Original final answer (English)
# The Great Whirl off Somalia, 2011–2020: when and where it forms, how variable it is, and which initiation mechanism the GLORYS12 fields can support

## Summary

**Life cycle (measured).** In the supplied monthly GLORYS12 fields (CMEMS `global-reanalysis-001-030-monthly`, 47–70 E, 4–26 N, 2011–2020) the Great Whirl (GW) is a strictly seasonal, recurrent anticyclone off Somalia. As a closed SSH anticyclone of amplitude ≥ 0.10 m it is present from **May–July** in every year, intensifies through **July–September**, reaches its annual maximum in **August–November**, and decays in **November–December**. Across the ten years the mature centre is at **8.4 ± 1.2° N, 54.3 ± 1.1° E**, all ten annual peak centres lie within 7.4–10.8° N, 53.4–57.0° E, and the half-amplitude radius is **155 ± 22 km** (equivalent diameter ≈ 310 km). Nothing of GW scale exists in **January–April**: the largest pre-season closed-contour amplitude in any year is 0.09 m (0.143 m across a 60-criterion ensemble), against a weakest annual peak of 0.23 m.

**Variability (measured).** Annual peak closed-contour amplitude is **0.29 ± 0.05 m** (0.23–0.36 m; 11–18 % coefficient of variation depending on the amplitude definition) and the radius varies by ±14 %. Timing is variable only at the margins: onset May–July (June in 7 of 10 years), peak August–November. The criterion-robust part is the *season* (peak in August–October in 86 % of 750 criterion-years; decay in November–December in 99 %); the per-year onset month is not robust — it moves by 2.1 months per 0.1 m change in amplitude threshold, and across a 40-criterion core ensemble the modal onset is June with 5–9 years each in March, April and May. With ten annual cycles (effective sample size ≈ 6.3 years) the 95 % interval on the interannual amplitude spread is itself wide (0.033–0.13 m).

**Mechanism (inference from the supplied fields, no winds).** The fields **do not support planetary (Rossby)-wave initiation in the form of a demonstrable pre-monsoon wave arriving at the Somali coast**: no GW-scale closed anticyclone exists at the site before May in any criterion-year, and the pre-monsoon large-scale sea-level rise that *is* present begins in mid-March but is **in phase across longitude** (8–12° N and 12–20° N), whereas a free first-baroclinic long wave would need 3.8–6.0 and 6–26 months respectively to cross the same longitudes. What the data show instead is an **eddy-scale anticyclone that spins up in place in the coastal band in May–July, coincident with or 0–2 months after every in-data monsoon-onset proxy, fed by local coastal mean-to-eddy conversion and not by import from the east**. That ordering is *consistent with* the local southwest-monsoon wind forcing hypothesis, and it is also consistent with instability of the monsoon-forced coastal jet; the supplied data cannot separate those two, and — because the reanalysis is wind-forced by construction — the local-wind branch is structurally untestable here. The single robust interannual amplitude relation (GW peak anti-correlated with monsoon-season coastal forcing, r = −0.76) is not usable as mechanism evidence: its two predictors are collinear at −0.87 and 52–72 % of it is a peak-versus-spread effect rather than a change in eddy energy.

The one published timing that the literature attributes to planetary-wave arrival — an April anticyclonic signature ~2 months before monsoon onset — is reproduced in these fields, but as a **basin-wide, zonally in-phase spring steric high** of large scale, not as the GW and not as a resolvable wave transit. Abstract-level literature only (search-only mode) was available, so published criterion thresholds and wave-identification tests could not be verified.

---

## 1. Data and what was actually computed

Supplied read-only sources, one directory per variable with year subdirectories 2011–2020 under `/import/home3/share/mafzhang/CMEMS_ARABIAN_MONTHLY/`: `thetao`, `so`, `uo`, `vo`, `zos`, `mlotst`. Inspection confirms **monthly** files only (12 `.nc` per year per variable, e.g. `cmems_monthly_2015-07_*.nc`); no daily or 5-day output exists in the workspace. Winds are not supplied and none were sought. The domain is 47–70 E, 4–26 N; `thetao`/`so`/`uo`/`vo` have 35 depth levels and the profiles end near 900 m.

Independent lines of work were run on these fields: closed-contour SSW detection and tracking (B1.1), seasonal-band propagation and coast-versus-basin lead-lag analysis (B1.2 → corrected by B1.2.1 → B1.2.1.1 → B1.2.1.1.1), onset timing relative to ocean-only monsoon proxies (B1.3), vertical/thermocline structure (B1.5), gyre-versus-eddy scale separation (B1.6), scale-resolved eddy energy and vorticity budget (B1.6.2), interannual covariation with coastal-forcing proxies (B1.6.1, B1.6.1.1), a 75-member detection-criterion ensemble (B1.7), an abstract-level literature comparison (B1.4), and an adversarial reading of what the combined evidence does and does not discriminate (B1.8).

## 2. When and where the Great Whirl forms, intensifies and decays, year by year

Detection: outermost closed SSH contour around the strongest maximum in 4–12° N, 47–58° E, "present" when its amplitude ≥ 0.10 m; onset = first month of the longest qualifying run starting in or after May; peak = month of maximum amplitude; decay = first month after the peak below half that year's peak. Identity was verified as a genuine anticyclonic circulation from the velocity fields (mean ζ/f = −0.37, clockwise swirl 0.42 m s⁻¹ mean, up to ≈1.3 m s⁻¹ in August–October).

| Year | onset (≥0.10 m) | peak month | peak amplitude (m) | peak SSH (m) | peak centre | half-amplitude radius (km) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | Jun | Nov | 0.24 | 0.61 | 10.8° N 55.1° E | 116 |
| 2012 | Jun | Oct | 0.27 | 0.64 | 7.6° N 53.7° E | 155 |
| 2013 | Jun | Nov | 0.23 | 0.56 | 7.5° N 54.8° E | 187 |
| 2014 | Jun | Aug | 0.28 | 0.71 | 8.5° N 53.5° E | 142 |
| 2015 | Jun | Oct | 0.23 | 0.63 | 7.8° N 53.9° E | 163 |
| 2016 | May | Oct | 0.36 | 0.73 | 10.0° N 57.0° E | 132 |
| 2017 | Jun | Sep | 0.35 | 0.72 | 7.5° N 53.4° E | 180 |
| 2018 | Jun | Aug | 0.28 | 0.67 | 7.4° N 53.5° E | 157 |
| 2019 | Jul | Sep | 0.33 | 0.76 | 8.8° N 54.4° E | 146 |
| 2020 | May | Sep | 0.33 | 0.79 | 8.2° N 53.6° E | 171 |

- Onset is May in 2 years (2016, 2020), June in 7 and July in 1 (2019). *(Note a slip inside the B1.1 summary, which lists 2019 among the May onsets while its own per-year table gives July 2019; the table above follows the per-year table.)*
- Decay: amplitude falls below half the annual peak in November (6 years) or December (4); the last month above the 0.10 m threshold is November in all ten years (October in 2012, 2014, 2015).
- Geographic evolution: the nascent May–June rise is centred near 7–9° N, 52–54° E; mature maxima are near 8.4° N, 53.3° E, and the centre migrates northward from ≈6–8° N in June to ≈8–11° N in September–October. In 2016 the mature centre was the farthest north and east (10.0° N, 57.0° E).
- Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-e43c8eef4e/outputs/great-whirl-lifecycle-2011-2020.png` (amplitude by month for every year with the annual maxima; May–June and August–October climatological SSH-rise maps with all ten peak centres; longitude–month Hovmöller).

## 3. How variable it is, and how much of that variability is real

Three uncertainty layers must be kept apart, because they scale differently.

1. **Criterion (dominant for dates).** A 75-member ensemble of detection criteria (40 closed-contour variants, 30 eddy-SSH-residual variants, vorticity and band-SSH indices; 750 criterion-years) gives: annual peak in August–October in 86 % of criterion-years (bootstrap 90 % CI 0.74–0.97); November–December decay in 99 % (0.96–1.00); no GW-scale closed anticyclone in January–April in 0 of 600 GW-box criterion-years; onset month *not* robust (±1–2 months; 2.1 months per 0.1 m of threshold); lifetime 143–298 d across core criteria (median 183 d), which straddles the published 140–198 d range and shows that published lifetime differences are largely definitional. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/statistics-d9565197c4/outputs/gw-criterion-uncertainty.png`.
2. **Sampling.** Monthly means quantise every date to ±1 month; the underlying daily-scale variability of the GW (its 10–20 day wobbles reported in the literature) is not present in these fields at all.
3. **Sample size for interannual statements.** Ten annual cycles have an effective sample size ≈ 6.3 years, so every interannual correlation reported below has a confidence interval that includes zero at that n_eff, and the interannual amplitude spread 0.288 ± 0.051 m (CV 18 %) has a 95 % interval of 0.033–0.13 m — the spread is real but its magnitude is weakly constrained.

Robust variability statements: the season dominates (pre-monsoon April amplitude ≤ 0.09 m vs August–October 0.15–0.35 m; the mature months carry 3–10× the April value); peak amplitude range 1.6× (0.23–0.36 m); peak month spans four calendar months; radius varies ±14 %. Consistent with B1.1's remark, the strongest years (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020) are years in which the May–June amplitude was already 0.13–0.22 m, i.e. the early-season anomaly is larger when the season is strong — but with n_eff ≈ 6 this is a description of four years, not an established relationship.

**A counter-intuitive but inadmissible relation.** GW eddy amplitude is *anti*-correlated with the monsoon-season coastal-forcing composite (coastal set-down, Somali coastal jet, coastal cooling; mutually correlated r = 0.52–0.97): r = −0.76 (0.95 % CI −0.94 to −0.24 at n_eff ≈ 9.9; −0.97 to +0.09 at n_eff 6.3), with the sign reproduced by the closed-contour amplitude (−0.57), the eddy-scale SSH (−0.61 to −0.69) and an independent vorticity-extreme index (−0.69). The two candidate explanations — January–March preconditioning (zero-order r = +0.80) versus monsoon-season forcing (r = −0.76) — are collinear at r = −0.866, so neither unique contribution excludes zero (+0.44 [−0.08, +0.92] and −0.22 [−0.90, +0.43]), and the ranking flips with the amplitude metric. Decomposition shows relocation contributes essentially nothing (the JAS eddy-scale maximum stays in the box in 10/10 years) while **52–72 % of the box-peak anti-correlation is a peak-versus-spread (concentration) effect**, the box-averaged eddy energy term itself being anti-correlated at only −0.64 to −0.32. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-cf3a80e145/outputs/gw-amplitude-axis-and-artefacts.png`.

## 4. Which initiation mechanism the data support

The mechanism question was attacked from six independent angles. Several of the published claims survive; the planetary-wave claim does not survive in any form the monthly fields can test.

**(a) Timing relative to the monsoon onset (measured; onset inferred from ocean proxies, not from winds).** Near-coast upwelling cooling, the Somali coastal jet (0–50 m alongshore velocity, 4–9° N), coastal sea-level set-down and coastal-minus-offshore mixed-layer change all reach half their annual amplitude in June (9/10, 8/10 and similar fractions of years). The GW index reaches half its annual amplitude in July (9/10 years) — i.e. +1 month behind the cooling in 8/10 years, behind the jet in 7/10, never before them, and the lag *shape* is significant in a block-bootstrap test; across a criterion ensemble the median lag is +0.66 to +1.07 months with 0/10 negative years for cooling, set-down and mixed-layer proxies (reversal frequency bounded only at ≤ 26 %). The GW's own pre-monsoon value is its annual minimum (8.9 cm in February vs 31.8–32.1 cm in August–September). Figures: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-865ffdd3d6/outputs/gw-monsoon-onset-timing.png` and `.../ocean-process-865ffdd3d6/outputs/gw-monsoon-spatial-structure.png`. *Limitation:* the proxies are ocean responses, so this ordering cannot by itself distinguish a wind-forced GW from a GW that is part of the same ocean response; and no wind onset date exists in the task data.

**(b) Is the pre-monsoon high a wave arriving at the coast? (No, not in its slow free-wave form.)** A westward-tilted annual-band SSH signal does exist at 5–10° N with phase marching west at 16–55 cm/s and a latitude dependence close to βc₁²/f² (implied first-mode speed 1.8–2.3 m/s), and D20 propagates the same way (r = −0.95 to −0.99). But three successive refinements removed the wave reading:
- The Somali coastal April maximum does **not lead** the basin: it lags the 65–69 E, 4–8° N band by 1.0 month in SSH (9/10 years) and 2.0 months in D20 and T at 92 m (10/10 years), and is simultaneous at 8–10° N, while the mid-basin 55–60 E box peaks 1–2 months later than the coast. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-183a569fac/outputs/gw-premonsoon-leadlag.png`.
- The pre-monsoon rise is not a single propagating phase line: in phase at 8–12° N (measured tilt 0.2–0.4 month against a 3.8–6.0 month mode-1 prediction) with only a 1.3–2.0 month westward tilt at 5–8° N whose sign is robust but whose speed (24–113 cm/s) is not.
- At 12–20° N, where a mode-1 transit across 50–70 E would take 6–26 months and is therefore resolvable monthly, the SSH rise half-date differs by ≈0.16 month (about 5 days) between the band ends, thermal indices tilt weakly *eastward* (0/10 years westward), 73 of 84 configurations are east-later, and the uniform-ramp test prefers in-phase over any ramp. The only westward tilt (fully-ocean 58–70 E bins, ≈1 month) implies 33–39 cm/s, 3–10× the first-baroclinic speed at 16° N, so it is not a free mode-1 wave, and it disappears when all bins are included. Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-6dd2985be2/outputs/gw-north-12-20N-phase.png`.
- What remains of the published "April onset" is therefore a **basin-wide, zonally in-phase spring steric high** over 5–12° N whose band-mean rise begins in mid-March and leads the monsoon proxies by 1.7–2.9 months. That is reproduced, but it is not the Great Whirl and it is not a resolvable wave transit.

**(c) Is the GW itself a pre-monsoon arrival? (No.)** No GW-scale closed anticyclone exists at the site in January–April in any of 600 GW-box criterion-years, and the eddy-scale SSH residual at the site is at its annual minimum in January–May. The GW is an **eddy-scale anticyclone riding on a pre-existing large-scale high, not the growth of that high**: the 2–6° low-pass SSH at the site actually peaks in April–May in 10/10 years and *falls* through the monsoon, while the April→July rise of +0.184 m decomposes into eddy-scale +0.236 m and large-scale −0.052 m, and the low-pass field contains no closed anticyclonic contour anywhere in 5–12° N, 48–58° E in any month. The partition is filter-dependent (eddy fraction 0.36–1.31 across filters) but its sign and timing are robust. Figures: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-182964391c/outputs/gw-gyre-vs-eddy-scale-separation.png` and `.../gw-vorticity-scale-split.png`.

**(d) Where does the eddy's energy come from? (In place, at the coast — not from the east.)** June–July EKE is 0.184 m² s⁻² in the coastal strip (0–100 km offshore, 4.5–13° N) and 0.128 m² s⁻² in the GW box but only 0.015 m² s⁻² in the 57–62° E band; eddy vorticity variance along the coast is 5.8–13.9 × 10⁻¹¹ s⁻² against 3–6 × 10⁻¹² s⁻² offshore. The only mean-to-eddy conversion that survives scale-splitting is coastal barotropic conversion C_BT (+3.6 to +4.9 × 10⁻⁸ m² s⁻³, same order as the observed June→July growth) and it is ≈0 in the east; boundary import is coastal- and south-face dominated, the east face carrying an order of magnitude less; there is no eastern eddy reservoir and no eastern time lead (max |r| = 0.38–0.39 at zero lag). Figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-20e5cd2946/outputs/gw-eddy-energy-budget.png`. *Limitation:* the budget does **not** close (term sum 3.1× the observed GW-box tendency; wrong sign in the coastal strip), C_BT's year-to-year spread is comparable to its mean, and monthly means cannot separate wind-forced in-place adjustment from in-place instability of the coastal jet.

**(e) Vertical structure. (Baroclinic and column-deep — consistent with both.)** The May–July onset is a mode-1-like thermocline displacement, not a surface-trapped response: relative to the same-year January–March baseline, isopycnals from σ₀ ≈ 23.6 to 27.3 deepen by 20–35 m in April–May and 40–46 m at σ₀ 25.3–26.3 in July–September, D20 deepens by 17–37 m, the subsurface salinity maximum deepens from 47 m to 92 m, the anticyclonic azimuthal flow reaches 0.36–0.58 m s⁻¹ at 78–110 m and 0.26–0.43 m s⁻¹ at 156 m, the SSH rise is steric to within 0.01–0.015 m, and the mixed layer simultaneously *shoals* by 10–17 m. This rules out a surface-trapped mechanism but, as the Expert states, local Ekman pumping and a first-baroclinic Rossby wave displace the thermocline in exactly the same way. Figures: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q20/attempt-1791186095912809286-48ef6d53/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q20--707590a1321b/agents/ocean-process-75592b6e74/outputs/great-whirl-onset-vertical-structure.png` and `.../great-whirl-onset-velocity-structure.png`.

**(f) Adversarial reading (B1.8).** Neither mechanism is *discriminated* as the initiator; the evidence falsifies only specific testable versions — a GW-scale closed pre-monsoon anticyclone at the site, a single free first-baroclinic westward phase line crossing the band before the monsoon, eddy-energy/vorticity import from the east during spin-up, and surface-trapped initiation. Not falsified, therefore not discriminated: local southwest-monsoon wind forcing of the eddy (the ocean-only ordering is consistent with it, but GLORYS12 is wind-forced by construction, so the test is circular); intrinsic mesoscale variability and barotropic/baroclinic instability of the monsoon-forced coastal jet (in-place coastal generation, positive but year-unstable C_BT, criterion-robust 11–18 % interannual amplitude spread); and an unresolvable fast, boundary-trapped or sub-monthly remote signal (the only wave-compatible evidence is the 1.3–2.0 month tilt at 5–8° N, one monthly sample wide, not reproduced by the harmonic-phase or uniform-ramp estimators, and absent at the GW's own mature latitudes).

**Answer to the mechanism clause, worded to the evidence.** The supplied fields **support a local, seasonally forced initiation of the Great Whirl eddy**: it is generated in place on the Somali coast in May–July, at or after the in-data monsoon-onset signatures, from coastal mean-flow to eddy conversion, and it is not the arrival of a pre-monsoon wave. The published planetary-wave attribution is **not supported** for the GW eddy itself; the pre-monsoon anticyclonic signal the literature reports for April is present in these fields but as a basin-wide in-phase spring adjustment, and the wave hypothesis is only falsified in its slow-free-wave, coast-arrival form. Because no winds exist in the task data and the single reanalysis stream is wind-forced by construction, the data can neither confirm the wind forcing nor exclude a wave that is too fast, too boundary-trapped or too sub-monthly to appear in monthly means — no mechanism is a measured quantity in this evidence set.

## 5. What would change the answer, and what remains untested here

- **Winds.** A co-located daily wind-stress-curl / Ekman-pumping product (ERA5, CCMP) for 2011–2020 is the only comparison that separates in-place wind-forced adjustment from in-place instability of the coastal jet, and it would test whether local Ekman pumping accounts for the March–May thermocline deepening that leads the monsoon proxies. Winds are not supplied and were not acquired.
- **Sub-monthly fields.** The 5–8° N wave-compatible tilt (1.3–2.0 months) is one to two monthly samples wide, and the June–July coastal spin-up collapses into a single monthly step; 5-day or daily GLORYS12 for February–July would decide whether the tilt is a propagating front or a static phase offset, and whether the spin-up is smooth forced growth or discrete instability bursts. The workspace contains only monthly files (verified by directory inspection).
- **Longer or independent record.** With n_eff ≈ 6.3 and collinear predictors a 30-year record, the 1993–present altimeter record, another reanalysis, or a twin experiment with the local monsoon winds suppressed are needed to break the preconditioning-versus-monsoon degeneracy and to test the wind branch at all.
- **Domain.** 47–70 E excludes the eastern-boundary generation region of a Rossby wave, so wave generation could not be observed, only its coastal signature.
- **Literature.** Acquisition mode was `search_only`, so detection thresholds, per-year published dates and the wave-identification tests behind the Rossby-wave attribution are abstract-level and unverified; the criterion ensemble's finding that published lifetime differences (140–198 d) are reproduced by definitional choices alone should be read with that limit.

## Research Tree

ROOT **B1 [closed]** — Using GLORYS12 monthly SSH, velocity, temperature and salinity (47–70 E, 4–26 N, 2011–2020), when and where does the Great Whirl form, intensify and decay in each year, how variable is it, and which proposed initiation mechanism (local southwest-monsoon wind forcing vs. pre-monsoon planetary/Rossby wave arrival at the Somali coast) do the data support?
*Closed with reason: every selected frontier question was adjudicated; remaining uncertainties (sub-monthly aliasing, absent winds, n_eff ≈ 6.3, one wind-forced reanalysis stream) cannot be reduced with the supplied data.*

- **B1.1 [completed]** When and where does the GW form, intensify and decay in each year 2011–2020, and how strong and how large is it?
  - Result: closed SSH anticyclone ≥ 0.10 m from May–July, intensifying July–September, annual maximum August–November, decay November–December; mature centre 8.4 ± 1.2° N, 54.3 ± 1.1° E, half-amplitude radius 155 ± 22 km; peak amplitude 0.29 ± 0.05 m; no GW-scale feature in January–April.
  - Limit: monthly dates ±1 month; the amplitude threshold is the largest single control on the reported onset/decay months.
- **B1.2 [completed, corrected by B1.2.1]** Is there a westward-propagating baroclinic signal reaching the coast before the monsoon?
  - Result: initially reported as a westward-tilted annual-band signal at 16–55 cm/s with c₁ = 1.8–2.3 m/s, but the coast-versus-basin lag was unresolvable and the harmonic phase speeds disagree with the direct peak-month timings; the corrected reading (B1.2.1, B1.2.1.1) is a basin-wide in-phase spring adjustment, not a demonstrable coastal wave arrival.
  - **B1.2.1 [completed]** Does the coastal April maximum lead the mid/eastern basin?
    - Result: no — the coast lags the 65–69 E, 4–8° N band by 1.0 month (SSH) and 2.0 months (D20, T92) and is simultaneous at 8–10° N; the mid-basin box peaks 1–2 months later than the coast.
    - **B1.2.1.1 [completed]** Is the pre-monsoon rise a propagating phase line or in phase?
      - Result: in phase at 8–12° N (0.2–0.4 month against a 3.8–6.0 month mode-1 prediction) with a 1.3–2.0 month westward tilt only at 5–8° N whose sign is robust and speed is not (24–113 cm/s); not a single mode-1 wave.
      - **B1.2.1.1.1 [completed]** Same diagnostic at 12–20° N, where a mode-1 transit is resolvable.
        - Result: no westward phase tilt (≈0.16 month end-to-end, slope CI straddling zero; thermal indices weakly eastward, 0/10 years westward; 73/84 configurations east-later); the only westward SSH tilt implies 33–39 cm/s, 3–10× the first-baroclinic speed at 16° N, and vanishes with all bins. In-phase seasonal adjustment confirmed at northern latitudes.
- **B1.3 [completed]** Does GW formation coincide with or precede the in-data monsoon-onset signatures?
  - Result: it does not precede them — coastal cooling, coastal jet, coastal set-down and mixed-layer change reach half amplitude in June, the GW half-amplitude onset in July, lagging by 0–2 months and never negative; the GW's pre-monsoon value is its annual minimum; no pre-monsoon anticyclonic anomaly at the site (eddy-scale index).
  - Limit: onset is inferred from ocean proxies, never measured winds.
- **B1.4 [completed]** Published criteria, timing, location and mechanisms.
  - Result: two-stage season — an April anticyclonic signature ~2 months before monsoon onset near 5–10° N, then a GW-proper intensifying after early-June onset, peaking July–September, decaying ~1 month after the winds die; published lifetime 140–198 d is criterion-dependent; the pre-monsoon onset is attributed to annual planetary/Rossby-wave arrival at the western boundary, local monsoon forcing to the May–June intensification and the GW's latitude, and intrinsic mesoscale variability to the non-seasonal variance. No inspected source attributes the April onset to local winds.
  - Limit: abstract-level only (search-only mode); the pre-monsoon onset is an average, not a per-year criterion.
- **B1.5 [completed]** Is the onset surface-intensified or mode-1-like?
  - Result: mode-1-like and column-deep (isopycnal deepening 20–35 m in April–May and 40–46 m at σ₀ 25.3–26.3 in July–September, D20 +17–37 m, salinity maximum 47→92 m, subsurface swirl 0.36–0.58 m s⁻¹ at 78–110 m, steric SSH) with a simultaneously shoaling mixed layer; rules out a surface-trapped response but does not separate local Ekman pumping from a baroclinic wave.
- **B1.6 [completed]** Is the GW the basin-scale coastal gyre or an eddy riding on it?
  - Result: an eddy-scale anticyclone riding on a pre-existing large-scale high — the low-pass SSH at the site peaks in April–May in 10/10 years and falls through the monsoon while the eddy-scale residual rises from its January–May minimum to an August–October maximum; no closed anticyclonic contour in the low-pass field anywhere in 5–12° N, 48–58° E.
  - **B1.6.1 [completed]** Does GW interannual amplitude covary with the monsoon-forced coastal proxies?
    - Result: yes, but with the opposite sign (r = −0.76; sign reproduced by four indices); timing covariation unmeasurable because the proxies have almost no onset variance; the monthly lag correlations are a seasonal-cycle phase relation (|r| ≤ 0.47 after deseasonalising).
    - **B1.6.1.1 [completed]** Preconditioning or monsoon strength, once collinearity is accounted for?
      - Result: not identifiable — the two axes are collinear at r = −0.866, both partial correlations include zero, the ranking flips with the amplitude metric; relocation contributes ~nothing and 52–72 % of the peak-based covariation is a peak-versus-spread effect.
  - **B1.6.2 [completed]** Is eddy vorticity/EKE generated in place or imported from the east?
    - Result: in place at the coast — coastal EKE 0.184 vs 0.015 m² s⁻² (57–62° E), vorticity variance 5.8–13.9 × 10⁻¹¹ vs 3–6 × 10⁻¹² s⁻², the only surviving conversion is coastal barotropic (+3.6 to +4.9 × 10⁻⁸ m² s⁻³), no eastern lead; an import-from-the-east origin is not supported. Budget does not close; monthly means cannot separate instability from wind-forced adjustment.
- **B1.7 [completed]** How robust are the phenology, the spread and the lead-lag contrasts?
  - Result: robust = August–October peak (86 % of criterion-years), November–December decay (99 %), absent January–April anticyclone (0/600 criterion-years), amplitude spread magnitude (0.288 ± 0.051 m) and the sign of the GW-versus-proxy lag; artefacts = per-year onset month, decay month to the extent it is definitional, and lifetime (143–298 d). The "no pre-monsoon signal" claim holds only for GW-scale structure in 4–12° N, 47–58° E; a large-scale band-mean rise begins in mid-March and leads the proxies by 1.7–2.9 months.
- **B1.8 [completed]** Adversarial reading of what the evidence discriminates.
  - Result: neither mechanism is discriminated; falsified are the GW-scale pre-monsoon anticyclone at the site, the single free first-baroclinic westward phase line, eastward eddy-energy import during spin-up, and surface-trapped initiation; not falsified are local wind forcing (structurally unfalsifiable inside a wind-forced reanalysis with no winds supplied), instability of the monsoon-forced coastal jet / intrinsic mesoscale variability, and an unresolvable fast, boundary-trapped or sub-monthly remote signal.

# The Great Whirl in GLORYS12, 2011–2020: formation, variability, and initiation mechanism

## What was done

GLORYS12V1 monthly means (`zos`, `uo`, `vo`, `thetao`, `so`, `mlotst`; 1/12°, 35 levels, 2011–2020, 47–70 °E / 4–26 °N) were used as supplied, read-only. The Great Whirl (GW) was isolated by high-pass filtering SSH (subtract a 5°-σ Gaussian background, with land-normalisation) and taking the largest positive anomaly in a Somali-basin box (50–56.5 °E, 5–11.5 °N) chosen to exclude the Socotra Eddy. Timing uses a half-peak-amplitude convention. The test of the two rival mechanisms is deliberately independent of SSH: it uses the coast-minus-offshore thermocline depth, sea level and SST contrast, plus the relative-vorticity and EKE fields. **Winds were not supplied**, so the monsoon is dated from the ocean response it drives.

## When and where, year by year

Peak eddy-SSH amplitude of the GW core (>½-amplitude equivalent radius in brackets):

| Year | Onset | Peak | Demise | Length | Peak amp | Peak centre | Radius |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2011 | Jun | Sep | Nov | 6 mo | 33.2 cm | 53.8 °E, 9.0 °N | 204 km |
| 2012 | Jun | Oct | Nov | 6 mo | 31.5 | 53.1, 8.7 | 169 |
| 2013 | Jun | Sep | Nov | 6 mo | 31.7 | 53.2, **11.1** * | 180 |
| 2014 | **Jul** | Aug | **Oct** | 4 mo | 36.9 | 53.5, 9.2 | 167 |
| 2015 | Jun | Oct | Nov | 6 mo | 27.4 | 53.3, 8.7 | 182 |
| 2016 | Jun | Oct | Nov | 6 mo | 39.6 | 56.5, **11.5** * | 61 * |
| 2017 | Jun | Aug | Nov | 6 mo | 38.8 | 53.7, 8.9 | 180 |
| 2018 | Jun | Aug | Nov | 6 mo | 34.1 | 53.6, 8.9 | 178 |
| 2019 | **Jul** | Aug | **Oct** | 4 mo | 38.0 | 53.4, 8.4 | 202 |
| 2020 | Jun | Sep | Nov | 6 mo | 40.7 | 53.7, 8.7 | 191 |

\* In 2013 and 2016 the GW merged with the Socotra Eddy into one connected anticyclonic band, so the box maximum moved north of 10.5 °N; those two centres and the 2016 radius are not clean GW values. **Excluding them the peak core is 53.08–53.83 °E, 8.42–9.17 °N and the radius 167–204 km.**

**Where.** The feature is remarkably stationary. During July — the month of fastest growth — the maximum sits at **52.6–53.9 °E, 6.4–8.8 °N in all ten years**; it then drifts north ~1–2° to lock onto ≈53.4 °E, 8.7 °N at peak.

**When.** Onset (half-peak) is **June in 8/10 years, July in 2/10**. Peak is August (4 yrs), September (3), October (3). Demise is **November in 8/10**, October in 2/10. Season length 4–6 months.

**How variable.** Timing is tightly phase-locked — onset s.d. only **0.42 months**, demise s.d. 0.42, peak s.d. 0.88. Amplitude varies much more: **27.4–40.7 cm, mean 35.2 ± 4.3 cm (±12 %)**. Both results are unchanged for background-filter scales from 3° to 9°.

## Which mechanism the data support

**Both mechanisms are real, but they act at different stages.**

**Pre-monsoon (Feb–May): the Rossby wave, unambiguously.**

- The spring thermocline maximum marches west at **≈0.36 m s⁻¹** — it sits at 68–70 °E in February, 56–62 °E in March, and reaches the Somali coast (50–54 °E) in **April**.
- Harmonic phase speed at 4–8 °N is **−0.17 ± 0.06 m s⁻¹ (z20)** and **−0.38 ± 0.13 m s⁻¹ (SSH)**, westward in **10/10 years for each field**. It is not a windowing artefact: every longitude sub-window from 50–62 °E to 62–70 °E yields a westward speed of −0.10 to −0.30 m s⁻¹.
- Both estimates lie between the first- and second-mode long Rossby-wave speeds computed from the GLORYS stratification (mode 1 −0.49 to −0.86 m s⁻¹, mode 2 −0.07 to −0.13 m s⁻¹ at 6–8 °N).
- **The decisive adiabatic test.** In April the coastal thermocline is **10.3 m deeper** than offshore (9/10 years) and coastal sea level **higher** (8/10), while the coast–offshore SST difference is **+0.04 °C — its annual maximum, no cooling at all** (10/10 years). Deep + high + *not cold* is impossible under local wind-driven upwelling, which must shoal the thermocline and cool the SST together. This is a remote, adiabatic western-boundary signal.

**Monsoon (June onward): local southwest-monsoon forcing.**

- June flips every sign at once: coastal SST drops **2.2 °C** below offshore, coastal SSH falls **7.0 cm** below, the coastal thermocline shoals **11 m**, and the Somali Current spins up from 9.9 cm s⁻¹ (May) to **54.7 cm s⁻¹** (July).
- There is a small but statistically robust pre-monsoon GW build-up (+3.2 cm over the winter background, positive in 10/10 years, paired t = 5.75, p = 0.0003) — but it is only **~20 % of the seasonal rise**. **61 % of the rise is added in June–July alone**, and the fastest growth (+8.8 cm month⁻¹ in July) coincides exactly with the Somali Current maximum and the coastal SST minimum (25.8 °C).
- Independent confirmation from velocity, not SSH: GW-box mean relative vorticity is ≈0 in December–April and strongly anticyclonic June–October (−0.14 → **−0.24** in August → −0.18 ×10⁻⁵ s⁻¹), with EKE peaking in September. The GW core is warmer than its surroundings from the surface to ~270 m, peaking at **+1.68 °C at 186 m**.

**Answer:** the planetary Rossby wave **preconditions** the western boundary (deep thermocline, anomalous coastal sea level) but does not by itself generate the Great Whirl; the **local southwest-monsoon winds initiate and intensify it**.

**Interannual amplitude is explained by neither.** Across 12 tests at n = 10, only `GW peak amplitude ~ Jun–Aug coastal v` reaches p = 0.041 uncorrected, and it fails Bonferroni correction (threshold 0.0042); it is also partly circular, since the GW's own circulation contributes to that coastal velocity. No wave predictor correlates with GW amplitude (|r| ≤ 0.40, p ≥ 0.25). GW *timing* is monsoon-locked; GW *amplitude* is not slaved to monsoon strength.

## Blockers, caveats and negative results

- **Monthly resolution** cannot order GW onset (early–mid June) against monsoon onset (late May–early June); the Rossby arrival in April and monsoon onset are separated by only two samples.
- **No wind fields**, so wind predictors are ocean-response proxies, and the velocity proxy is partly contaminated by the GW itself.
- The annual cycle **is not a free wave** — the measured speed is an apparent phase speed of a forced signal; with 12 monthly samples the wavelength is only partly resolved and the mode number cannot be uniquely identified.
- **n = 10** gives very low power: the honest reading is "not detected", not "absent".
- **2013 and 2016** GW–Socotra Eddy merging contaminates those peak locations.
- Literature mode was `search_only` with no supplied papers, so no external literature was consulted; the mechanism framing comes from the research question itself. No credentials were read and no data left the machine.

## Deliverables (workspace root)

- **`analysis.ipynb`** — the single executed notebook (44 cells, 0 errors) walking through data inventory, GW detection/tracking, the event table, the Rossby phase analysis (including the window-robustness and raw month-of-maximum checks), the adiabatic coast-vs-offshore test, the correlation tests, vertical structure, and all eight figures inline.
- **`code/`** — `gw_common.py`, `step1_eddy_field.py`, `step2_rossby.py`, `step3_indices.py`, `step4_variability.py`, `step5_figures.py`, `viz_style.py`, `build_notebook.py`
- **`figures/`** — fig1 climatological eddy-SSH maps; fig2 seasonal timing; fig3 year×month timeline; fig4 Rossby Hovmöller + per-year phase speeds; fig5 coast-minus-offshore mechanism test; fig6 structure (maps + quiver + vertical sections); fig7 predictor-vs-amplitude scatters; fig8 velocity/vorticity check
- **`outputs/`** — `gw_events.csv`, `gw_track.csv`, `gw_yearly.csv`, `gw_correlations.csv`, `filter_sensitivity.csv`, `coastal_series.csv`, `indices_clim.csv`, `indices_monthly.csv`, `rossby_modes.csv`, `rossby_phase.csv`, plus NetCDF fields (`z20`, `ssh_eddy`, `ssh_eddy_clim`, `hovmoller`, `gw_vertical`)

Original final answer (English)
Great Whirl (GW) analysis using GLORYS12 monthly SSH/velocity/temperature/salinity 2011-2020 (47-70E, 4-26N).

## Methods
- Loaded all 120 monthly files of sea surface height (zos), surface u/v, SST, mixed-layer depth. SSH anomaly (SLA) = zos minus its 2011-2020 mean. GW region = 49-58E, 5-13N (Somali coast / western Arabian Sea).
- Computed: GW-box max SLA and its location each month; per-year GW event metrics (peak month/amplitude/position, onset, decay, active months); surface relative vorticity from u/v to confirm anticyclonic core; longitude-time (Hovmoller) composites to test for westward (Rossby wave) propagation; SST and MLD at the GW.
- Figures: fig1_seasonal_cycle.png, fig2_yearly_cycles.png, fig3_hovmoller.png, fig4_composite_hovmoller.png, fig5_monthly_maps.png, fig6_anomaly_hovmoller.png, fig7_annual_hovmoller.png, fig8_sst_mld_sla.png, fig9_summary.png; tables under /workspace/scratch/gw_metrics.csv, gw_events.csv, vort_metrics.csv.

## When the GW forms, intensifies, decays
- Seasonal composite of GW-box maximum SLA (cm): Jan 10.1, Feb 11.0, Mar 11.8, Apr 15.2, May 16.2, Jun 9.1, Jul 18.0, Aug 19.1, Sep 16.0, Oct 16.8, Nov 4.8, Dec 9.9.
- The dominant intensification is June->August; the GW core reaches peak late-August/September. Per-year peak SLA months: 2011 Sep, 2012 Jul, 2013 Sep, 2014 Sep, 2015 Oct, 2016 Oct, 2017 Aug, 2018 Aug, 2019 Sep, 2020 Sep (mode = September, 5/10 years).
- GW-box relative vorticity (1e-6/s) composite becomes anticyclonic (negative) from March (-1.6), strengthens to July (-11.9), remains strongly anticyclonic through Sep (-8.9) and decays in Nov (-1.6) / Dec (+0.7). This confirms spin-up in late spring, mature anticyclone Jun-Sep, decay Oct-Nov.
- Onset (SLA>10 cm in the box) is detected from April in essentially every year; the anomaly stays positive over the western box until October-November (decay_month = 10-12). So the GW "season" spans roughly April-May (precursor) -> June-September (mature) -> October-November (decay), with a brief June minimum in the coastal-band composite.

## Where
- Per-year GW peak is centred at mean 55.2E (std 1.7, range 53-58E) and mean 10.4N (std 1.4, range 8.8-13N). The core sits offshore of Somalia in the western Arabian Sea, consistent with the classic GW location. The monthly maps (fig5) show the positive SLA/anticyclonic core hugging the coast at ~5-10N in spring, expanding and migrating slightly eastward/northward to ~9-13N, 53-57E at the summer peak.

## Variability
- Peak SLA amplitude: mean 30.0 cm, std 4.6 cm, range 22.6 cm (2012) to 36.0 cm (2019). Note a weak increasing tendency over the decade (2011 26.8, 2012 22.6, 2013 28.9, 2014 30.5, 2015 29.2, 2016 34.1, 2017 32.0, 2018 24.0, 2019 36.0, 2020 35.6).
- Peak month is variable (Jul-Oct), and peak position moves within ~5 deg of longitude and ~4 deg of latitude — the GW is a robust but interannually variable feature.
- The seasonal cycle explains ~55% of GW-box SLA variance; the remaining ~45% is interannual/intra-seasonal.

## Mechanism the data support
Two pieces of evidence bear on the two mechanisms:
1. Local SW-monsoon wind mechanism: the mature GW (strong positive SLA + anticyclonic vorticity) coincides with the summer monsoon (Jun-Sep) and with maximum SST (29.9C in May, 27.7/26.3C in Jun/Jul — upwelling cooling) and a shoaling/restratifying mixed layer. The bulk intensification is clearly in phase with the monsoon season, which is consistent with local wind forcing as the sustaining driver.
2. Rossby-wave mechanism: the composite longitude-time (Hovmoller) SLA has a clear WESTWARD phase tilt. The month-of-maximum by longitude shows the coastal band (49-53E) peaks earliest, in APRIL (month 4), while 53-56E peaks in May and further offshore reaches maximum later. The coastal band already has +9.2 cm SLA in April and +7.3 cm in May, i.e. a strong positive SSH anomaly appears at the coast BEFORE the June-July monsoon intensification. Lead-lag correlation between a far-eastern box (60-65E) and the coast is maximal at lags 0 to +1 month with comparable magnitude (r~0.6-0.7), indicating coherent westward-advecting SSH. This pre-monsoon coastal anomaly that precedes the monsoon-driven peak is the expected signature of a westward-propagating planetary (Rossby) wave reaching the coast.

Conclusion: Monthly GLORYS12 data support a TWO-STAGE picture — a pre-monsoon (April-May) positive SSH anomaly at the Somali coast that propagates westward from the interior and is present before the monsoon, followed by the monsoon-season (June-September) intensification of the Great Whirl. Thus BOTH processes appear to operate: the Rossby-wave mechanism is supported as the INITIATION/precursor trigger (coastal positive SLA appears in April-May, before the monsoon and with westward phase tilt), while the local SW-monsoon winds are required to build the GW to its full summer amplitude (peak in Aug-Sep, coincident with the monsoon and maximum anticyclonic vorticity). The data do not support a purely wind-only initiation, because the coastal anomaly clearly precedes the monsoon peak.

## Missing evidence / unresolved questions
- No wind fields were supplied, so the wind-forcing mechanism could not be tested directly; the monsoon link is inferred indirectly from the seasonal timing of SST/MLD/velocity. A wind-stress-curl budget would be needed to quantitatively separate the two mechanisms.
- Monthly means cannot resolve sub-monthly spin-up, eddy-eddy interactions, or the exact day/position of GW formation; higher-frequency output is required.
- Salinity (so) was available but not central to the SSH/vorticity diagnostics; it was not used beyond noting availability.
- The apparent upward trend in peak amplitude over 2011-2020 is based on only 10 years and should be treated cautiously.
- The Rossby-wave interpretation rests on the timing and westward phase tilt of SSH; a definitive test would require full 2-D wavenumber-frequency analysis, which monthly data partly limit.

Original final answer (English)
# How Persian Gulf Water spreads and is diluted in the Arabian Sea (GLORYS12 monthly, 2011-2020, 47-70 E / 4-26 N)

## Summary

In the supplied GLORYS12 monthly reanalysis the high-salinity water that leaves the Gulf of Oman at 200-350 m appears as a subsurface salinity maximum on isopycnals σ0 ≈ 26.2-26.6 kg m⁻³, with core depth 239 m (10-90 % 185-315 m), core salinity 36.54 ± 0.21 PSU and core potential temperature 18.3 ± 1.3 °C at the exit. Its one demonstrated coherent spreading path is the Omani continental-slope / Ras al Hadd boundary current, flowing equatorward at 6-11 cm s⁻¹ near 22-23 N and ~5 cm s⁻¹ along the Arabian coast at 16.5-19 N; an offshore basin-interior anomaly of comparable amplitude exists but an eddy-mediated interior route is *not* demonstrated with monthly means. Along that boundary path the anomaly propagates at about 4-12 cm s⁻¹ (season-dependent), reaching 355 km in 33-102 days and 1000 km in 167-222 days (fixed-266 m and isopycnal-following estimates agree within ~1 cm s⁻¹ and ~28 days), so the western-boundary route answers "how fast" for the boundary branch, while the published tracer-based spreading speed of 1.6 cm s⁻¹ is commensurate with the reanalysis *interior* rate (1.2-1.9 cm s⁻¹), not with the jet. The high-salinity water leaves the Gulf of Oman most strongly in **October-November** (transport-weighted salinity 36.72 PSU in October versus 36.31 PSU in April; salt flux a factor 4.2 larger than the May minimum) but it reaches **farthest in late winter to spring**, because the autumn pulse arrives late; the only statistically clean seasonal separation of the boundary flow is a **southwest-monsoon stall/reversal** at ~725 km downstream (reversed in 5 of 10 years; no reversed years in the northeast monsoon). Dilution is dominated by **lateral isopycnal exchange** with colder, fresher water on the *same* density surfaces: the reanalysis core anomaly cools 1.52 °C while freshening 0.35 PSU (ratio 4.3 °C PSU⁻¹, close to the isopycnal β/α = 3.2), entrainment of the overlying fresher layer is bounded at ≤10 % of mass, the mixed layer never touches the 230-270 m core, and vertical diffusion is excluded by the sign of the resolved curvature. However, about **half of the headline "0.7 PSU per 1000 km" decay is the along-path freshening of the isopycnal background** rather than salt loss: the locally referenced decay is 0.32 ± 0.04 PSU per 1000 km, and against the water actually adjacent on the same density surface the contrast does not decay (+0.05 ± 0.03 PSU per 1000 km). The surviving uncertainty is structural rather than numerical: several competing explanations (eddy aliasing, a locally generated interior anomaly, a tracked maximum that may be a strait-mixing thermocline feature rather than the dense outflow) are compatible with these monthly-mean diagnostics but cannot be separated with the supplied files.

---

## 1. What the supplied data are, and the source water

Data: GLORYS12 monthly reanalysis (cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1M-m, 1/12°, 35 levels, monthly means 2011-2020) for thetao, so, uo, vo, zos and mlotst over 47-70 E / 4-26 N. Every result below is a ten-year statistic of 120 monthly-mean fields; no daily output, no tracer, no independent observation is present in the task sources, and the assigned literature mode was search-only (abstract/metadata level).

At the Gulf of Oman exit (58-62 E, 22-25.5 N) the PGW signature is a subsurface salinity maximum at 239 m (median 225 m) with core salinity 36.54 ± 0.21 PSU, core θ = 18.3 ± 1.3 °C and core σ0 = 26.38 ± 0.27 kg m⁻³; a ΔS = 0.10 PSU threshold around the core defines a 184-295 m layer of 111 ± 46 m thickness. The core exceeds the salinity minimum directly above it by 0.27 ± 0.15 PSU. Its monthly cycle: shallowest in September (219 m), deepest in January (258 m), saltiest in October-November (36.61 PSU), freshest in January-February (36.47 PSU), thinnest in October-November (96 m), thickest in February-March (123 m). The material caveat is that this is a *model* core far fresher than the classical observed PGW (S > 38 PSU), so the absolute salinities reported here are model-specific and must not be quoted as observational PGW values.

![PGW core at the Gulf of Oman exit: sections and map](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-4c3680c035/outputs/pgw-core-exit-sections-map.png)
![PGW core seasonal cycle at the exit](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-4c3680c035/outputs/pgw-core-seasonal-cycle.png)
![Downstream evolution of the PGW core in the model](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-4c3680c035/outputs/pgw-downstream-dilution.png)

Downstream, the core σ0 stays nearly constant (26.37 → 26.38 kg m⁻³) while core salinity falls from 36.83 PSU (inner Gulf of Oman) to 36.45 (exit), 36.25 (Omani slope 58-60 E / 19-22 N) and 35.77 PSU (55-57 E / 13-16 N), the layer deepening (~230 → 252 m) and thickening (83 → 235 m); in the central Arabian Sea (60-64 E / 12-18 N) the intermediate salinity maximum is nearly absent. The literature line independently places the PGW core on σ0 ≈ 26.5 at ~220 m with a core salinity decaying from ~37.5-38 PSU near the source to ~36.5 PSU at 57 E / 18 N, so the model's **pathway geometry and density class are consistent with the published picture, while its salinity amplitude is not** ([literature pathway synthesis figure](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/literature-3f35434f15/outputs/pgw-literature-pathways.png)).

## 2. Along which paths

**Demonstrated: the Omani-slope / Ras al Hadd boundary current.** A coherent equatorward mid-depth current carries the salinity maximum within 0-100 km of the slope: 6-11 cm s⁻¹ at 22-23 N, 3-8 cm s⁻¹ at 20-21 N, ~5 cm s⁻¹ westward along the Arabian coast at 16.5-19 N, 53-56 E. The same mid-depth salinity maximum also fills the offshore interior (core amplitude 0.17 PSU in 59.5-63.5 E / 16-20 N, equal to the slope box), but the 266 m interior mean flow is only 0.2-0.8 cm s⁻¹, so **an eddy-mediated interior route is compatible with the anomaly pattern but not demonstrated**.

![Map of the demonstrated and candidate PGW pathways](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-edf5496582/outputs/pgw-pathways-map.png)
![Supporting sections for the branch identification](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-edf5496582/outputs/pgw-sections.png)

**Not demonstrated: Socotra-Irwin and Laccadive branches.** Core amplitude falls to 0.09 and 0.07 PSU there, with 0 of 10 years above 0.2 PSU (versus 8 of 10 at the source). A local salinity maximum on the PGW isopycnals occurs in 93-100 % of columns from the Gulf of Oman through Ras al Hadd and the western interior, in 43 % of columns at 53-58.5 E / 13-17 N, in only 3-4 % in the Socotra-Irwin sector and Gulf of Aden, and in ~0 % south of 14 N at a 0.05 PSU threshold.

**Correction of an earlier claim in this study.** One node first attributed the strong Gulf of Aden subsurface salinity maximum (0.32 PSU at ~323 m) to Red Sea Outflow Water on the basis of a 156-454 m search band. That search band had clipped the feature: on re-inspection the Gulf of Aden/Socotra maximum sits at **~586-611 m on σ0 = 27.16 kg m⁻³ with θ = 11.9-13.9 °C**, i.e. ~0.8 kg m⁻³ denser and 4-6 °C colder than the model PGW core. A two-endmember mixing line (freshest water above the core → RSOW core) *over-predicts* the observed salinity on σ0 = 26.4 in that sector (box-mean residuals -0.003 to -0.052 PSU; sector 99th percentile +0.014 PSU), and a PGW contribution would have to be 14-30× larger than the residual allows. The same diagnostic returns +0.379 PSU in the Gulf of Oman source box where PGW genuinely exists, i.e. the method would have detected PGW. **Conclusion (bounded, not absolute): PGW is not detectable as an advected high-salinity core in the Gulf of Aden/Socotra sector, and its possible contribution there is bounded at ≤2-4 % of the local water mass (≤0.03 PSU)**; one marginal 17-column coastal bump strip at 47.1-48.9 E / 11.1-11.5 N is the only persistent southern PGW-class feature.

![Attribution of the Gulf of Aden maximum to Red Sea Outflow Water](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-80a0547bdd/outputs/aden-rsow-attribution.png)
![Isopycnal salinity anomaly map used for the attribution](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-80a0547bdd/outputs/isopycnal-salinity-anomaly.png)
![Testing whether any PGW survives on σ0 ≈ 26.4 in the south-west](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-681f110630/outputs/pgw-density-aden-attribution.png)

**How far the boundary branch is quantitatively sufficient, and where it ends.** A gate-by-gate σ0 26.2-26.6 layer budget (47 gates, 5 km cross-axis sampling) shows the downstream branch within 100 km of the axis carrying 0.34 Sv at 36.46 PSU at the exit, 0.50 Sv / 36.33 PSU at 20.4 N, 0.41 Sv / 36.14 PSU at 18.5 N, then collapsing to 0.18 Sv / 35.79 PSU at 16.5 N; its transport-weighted salinity falls 0.35 PSU per 500 km (exit → 20.4 N) and 0.43 (20.4 → 18.5 N), **independently reproducing the core-based -0.352 PSU per 500 km**. But at no gate is the layer *net*-exported (full-section net -0.04 to -0.20 Sv; downstream in only ~50 of 120 months), so the supply is a **branch inside a recirculating layer, not a one-way conveyor**.

![Gate-by-gate transport and salinity budget of the PGW layer](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-d1e7db690c/outputs/pgw-gate-layer-budget.png)

The transport loss is localized in one **60-km step at 17.75 → 17.24 N** (0.471 → 0.251 Sv; excess-salt flux 0.395 → 0.188 Sv·PSU) while the layer thickens from 72.8 to 82.9 m. Of the lost excess salt, ~62 % leaves across the 100-km line into the interior, ~24 % crosses the axis line toward the coast and ~14 % is unexplained by lateral divergence. The interior band is itself fresher at 16.5 N than at 20.4 N (35.754 versus 36.121 PSU) and the branch-interior salinity contrast collapses from +0.21 PSU to +0.03 PSU, so **the anomaly is dispersed laterally into the interior rather than handed over as a distinct salty tongue, and is not destroyed locally at the collapse**. Widening the band to 0-200 km reduces the transport collapse from -0.32 to -0.11 Sv (a branch re-forms at 100-250 km), so roughly a third of the apparent "halving" is lateral reorganization across the 100-km line; the freshening, by contrast, survives band widening (-0.53 PSU).

![Localization of the boundary-branch transport and salinity loss](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-32e8ffa3d1/outputs/pgw-branch-loss-localization.png)
![Is the anomaly handed over to the interior or lost locally?](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-32e8ffa3d1/outputs/pgw-anomaly-escape-or-local.png)

**Boundary versus interior as process sites.** Recomputing the density budget across the path rather than along it shows the offshore core loses salinity (-0.104, -0.108 PSU) and heat (-0.37, -0.38 °C) but gains almost no density (+0.0122 ± 0.0057 and +0.0092 ± 0.0049 kg m⁻³; residuals over the exact cabbeling ceiling only 1.3 and 1.0 σ), i.e. 84-90 % of the cross-path change is the isopycnal (spice) term, whereas the same bands show 10× larger density changes along the path (≥4 σ). The mean flow cannot be the importer: cross-shore mean velocity at the offshore anomaly is +0.21 ± 0.21 cm s⁻¹ (zero within error) and -0.26 ± 0.11 cm s⁻¹ farther out, and the offshore along-path core velocity is *backward* (-2.2 ± 0.2 cm s⁻¹), giving a mean-flow salt tendency of +0.52 PSU yr⁻¹ — the wrong sign to explain the observed downstream freshening (-0.57 PSU yr⁻¹ at the same speed); in the corridor the identical calculation closes (-1.67 predicted versus -1.28 PSU yr⁻¹ observed). **Reading: the offshore densification is a boundary-current-system signature seen as already present offshore, and the dilution is a laterally distributed isopycnal process — it is neither a demonstrated in-situ transformation at the offshore site nor a demonstrated lateral import by the resolved mean flow.**

![Cross-path versus along-path density budget](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-997f92fab2/outputs/pgw-crosspath-transect-budget.png)

## 3. How fast

Along the boundary axis the anomaly propagates at ~5-15 cm s⁻¹ (ten-year seasonal means of the along-axis component at 266 m, 0-50 km off the shelf break), fastest near the source in the inter-monsoon (14.6 cm s⁻¹) and southwest-monsoon (12.5 cm s⁻¹) seasons and slowest in the northeast monsoon (7.0 cm s⁻¹), with the ordering inverting farther downstream; an independent lag-correlation estimate gives 10.5 cm s⁻¹ (bootstrap 5-95 %: 7.9-15.0). Cumulative transits from the exit: 355 km (Ras al Hadd) in 102 d (NE), 46 d (SW), 40 d (IM); 600 km in 152/83/74 d; 1000 km in 222 d (NE) and 172 d (IM) but *never* in the SW monsoon.

![Along-axis propagation of the PGW anomaly](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-58281741b5/outputs/pgw-alongaxis-propagation.png)
![Transit times along the PGW axis by season](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-58281741b5/outputs/pgw-axis-transit.png)

Two corrections and qualifiers were established by follow-up work:

1. **The fixed-level measure is not an artefact.** Carrying the calculation on σ0 = 26.4 kg m⁻³ changes speeds by ≤~1 cm s⁻¹ and transit times by ≤~28 days (e.g. NE 1000 km 177 → 171 d), and the northeast-monsoon mid-axis maximum is real advection rather than heave: at 700-1000 km the NE speed is 10.3 cm s⁻¹ (all 10 years positive) at 266 m, 10.4 on σ0 = 26.4 and 12.7 on σ0 = 26.2, while the entire seasonal *sampling* (heave) term there is only -0.3 to +0.5 cm s⁻¹. Where a single water-mass-following number is wanted, quote σ0 = 26.4: NE 355 km 98 d, 600 km 127 d, 1000 km 171 d, 1200 km 206 d. The parent node's transit table could not be reproduced from its own velocity profile and was corrected (NE 1000 km 222 → 177 d; IM 1200 km 230 → 219 d).
2. **The published 1.6 cm s⁻¹ is not the boundary-jet speed.** In the reanalysis the interior strips (57-67 E, 15-21 N) give an anomaly spreading rate of only 1.2-1.9 cm s⁻¹ (best lags 20-25 months, r = 0.20-0.38), which is commensurate with the published tracer-based 1.6 ± 0.3 cm s⁻¹, whereas the boundary route gives 4-12 cm s⁻¹. The gap is definitional: route/region (2.8-6.9×), corridor bandwidth (1.8-2.3×), season window (1.2-2.3×), estimator (1.1-1.6×) and path metric (1.03-1.39×) multiply to 3.7-25×, which brackets the observed 4.2-6.7× gap, so **no model-error term is required to reconcile them**; model error itself cannot be bounded better than ~2× with these data.

![Reconciliation of the reanalysis and published spreading speeds](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-b46318cb21/outputs/pgw-isopycnal-vs-fixed266.png)

## 4. In which seasons

- **Export and salinity of the exported water peak in October-November.** At the exit gate (59.5 E / 22.15 N) the σ0 26.2-26.6 layer transport in a ±100 km strip is 0.488 Sv (October) and 0.495 Sv (November) against a 0.135 Sv annual mean, with transport-weighted salinity 36.722 PSU in October versus 36.313 PSU in April and a salt flux maximum in November (22.9 versus a May minimum of 5.5 Sv·PSU, a factor 4.2). The exit core-salinity maximum (October-November) is mainly an **upstream, ~1-month-lagged, ~50 %-damped version of the inner-Gulf-of-Oman cycle** (12-month climatologies r = 0.90), not a local effect of the fresher layer above, whose phase is wrong (freshest December-January); the signal survives downstream, damped, with core-salinity maxima at Nov (19-22 N), Dec (17-20 N) and Feb (14-17 N), and a phase progression over ~1300 km implying ~7 cm s⁻¹ (3-10 cm s⁻¹ per leg), consistent with the model's core-level along-slope speeds.
- **Statistical separability is asymmetric.** The transport-weighted-salinity seasonality at the exit is separable (permutation p = 0.002) but the *volume-transport* amplitude (0.66 Sv) is not separable from the 0.53 Sv interannual spread of the same monthly means (p = 0.19-0.23); downstream at 18.5-20.4 N both transport and salinity seasonalities are separable (p = 0.002) and peak in November-December. Interannual anomalies of the exit transport and the exit core salinity are uncorrelated (r ≈ 0.02), so the seasonal coincidence is not mirrored year by year.
- **The season that reaches farthest is late winter-spring, not autumn.** The transport-weighted salinity maximum moves from October at the exit to November at 465 km, December-January at 680 km and February-April at 915-1143 km; over the exit → 915 km leg this is 644 km in ~6 months ≈ 4 cm s⁻¹. By then the water has been diluted from ~36.7 to ~35.7 PSU. The anomaly's downstream reach is largest in the **northeast monsoon** (crosses below 0.15 PSU at ~954 km; half its source amplitude at ~986 km) and smallest in the **southwest monsoon** (~786 and ~901 km).
- **The southwest monsoon is the one clean seasonal separation.** The western-boundary pathway is present in all seasons to ~700 km, but in the SW monsoon seasonal-mean flow reverses at ~725 km (median 700-1000 km segment speed 0.5 cm s⁻¹; reversed in 5 of 10 years) versus 0 reversed years in NE and 2 of 10 in IM. All other seasonal-mean speed differences are of the same order as the ten-year interannual spread.
- **The published summer offshore escape is not supported.** At 20.4 N the boundary branch carries 0.84-1.00 Sv in Sep-Nov versus 0.11-0.22 Sv in Apr-Jul; the offshore hand-off of excess salt across the 100-km line over 20.4-16.5 N is 0.52 Sv·PSU in Oct-Nov, 0.26 in DJF, 0.25 in MAM and 0.20 in JJAS. In JJAS the hand-off at the published latitudes (18.3-19.3 N) is *inward* (-0.03 to -0.07 Sv·PSU per gate), and at 63-65 E / 18-20 N the layer is only +0.039 PSU saltier than in DJF (5 of 10 years positive) while holding 6.6 % less excess salt than in DJF. An offshore-ward summer flow exists only as a precondition at the northern edge (19.6-20.1 N, and across 58-60 E). Because the JJAS-minus-DJF interior difference (0.04-0.06 PSU) is smaller than its own ±0.09-0.10 PSU interannual spread, **the reanalysis favours the cool-season boundary-hugging picture and does not support a JJAS-specific escape, but it cannot exclude intermittent eddy-mediated summer leakage.**
