## 5. By which processes it is diluted

**The dominant process is lateral isopycnal exchange with same-density water, not entrainment, surface forcing or vertical diffusion.** Along the Omani-slope/Ras al Hadd path the core anomaly above the far-field value on its own isopycnal falls from 1.39 to 1.04 PSU in 500 km, while the core cools 1.52 °C and freshens 0.35 PSU (ratio 4.3 °C PSU⁻¹, close to β/α = 3.2 and far from the -6 to -9 °C PSU⁻¹ of the overlying water). The anomaly decays by 0.14-0.37 PSU on *every* isopycnal from σ0 25.9 to 27.0 with no density class gaining salt. A non-negative θ-S mixing inversion bounds the entrainment share of each 100-km salinity change at ≤10 % of mass, while the same-density ambient can supply 48-98 % of it. The mixed layer stays above 80 m along the corridor (median 13 m; largest single grid-cell month 78 m), so air-sea buoyancy forcing never touches the 230-270 m core; the interface above the core is doubly stable in 99 % of cases and salt-finger favourable only weakly below (Rρ ≈ 7). A purely vertical explanation would need K_z ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻¹, 4-40× the plausible range.

![Process attribution of the downstream dilution](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-7e317b63dd/outputs/pgw-dilution-attribution.png)

**How much of the decay is actually dilution.** Recast against a locally varying isopycnal background instead of one far-field box, the corridor decay is **-0.32 ± 0.04 PSU per 1000 km** (negative in 10/10 years) against a far-field-referenced -0.72 ± 0.04 PSU per 1000 km, because the core freshens at -0.74 PSU per 1000 km while its local interior reference freshens at -0.42 PSU per 1000 km on the same density surface. Against the water actually adjacent to the core on its own isopycnal (100-300 km offshore) the contrast does **not** decay (+0.05 ± 0.03 PSU per 1000 km), and the core-minus-overlying-minimum contrast is preserved over the first 500 km (0.202 → 0.207 PSU). The excess-salt content tells the same story: the corridor-strip content falls 64 % over 600 km but the 0-600 km section content falls only 24.5 % and the 0-1500 km section content is conserved within uncertainty (-6 %), i.e. **the corridor's excess is redistributed offshore rather than removed locally**. The required lateral diffusivity is therefore not a single number: recomputed across defensible anomaly and length-scale definitions it spans 0.1-7.7 × 10⁴ m² s⁻¹, with the previously quoted 1.4 × 10⁴ m² s⁻¹ sitting inside that range rather than being pinned by it. The "e-folding 640 km" and "0.7 PSU per 1000 km" figures should be quoted only together with their definition.

![Excess-salt budget and definition sensitivity of the dilution rate](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-988b8f0b6c/outputs/pgw-excess-salt-budget.png)

**A cross-isopycnal term is required for the density change but cannot be certified as a diapycnal mass flux.** The corridor core densifies by +0.104 kg m⁻³ over 500 km (positive in 80 of 118 paired months). Cabbeling of isopycnal mixing reaches only 10-29 % of this (exact-gsw ceilings of +0.011 to +0.022 kg m⁻³ per 500 km; the θ-S trajectory runs at 4.33 °C PSU⁻¹, steeper than the steepest chord to any same-σ0 interior water, 3.27), so **70-80 % (+0.075 to +0.094 kg m⁻³ per 500 km) must come from mixing with water of a different density**. This requirement decays seaward (+0.082 / +0.075 / +0.027 kg m⁻³ per 500 km for the 0-100, 100-300 and 300-600 km bands) and the down-slope signature marking a boundary current is boundary-confined (core descent +30.8 / +20.8 / +4.4 m; along-path core velocity positive only in the corridor). Yet the layer budget cannot certify a diapycnal mass flux: the transport-weighted σ0 of the boundary branch is flat over the whole route (26.406, 26.410, 26.402, 26.424 kg m⁻³; per-500-km changes -0.021 to +0.046, all below the required value), the isopycnal (spice) term accounts for ≥100 % of the freshening on every leg, the Gulf-of-Oman-mouth to exit leg shows no dilution at all, and cross-gate closure residuals (0.18-0.58 Sv) are as large as the transports themselves. The only budget expression of the exchange is geometric: the band thickens monotonically (90 → 105 → 145 → 161 m), with the largest step (+40 m per 214 km) on exactly the leg where the step table puts the required densification. Vertical turbulent diffusion is excluded by sign: the resolved σ0 curvature at the core is concave (-2.7 to -5.0 × 10⁻⁵ kg m⁻⁴), so diffusion *lightens* the core and cannot produce the observed densification.

![Cabbeling versus cross-isopycnal transfer in the boundary corridor](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-8d908ddaf9/outputs/pgw-densification-cabbeling.png)
![The same test in the offshore bands](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q21/attempt-1791188969502813757-087e72ab/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q21--62c6638cff7c/agents/ocean-process-71255cca50/outputs/pgw-offshore-vs-corridor-cabbeling.png)

## 6. What is unresolved, and what would settle it

The remaining uncertainties are structural, not numerical, and none of them can be closed with the supplied monthly-mean fields:

1. **Eddy aliasing and the interior route.** Monthly means cannot separate anomaly propagation from mesoscale eddy transport, isopycnal heave or local generation. The interior spreading rate (1.2-1.9 cm s⁻¹) rests on weak lag correlations (r = 0.20-0.38 against an autocorrelation-adjusted significance threshold of ≈0.28-0.30), and the 60-km transport collapse at 17.75-17.24 N plus the 0.28 Sv·PSU offshore hand-off could be the averaged signature of meanders. A daily/5-day or eddy-resolving reanalysis subset, or a Lagrangian/tracer release seeded in the 230-270 m core at the exit, is the only discriminator. This was never resolvable here: the sources contain only monthly files.
2. **A locally generated interior anomaly.** Where stratification and the RSOW flank can account for a subsurface salinity maximum without advection (as demonstrated for the Gulf of Aden sector), the interior could act as a *source* of the fresher same-density water that dilutes the boundary core rather than as a pathway. The transect budget found no significant cross-shore density production (residuals only 1.0-1.3 σ) and a mean flow with the wrong sign to import it, but the eddy flux that would have to do the importing is exactly what monthly means remove.
3. **Is the tracked maximum the dense outflow at all?** The model's PGW core (36.54 PSU on σ0 26.38 at 239 m) is much fresher and lighter than the observed outflow (>38 PSU on σ0 ≈ 26.5-26.8 at 250-300 m). If the tracked maximum is a strait-mixing thermocline feature rather than the dense outflow, every speed and dilution rate here describes a surrogate water mass. Testing this needs an independent observed constraint on the boundary-jet core salinity and σ0 on the same route (Argo or shipboard); no such constraint is available under the assigned literature mode and no observational product is in the task sources, so model error is bounded only to ~2×.
4. **Definitional sensitivity of "the anomaly decays".** The two saved anomaly measures disagree in trend (core-minus-overlying-minimum preserved along the corridor, 0.202 → 0.207 PSU per 500 km, versus core-minus-far-field isopycnal anomaly 1.385 → 1.044 PSU), so "the anomaly decays" is a statement about one definition. The locally referenced, content-based rate (-0.32 PSU per 1000 km) is the one this report quotes; the far-field 0.70 PSU per 1000 km should be labelled as the total contrast to the remote (4-9 N) interior, which also contains the basin-scale θ-S gradient.
5. **No independent water-mass tracer.** The likely presence of PGW south of 14 N is bounded (≤2-4 % of the local water mass, ≤0.03 PSU) rather than excluded; oxygen, nutrients or CFC/SF6 data, absent from the sources, would be needed to tighten it.

Independent support for the parts that *are* robust: the along-path decay is negative in 10 of 10 years; the corridor preserves its vertical salinity step while the isopycnal anomaly falls on every density surface with no compensating gain; the θ-S direction excludes overlying-layer entrainment as the main term; the Gulf of Aden maximum is cleanly separated as RSOW; the southwest-monsoon boundary stall survives the isopycnal switch (so it is not a fixed-level artefact); and the model's pathway geometry and core density class match the published observational picture even though its salinity amplitude does not.

## Research Tree

ROOT (B1, active): *How does the high-salinity Persian Gulf Water (PGW) that leaves the Gulf of Oman at ~200-350 m spread and become diluted in the Arabian Sea (47-70 E, 4-26 N, 2011-2020): along which paths, how fast, in which seasons, and by which processes?*

- **B1.1 [completed]** Source term: properties, core depth, thickness, seasonal cycle of the PGW core at the Gulf of Oman exit.
  - Result: subsurface salinity maximum at 239 m, S = 36.54 ± 0.21 PSU, θ = 18.3 ± 1.3 °C, σ0 = 26.38 ± 0.27; 184-295 m layer, 111 ± 46 m; saltiest Oct-Nov; downstream core salinity 36.83 → 35.77 PSU; model core much fresher than observed PGW (stated limitation).
  - **B1.1.1 [completed]** Is the October-November exit salinity maximum upstream-set or locally produced, and does it survive downstream?
    - Result: upstream, ~1-month-lagged, ~50 %-damped version of the inner-Gulf-of-Oman cycle (r = 0.90); overlying layer phase is wrong; signal survives damped along the slope (~7 cm s⁻¹ phase speed).
    - **B1.1.1.1 [completed]** Does the autumn salinity maximum coincide with a seasonal transport maximum, and which season reaches farthest?
      - Result: in phase — October-November export (0.49 Sv versus 0.135 Sv annual mean; transport-weighted salinity 36.72 versus 36.31 PSU in April), but exit volume-transport seasonality is not separable (p ≈ 0.2) while the salinity/salt-flux seasonality is (p = 0.002); the season carrying the anomaly farthest is late winter-spring (Feb-May).
- **B1.2 [completed]** Along which pathways does the PGW maximum spread, and which branches carry it?
  - Result: the Omani-slope / Ras al Hadd boundary current is the only demonstrated advective path (6-11 cm s⁻¹ at 22-23 N, ~5 cm s⁻¹ at 16.5-19 N); a comparable interior anomaly exists but an eddy-mediated interior route is not demonstrated; no Socotra-Irwin/Laccadive branch.
  - **B1.2.1 [completed]** How fast does it propagate along that path, and how do speed and reach differ by season?
    - Result: 5-15 cm s⁻¹ seasonal-mean speeds; 355 km in 40-102 d, 1000 km in 172-222 d; largest reach in NE monsoon (~954 km), smallest in SW (~786 km); SW-monsoon reversal at ~725 km is the only clean seasonal separation.
    - **B1.2.1.1 [completed]** Does an isopycnal-following calculation change the transits or the seasonal ordering; is the NE mid-axis maximum real or heave?
      - Result: no change of conclusion (≤~1 cm s⁻¹, ≤~28 d); NE mid-axis maximum is real advection (heave term only -0.3 to +0.5 cm s⁻¹); the parent's fixed-level transit table is corrected (e.g. NE 1000 km 222 → 177 d).
  - **B1.2.2 [completed]** By which processes is the anomaly diluted downstream — diapycnal versus isopycnal?
    - Result: lateral isopycnal exchange with same-density fresher water dominates; entrainment ≤10 % of mass; no contact with surface forcing; vertical diffusion would need implausible K_z; required K_h ≈ 1.4 × 10⁴ m² s⁻¹ under that definition.
    - **B1.2.2.1 [completed]** Is the +0.10 kg m⁻³ per 500 km densification cabbeling or genuine cross-isopycnal transfer?
      - Result: cabbeling explains only 10-29 %; 70-80 % requires cross-isopycnal transfer, which opposes rather than produces the freshening; vertical diffusion excluded by sign.
      - **B1.2.2.1.1 [completed]** Does the offshore band show the same process balance?
        - Result: same in kind, weaker in magnitude (+0.082/+0.075/+0.027 kg m⁻³ per 500 km for 0-100/100-300/300-600 km); down-slope signature boundary-confined out to ~300 km.
        - **B1.2.2.1.1.1 [completed]** Is the offshore densification in-situ transformation or lateral import?
          - Result: neither demonstrated: cross-path change is 84-90 % isopycnal with density residuals only 1.0-1.3 σ, and the resolved mean flow cannot import it (wrong sign, zero within error offshore); "transformation along the boundary-current system, laterally distributed".
  - **B1.2.3 [completed]** Is the Gulf of Aden/Socotra salinity maximum RSOW rather than PGW?
    - Result: yes — RSOW on σ0 27.16 at ~599 m (corrects the earlier 323 m estimate from a clipped search band); PGW-class maxima in 3-4 % of columns there and ~0 % south of 14 N.
    - **B1.2.3.1 [completed]** Is the residual σ0 ≈ 26.4 excess RSOW flank or weak PGW?
      - Result: fully accounted for by local stratification/RSOW flank (residuals negative to +0.032 PSU); PGW contribution bounded at ≤2-4 % of the local water mass.
- **B1.3 [completed]** Published prior on PGW pathways, speeds and dilution (search-only mode).
  - Result: PGW core on σ0 ≈ 26.5 at ~220 m, along-coast boundary current after Ras al Hadd, salinity decaying from ~37.5-38 to ~36.5 PSU at 57 E/18 N; tracer-based mean speed 0.016 ± 0.003 m s⁻¹; tidal/entrainment dilution at the source, lateral and diapycnal mixing downstream; two contested seasonal pictures. Abstract-level evidence only.
- **B1.4 [completed]** Which speed answers "how fast", and can it be reconciled with the published 1.6 cm s⁻¹?
  - Result: a route-resolved spreading rate; the published value matches the reanalysis *interior* rate (1.2-1.9 cm s⁻¹), not the boundary jet; definitional factors (3.7-25×) bracket the gap, so no model-error term is required; model error bounded only to ~2×.
- **B1.5 [completed]** Which alternative explanations remain compatible, and which would change the answer?
  - Result: three would change it and cannot be settled with these files — eddy/standing-structure aliasing; a locally generated interior anomaly acting as a freshwater source rather than a path; and the model's fresh, light core possibly being a strait-mixing thermocline feature rather than the dense outflow. Four more change only the dilution numbers.
  - **B1.5.1 [completed]** Is the headline decay salt loss or partly background freshening / geometric spreading?
    - Result: about half is background (locally referenced -0.32 ± 0.04 PSU per 1000 km versus far-field -0.72); the local contrast does not decay (+0.05 ± 0.03); section excess-salt content conserved within -6 % over 1500 km; K_h spans 0.1-7.7 × 10⁴ m² s⁻¹ across definitions.
  - **B1.5.2 [completed]** Does the gate-by-gate layer budget show the boundary current can supply the anomaly, and where does the cross-isopycnal term act?
    - Result: sufficient from the exit to 18.5 N (0.34 → 0.50 → 0.41 Sv) but collapsing at 16.5 N; never net-exported (recirculating branch); the cross-isopycnal term is neither an exit process nor certifiable as a diapycnal mass flux (spice term ≥100 % of freshening; closure residuals 0.18-0.58 Sv).
    - **B1.5.2.1 [completed]** Where does the branch collapse, and is the anomaly handed to the interior or lost locally?
      - Result: one 60-km step at 17.75-17.24 N; ~62 % of the lost excess salt crosses the 100-km line; the interior is itself fresher at 16.5 N and the branch-interior contrast collapses from +0.21 to +0.03 PSU — lateral dispersal, not a distinct tongue, not local destruction.
      - **B1.5.2.1.1 [completed]** Does the reanalysis support a summer (JJAS) offshore escape as opposed to winter western-boundary spreading?
        - Result: supports cool-season boundary-hugging spreading with an Oct-Nov maximum; JJAS hand-off at 18.3-19.3 N is inward and the JJAS interior excess is within the interannual spread, so a summer escape is neither confirmed nor excluded.

Closed / unpursued directions (with reasons): daily-resolution or Lagrangian/tracer tests of the interior route, of the 60-km collapse and of the SW-monsoon stall require sub-monthly fields not present in the task sources; independent observational or tracer constraints (Argo/shipboard core properties, O₂/nutrients/CFC-SF6) are outside the supplied data and the assigned search-only literature mode, so model error and the southern PGW fraction remain bounded rather than measured; RSOW's own dilution budget is a different water mass and was not pursued; the one marginal southern PGW-class bump strip (47.1-48.9 E / 11.1-11.5 N) and the definitional sensitivity of K_h were left as named residual uncertainty because they do not change the reported paths, speeds, seasons or process attribution. No failed nodes.

# How Persian Gulf Water spreads and is diluted in the Arabian Sea
### GLORYS12V1 monthly reanalysis, 2011–2020 (47–70°E, 4–26°N)

## Data and method (summary)

The 120 monthly files of `thetao`, `so`, `uo`, `vo` (plus `zos`, `mlotst`) were read **in place, never copied**. PGW is defined as the subsurface salinity maximum inside the density band **σ₀ = 26.30–27.05 kg m⁻³**, which sits between Arabian Sea High Salinity Water above and Red Sea Water below. For each target density the depth of the isopycnal is found by a first-crossing search in every column (TEOS-10 via `gsw`), and S, T and velocity are interpolated onto it. Paths are computed with isopycnal-following RK4 drifters (1-day step, sub-stepping, coastal sliding) released in the Gulf of Oman. Dilution is measured by the excess-salinity fraction `f = (S_iso − S_background)/(S_source − S_background)`, with `S_background` the basin median on the same isopycnal.

## 1. The source

In the box immediately downstream of Hormuz (56.3–58.0°E, 25–26°N) the salinity maximum is **36.76 ± 0.10 psu at 260 m (range 222–318 m), σ₀ = 26.46**, with a small seasonal amplitude of 0.35 psu (min 36.61 in February, max 36.96 in August).

> **Model caveat, reported up front:** observed PGW is 37.5–39.5 psu. GLORYS12's Gulf-of-Oman core is **1–3 psu fresher**. Every absolute salinity below is therefore a model value; what is analysed is the *structure* (path, speed, seasonality, dilution length scale), which is far less sensitive to this bias.

## 2. Along which paths

Averaged over 2011–2020, the isopycnal salinity field shows a high-salinity ribbon leaving the Gulf of Oman and running **south-east along the Omani coast**. Because the basin-wide north–south salinity gradient dominates the raw field, the tongue is isolated with the **zonal anomaly at fixed latitude and density**; the +0.05 psu contour encloses a coherent tongue from the source to the central Arabian Sea (Fig. 2b,c).

The Lagrangian ensemble confirms and extends this (Fig. 3a). Drifters on σ₀ = 26.3/26.5/26.7 (488/462/450 particles) released 2011-01-15 and integrated five years show a **narrow, high-occupancy ribbon hugging the Omani coast to about 60°E/21°N**, after which the ensemble **fans out south and east into the central Arabian Sea**, reaching 70°E and ~5°N within five years. The occupancy maximum stays west of ~62°E; the median drifter ends at **61.5°E, 17.2°N** (σ₀ = 26.5). 92–94% of particles are still on a valid isopycnal after five years, and only 24–36% ever touch a domain edge (1–4% are at an edge at year 5), so boundary artefacts are minor.

The core depth is not constant: on the 26.3–27.05 band the salinity maximum sits at 220–320 m near the source and the tongue **deepens and erodes downstream** (Fig. 2d, Fig. 5d).

## 3. How fast

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Net drift speed (30-day lagged displacement), median | **4.8–4.9 cm s⁻¹** |
| 1-day displacement speed, median | 10.3 cm s⁻¹ |
| 90-day lagged speed, median | 2.8 cm s⁻¹ |
| Transit time to 500 km | **~6 months** |
| to 1000 km | 18–22 months |
| to 1500 km | 34–40 months |
| to 2000 km | 46–49 months, but only ~10% of drifters get there in 5 years |

The contrast between the 1-day (10 cm s⁻¹) and 30-day (4.9 cm s⁻¹) speeds is the signature of **looping/meandering rather than a steady jet** — most of the instantaneous motion does not contribute to net displacement. Spreading is slow: **~1000 km in about 1.5–2 years**.

## 4. In which seasons

Two independent measures agree on the same ordering (Fig. 4):

- **One-year displacement by release month** (120 monthly releases, 462 drifters each): **fastest for July–September**, peaking at **784 km for September** releases (August 747, July 729); **slowest for November–December** (615 and 614 km). Spread is 25% of the mean.
- **Equatorward reach:** 39% of September releases are south of 20°N after one year versus 20% of December releases.
- **Drifter depth after one year** is shallowest for August–October releases (249 m) and deepest for April (280 m) — the isopycnal is lifted during the upwelling season.
- **Eulerian tongue:** area is largest in **March (11.1 × 10⁵ km²)** and smallest in **July (7.7 × 10⁵ km²)**; the eastern limit is farthest east in **September (67.2°E)** and farthest west in **May (63.4°E)**.

**Interpretation.** Late-summer releases are fastest because the Omani coastal current is **southwestward (equatorward) during the SW monsoon (June–September)**, advecting PGW along the coast; the **NE-monsoon reversal** (December–February) opposes it, and late-autumn releases are the slowest. The two measures differ in phase because the Eulerian tongue *area* is set by the convergence of the anomaly field (largest when the alongshore current is weak and the anomaly accumulates), whereas the drifter displacement measures advection — they are complementary, not contradictory.

## 5. How much it is diluted

The excess-salinity fraction **decays exponentially with distance** (Fig. 5a,b):

| Isopycnal | e-folding length L | f at 500 km | f at 1000 km | f first < 0.05 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| σ₀ = 26.3 | 613 km | 0.74 | 0.44 | 1850 km |
| σ₀ = 26.5 | 590 km | 0.69 | 0.31 | 1250 km |
| σ₀ = 26.7 | 581 km | 0.71 | 0.39 | 1450 km |

So **half the PGW signal is lost within ~400–500 km (about 4–6 months of travel)** and the signal is effectively erased **1250–1850 km** downstream — well before the drifter ensemble reaches the domain edge. The salinity on the isopycnal converges to the basin-median background value (Fig. 5c), and the T–S curves along the path collapse toward the background line (Fig. 5e) — i.e. this is **mixing along the isopycnal toward a common water mass**, not a density-changing transformation.

## 6. By which processes

Three candidate mechanisms were tested (Fig. 6):

1. **Direct winter ventilation — ruled out.** The February mixed layer over the tongue is **30 m** deep while the core is at **266 m**: a ventilation gap of **~230 m**. No winter convection reaches PGW.
2. **Double diffusion — plausible, and favoured.** At the core in February the Turner angle exceeds 45° over **91% of the basin** (salt-fingering favourable); 9% is statically stable and **0% is diffusive-convective**. PGW is warm and salty overlying cooler, fresher water, exactly the salt-fingering configuration — a viable but slow diapycnal sink.
3. **Mesoscale lateral stirring — the dominant loss.** The median rate of change of the PGW fraction more than doubles with eddy kinetic energy, from **−0.015 yr⁻¹** in the quietest bin (EKE < 0.002 m² s⁻²) to **−0.19 yr⁻¹** at EKE ≈ 0.006–0.009 m² s⁻², then flattening (and turning slightly positive) in the highest-EKE bins where sample counts are small.

**Answer:** the tongue is diluted **predominantly laterally, by mesoscale stirring along isopycnals**, with an e-folding scale of ~600 km; salt fingering is the energetically available diapycnal sink; direct winter convection plays no role.

## 7. Answer to the question, in one paragraph

PGW leaves the Gulf of Oman as a 220–320 m salinity maximum on σ₀ ≈ 26.3–26.7, hugs the Omani coast south-eastward as a narrow ribbon, and turns south into the central Arabian Sea around 60–62°E, fanning out to reach 70°E and 5°N within five years. It travels slowly — a median net drift of ~4.9 cm s⁻¹, about 1000 km in 1.5–2 years and 1500 km in ~3 years — and spreads fastest for late-summer (July–September) releases, when the SW-monsoon equatorward coastal current carries it south, and slowest for November–December releases under the opposing NE monsoon. It is diluted by lateral mesoscale stirring along isopycnals, losing half its excess salinity within ~400–500 km (e-folding ~600 km) and the whole signal by 1250–1850 km, while salt fingering provides a slower diapycnal sink and winter convection is too shallow to matter.

## Caveats and limitations (honest accounting)

1. **Model salinity bias.** GLORYS12's Gulf-of-Oman core is 36.6–37.0 psu vs. an observed 37.5–39.5 psu. Absolute values are not trustworthy; the structure is.
2. **Monthly means filter the mesoscale.** The drifters follow monthly-mean velocities, so individual eddy pathways are not resolved and the EKE diagnostic is an explicit **lower bound**. Actual dispersion is likely faster and more diffusive than simulated.
3. **Domain boundaries.** Spreading beyond 70°E or south of 4°N is not represented; particles reaching the edge are held there. This is a modest effect (1–4% of particles at year 5) but it truncates the far field.
4. **Survivorship.** Particles whose isopycnal disappears (shelf/land) leave the statistics; ~6–8% by year 5. Statistics are therefore slightly biased toward particles that stayed in the open basin.
5. **Background definition.** `S_background` is the basin median on each isopycnal and itself contains some PGW influence, so `f` is a conservative (slightly under-)estimate of the excess salinity.
6. **Source region.** The Strait of Hormuz is just outside the domain; the source box is downstream of it, so the initial outflow is not resolved.
7. **Seasonal ensemble window.** Releases whose 2-year window runs past December 2020 are excluded from the 730-day statistics (96 of 120 usable); 108 of 120 are usable at 365 days, so the one-year seasonality above is the more robust result.
8. **Tongue-extent metric.** The eastern limit is defined as the easternmost longitude carrying at least 15 anomalous cells (≥ +0.05 psu), to prevent a single noisy cell from defining it; the uncorrected metric showed spurious 2° jumps.

No blockers were encountered. All supplied datasets were treated as read-only and no data were copied or sent anywhere.

# Spreading and dilution of Persian Gulf Water (PGW) in the Arabian Sea (47-70°E, 4-26°N), 2011-2020

## Data & method
I used the supplied GLORYS12V1 monthly reanalysis (120 months, 2011-01…2020-12; 1/12° grid; 35 depth levels, 0.5-902 m): thetao, so, uo, vo, zos, mlotst. A 10-year monthly climatology was computed for every field (intermediate .npy in /workspace/scratch; original inputs untouched). PGW is identified as the sub-surface salinity maximum in a 150-450 m (core search) / 200-400 m (tracking) window.

## 1. Paths
The annual-mean salinity field shows a pronounced sub-surface salinity maximum (>36) centred in the Gulf of Oman (Smax ≈ 36.9 near 58-60°E, 24-25°N) with its core at ≈220 m — the PGW source. The core salinity-maximum traces a single coherent pathway southward along the Oman continental margin (equatorward), then curling slightly south-west:
(59.0°E,24.0°N)→(58.5,22.5)→(58.0,21.0)→(57.5,19.5)→(57.0,18.0)→(56.0,16.0)→(55.0,14.0)→(54.0,12.0)→(53.0,10.0)→(52.0,8.0).
Total path ≈1935 km. Meridional section at 58°E shows the high-salinity tongue descending and thinning to the south (core deepens from ≈222 m at 24°N to ≈266 m at 14-18°N). Zonal section at 12°N shows the high-salinity signal confined to the west near the Oman/Makran margin.
Figures: fig01_salinity_structure.png, fig03_pgw_layer_maps.png, fig05_paths_dilution.png, fig09_zonal_meridional_sections.png.

## 2. Speed
Mean horizontal velocity in the PGW layer (200-300 m) along the path is 2-9 cm/s (path mean ≈5.0 cm/s; max ≈8.6 cm/s). Using these Eulerian monthly-mean speeds, the along-path advective travel time from the Gulf of Oman (24°N) to 8°N (1935 km) is ≈472 days (≈1.3 yr). This is an estimate; monthly Eulerian means under-sample mesoscale eddy transports, so true spreading is likely somewhat faster.
Table: table_pgw_path_transect.csv.

## 3. Seasonality
Box-mean PGW-layer (200-400 m) salinity maximum (table_pgw_seasonal_boxes.csv):

| Box | DJF | MAM | JJA | SON |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gulf of Oman (source) | 36.407 | 36.461 | 36.462 | 36.458 |
| Oman corridor | 35.814 | 35.831 | 35.766 | 35.744 |
| South Arabian Sea | 35.463 | 35.479 | 35.424 | 35.393 |

Source is saltiest in late spring-summer (peak June); the Oman corridor and southern basin peak in spring (corridor peak March; south peak May — a downstream lag consistent with the ~1-yr path). The minimum everywhere is in autumn (SON, September trough). The SW-monsoon (JJA) upwelling/alongshore current system enhances equatorward PGW transport at the source.
Figures: fig04_seasonal_pgw_layer.png, fig06_seasonal_cycle.png; table_pgw_monthly_cycle.csv.

## 4. Dilution processes
The PGW-core salinity maximum decays almost linearly with distance: Smax = 36.529 - 6.56e-4·distance(km), i.e. ≈0.66 psu per 1000 km, or 1.25 psu over the 1935-km path (36.68 → 35.43). An exponential fit to the anomaly above background (Sb≈35.0) gives a decay length scale ≈1360 km. This steady monotonic dilution is the signature of lateral (isopycnal) spreading and mesoscale eddy stirring along the boundary-current path.
- Diapycnal (vertical) mixing is weak after PGW leaves the Gulf of Oman: |dS/dz| ≈0.0026 psu/m at the source, decreasing to ≈0.0002-0.0006 psu/m downstream.
- Surface processes do not ventilate the 200-350 m PGW core directly: winter mixed-layer depth (~40 m in DJF) is far shallower than the core; MLD is ~11-22 m in JJA, ~13-16 m in MAM/SON (fig08_mld_seasonal.png).
- T-S diagram (fig07_section_ts.png) shows PGW as a distinct high-salinity branch that cools and freshens toward the background thermocline along the path.

## Key numbers (table_summary_metrics.csv)
- PGW source salinity max (Gulf of Oman, 24°N, ~222 m): 36.68
- PGW salinity max at 8°N: 35.43
- Salinity loss along path: 1.25 psu
- Path length: 1935 km; dilution rate: 0.656 psu/1000 km; decay scale: ~1360 km
- Mean PGW-layer current speed: 5.05 cm/s
- Advective travel time (24°N→8°N): ≈472 days (≈1.3 yr)

## Caveats / unresolved questions
- Eulerian monthly-mean velocities under-sample eddy transport; a Lagrangian particle-tracking calculation would give a more robust spreading rate.
- In the southern basin the "salinity maximum" in the 200-400 m window sometimes sits at the top of the window and partly reflects pycnocline/Red-Sea/other water masses, so absolute Smax there is a mixture; the monotonic decrease from the Gulf of Oman nevertheless tracks PGW robustly.
- Some path waypoints fell on land; nearest-wet sampling and linear interpolation of speed were used (flagged in table_pgw_path_transect.csv).
- No literature-search tool and no in-situ validation were available, so the results rely solely on the supplied GLORYS12 fields; no external citations were invented.

## Artifacts written to /workspace/outputs
Figures: fig01_salinity_structure.png, fig03_pgw_layer_maps.png, fig04_seasonal_pgw_layer.png, fig05_paths_dilution.png, fig06_seasonal_cycle.png, fig07_section_ts.png, fig08_mld_seasonal.png, fig09_zonal_meridional_sections.png.
Tables/report: table_pgw_path_transect.csv, table_pgw_seasonal_boxes.csv, table_pgw_monthly_cycle.csv, table_summary_metrics.csv, report.txt.</answer>

Original final answer (English)
# Loop Current eddy separation in the Gulf of Mexico, 2011–2017 (GLORYS12 daily SSH, temperature, salinity): events, intervals, pre-separation state, and why published intervals differ

## Summary

Using the supplied GLORYS12 daily `zos` (SSH above geoid), `thetao` and `so` for 2011-01-01 to 2017-12-31, one fixed model record yields **anywhere between about 3.5 and 20 months for the mean separation interval depending only on how "separation" is defined** — a range that contains the entire published spread (8.0–11.0 months). The defensible 2011–2017 event list is therefore reported as a small set of criterion-consistent alternatives, not as one number:

- **SSH multi-definition core list (≥2 of 3 internally defined criteria agree): 6 events** — 2011-04-04 (±~3 weeks), 2011-11-12, 2012-12-04, 2013-11-16, 2015-01-19, 2016-11-01; intervals 222, 388, 347, 429, 652 d; mean 408 d, median 388 d. The strict three-criterion core is only **4 events** (2011-11-12, 2012-12-04, 2015-01-19, 2016-11-01; intervals 388, 776, 652 d; mean 605 d), and permissive single-criterion thresholds give 10–14 detections (mean interval 216–291 d).
- **Water-mass (eddy-identity) list: 10 physically distinct anticyclones** (range 7–11 over the amplitude/area/smoothing grid, 1.0–1.6 events yr⁻¹) with formation dates 2011-04-03, 2011-08-16, 2011-09-05, 2012-05-27, 2014-08-19, 2014-11-24, 2015-05-23, 2015-10-24, 2016-06-07, 2017-06-09; intervals 135, 20, 265, 814, 97, 180, 154, 227, 367 d; mean 251 d (8.2 months), median 179 d (5.9 months). This rule is the one that supplies the "one eddy counted once" identity that the literal published-style criteria lack.
- **Joint SSH-plus-warm-core whole-record scan: 12 bodies** (mean 194 d, median 176 d). Re-adjudicating the three bodies inside the 2012–2014 gap, none is catalogue-class, which corrects that scan to **9 events, mean 266.5 d (8.8 months), median 195.5 d (6.4 months), longest interval 946 d**.

**The same long gap survives every convention.** No convention tested breaks the 2012–2014 separation hiatus: 776 d between the SSH event dates 2012-12-04 and 2015-01-19, 814 d between the water-mass formations 2012-05-27 and 2014-08-19, 946 d between joint bodies (2012-05-29 → 2014-12-31). The 2013-11/2014-02/2014-05 SSH candidates are excluded: the eastern Gulf had 0 days with a 20 °C-isotherm-depth anomaly above 100 m in 2013 and in 2014-01 to 2014-08, versus 126 days in 2015; the three candidate bodies reach only 59 %, 66 % and 86 % of ring size at the reference 50 m amplitude, one is a quasi-stationary western-Gulf remnant of the 2012 eddy, and the 20 600 km² warm-core gate (versus 9 000 km² in the loose scan) is what separates the verdicts.

**State of the Loop Current before each separation** (GLORYS12 SSH-anomaly ridge index): every one of the ten separated eddies pinches off from an *extended*, northward-penetrating loop — ridge near 25.5–28.3 °N at formation, 8 of 10 at or above 26.0 °N, seven of them within only 2–13 d of the onset of an extended episode, and none following a collapse to ≤23.5 °N in the preceding 25 d except the 2011-04-03 eddy (4 d). For the four SSH tier-1 events the ridge sits at 27.1 ± 0.9 °N 90 d before and 26.7 ± 0.5 °N 30 d before, and reads 22.2 ± 1.3 °N on the event date, i.e. the "event" is the collapse of an already-long-extended loop, with the ridge maximum 8–181 d (median 75 d) earlier. No single common precursor signature exists beyond extension: loop configuration and the Yucatan/Campeche setting vary event to event, and the five eddies the SSH core list missed are statistically indistinguishable in pre-formation state from the five it counted (Mann–Whitney p ≥ 0.42 at every lag, n = 5 vs 5). Extension is close to necessary but far from sufficient: only 8 of 28 extended episodes (ridge ≥26 °N) produced one of the ten cores; the best empirical discriminator is the loop's *history* rather than its instantaneous extent (7 of 15 episodes beginning as a modest dip within an already-extended loop shed, versus 1 of 13 beginning after a collapse to ≤23.5 °N; Fisher p = 0.038; pre-onset ridge area AUC 0.86, p = 0.004), with part of the signal being a warm-season preference (7 of 16 May–October episodes shed versus 1 of 12 November–April).

**Why published estimates differ — weighed, not asserted.** The tree measured the components and then had the result challenged adversarially, which changed the conclusion level (this is a correction to the earlier reading):

- *Event definition / detection criterion is a large sensitivity, but attribution is not identified.* On the fixed record, eight defensible definitions span mean intervals 5.2–19.9 months (factor 3.8, SD 4.7 months), about five times the published spread (8.0–11.0 months, range 3.0, SD 1.2 months). But the endpoints of that span imply shedding rates (0.57 and 2.0 yr⁻¹) outside the published 1.1–1.6 yr⁻¹ band; restricting to rate-compatible variants collapses the GLORYS12 mean-interval range to **9.5–11.2 months, inside the published spread**. So the data show that definition has large leverage, not that definition explains the published differences (see below).
- *Date-marker convention is a genuine null for the mean.* With a fixed event list, dating every event at the extension peak, mid-retreat or contour crossing moves the 7-year mean by at most 0.4 months, even though individual dates move by up to 156 d and the water-mass formation date precedes the matching SSH event date by 56–191 d for the same eddy. Marker convention matters mainly where it changes the count.
- *Record length / sampling is as large as the published spread.* The SD of a mean interval is 1.3–1.6 months for a 20–30-year record and 2.6–5.2 months for 7 years, versus a published spread of 1.2 months; the between-study heterogeneity test is marginal (Q = 15.2, df 7, p = 0.034 at interval CV 0.4; p = 0.21 at CV 0.5; p = 0.70 at CV 0.72), so the published means are statistically compatible with sampling noise alone and any systematic between-study SD is bounded at ≲1.1 months.
- *Period/regime and region are neither separable nor demonstrably non-zero here.* Vukovich's 2001–2010 decade counts (11, 11, 16 rings) are not distinguishable from homogeneous sampling under Poisson (p = 0.52), and the literature corpus contains no regional contrast independent of method.
- *A competing reading is not excluded.* Only one model record and no altimetry were available, so the tree could vary event definition inside GLORYS12 but could never test a GLORYS12-specific eddy census; every published criterion was a reconstruction from abstract-level text, so the criterion-matched residual (24 detections at 3.5 months; 17 at 4.1 months; 3 at 18.0 months for a deep-retreat reading of the same criterion string) is a null about the reconstructions, not about the published algorithms.

Two threshold-free results stand independently: in 2015, six literal SSH detections over 87–89 °W collapse to **two coexisting rings** (one born 2014-11-24 drifting 559 km west, one born 2015-05-23 drifting 285 km west, coexisting 92 days at 344–581 km centroid separation, visible as two simultaneous ≥17 cm closed highs); and the 2013–2014 eastern-Gulf warm-dome quiescence is a fact about the fields, not an artefact of a threshold choice within the tested range.

---

## 2. Separation events and intervals, 2011–2017

### 2.1 SSH kinematic lists (node B1.1)

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| permissive | any single definition | 10–14 | — | — | 216–291 d / — |
| **core** | ≥2 of 3 definitions | **6** | 2011-04-04, 2011-11-12, 2012-12-04, 2013-11-16, 2015-01-19, 2016-11-01 | 222, 388, 347, 429, 652 | 408 d / 388 d |
| strict | all 3 definitions | 4 | 2011-11-12, 2012-12-04, 2015-01-19, 2016-11-01 | 388, 776, 652 | 605 d / 652 d |

Event dates carry ±1–2 weeks (up to 37 d for the 2016 event); the count is bounded (4 to ~14), not uniquely determined. ### 2.3 Joint census and the reconciliation of the count (nodes B1.3.1.1.1.1, B1.3.1.1.1.1.1)

Requiring, on the same day, a detached core-size SSH body (≥2.06 × 10⁴ km², ≥0.15 m) and a detached warm core (d20 anomaly ≥50 m, ≥~9 000 km², ≥20 joint days) gives 12 bodies with formation dates 2011-01-18, 2011-07-13, 2011-10-27, 2012-05-29, 2013-07-18, 2013-12-24, 2014-04-04, 2014-12-31, 2015-06-11, 2015-08-18, 2016-03-24, 2016-11-19 (mean 194 d, median 176 d). Eight match a catalogued core; three of the other four lie inside the 2012–2014 gap and were re-adjudicated:

| body | max detached warm-core area at ≥50 m | % of ring size | days above 20 600 km² | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2013-07-18 | 12 100 km² | 59 % | 0 | threshold-marginal sub-ring-size detached anomaly — not counted |
| 2013-12-24 | 13 687 km² | 66 % | 0 | quasi-stationary (2.5–33 km drift over 53–129 d) at 25.1 N 95.0 W, ~550 km west of the Loop Current — decayed remnant of a previously separated eddy, a non-separation |
| 2014-04-04 | 17 755 km² | 86 % | 0 | sub-ring-size quasi-stationary feature just west of the Florida shelf (0.9 km d⁻¹ drift) — not counted; "small shed ring" vs "Loop Current lobe" cannot be closed without velocity |

The separating gate is the **warm-core area at the reference 50 m amplitude** (20 600 km² versus the loose scan's 9 000 km²); amplitude (50 versus 45 m) is the second gate and admits 2013-07-18 and 2014-04-04. Corrected joint count: **9 events, mean 266.5 d (8.8 months), median 195.5 d (6.4 months), longest interval 946 d**; the intermediate 45 m choice gives 11 events, mean 213 d (7.0 months). ### 2.4 The 2011-04-04 event (nodes B1.1.1.1)

The 222-day first interval of the SSH core list is the least robust: the longest continuous detached episode is 19 d (2011-04-19 to 05-07), one day under the 20-day gate, and the event is a **real but marginal detachment** (moderate confidence, ≈2:1) with the weakest pre-separation Loop Current state of the core list. If the same 20-day standard that removed the 2013–2014 candidates is applied consistently, 2011-04-04 also drops and the pooled core-list mean becomes 454 d instead of 408 d; at a 45 m amplitude threshold the 2011-versus-2013/2014 contrast disappears altogether. Both statistics must be carried as a stated sensitivity. Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-42d4ec4ec0/outputs/lc-2011-detachment-diagnosis.png`.

### 2.5 Right-censoring

The record ends 425 d after the 2016-11-01 event (dominated by the water-mass eddy 10 formed 2017-06-09), so the final interval is right-censored and no statement about an event after 2017 is possible.

## 3. State of the Loop Current before each separation

Measured on the GLORYS12 SSH-anomaly ridge index (the strongest anomaly component touching the Yucatan source box; "ridge" = the part reaching half the component's peak). All absolute values are threshold-dependent (hand-set anomaly floors; at a 0.10 m floor the same events read up to 1.4° further north at 90 d lead and the 2011-04-04 pre-state flips from retracted to extended).

- **All ten water-mass eddies pinch off from an extended loop.** Ridge latitude at formation 25.5–28.3 °N; 8 of 10 at or above 26.0 °N; seven form within 2–13 d of an extended episode's onset (i.e. during re-extension, not after a long mature phase); eddy 6 forms 51 d into a 104-day episode; eddies 2 and 10 form outside any ≥26 °N episode in a moderate 25.7–25.8 °N state; only eddy 1 follows a collapse to ≤23.5 °N in the preceding 25 d (4 d).
- **The five eddies the SSH core list missed are not a distinguishable class.** Group-mean ridge latitude at −90/−60/−30/0 d: counted five 24.65 ± 2.80 / 26.43 ± 1.04 / 27.02 ± 1.04 / 26.85 ± 0.71 °N versus missed five 25.15 ± 2.15 / 25.63 ± 0.93 / 26.97 ± 1.12 / 26.73 ± 1.06 °N (p = 1.00, 0.46, 0.92, 1.00); ridge area identical at −90 d. The only near-significant contrast is in the *opposite* direction (stronger 30-d-before ridge for the missed five, 0.53 ± 0.10 versus 0.38 ± 0.09 m, p = 0.06). They differ in what the SSH criterion demands of an event, not in the preceding loop configuration. Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-b6020c11c4/outputs/lc-state-before-10-eddies.png`.
- **For the four SSH tier-1 events** the ridge is at 26.7 °N 180 d before, 27.1 ± 0.9 °N 90 d before, 26.7 ± 0.5 °N 30 d before, collapsing to 22.2 ± 1.3 °N on the event date (ridge area 54 000 → 68 000 → 59 000 → 3 000 km²). The marginal SSH candidates are weaker or fully retracted at long lead (2013-11-16: 25.4 °N, 21 500 km², 0.31 m at 30 d; 2014-02-09: 0.21 m, 17 500 km² — the weakest of any candidate). Loop configuration and the Yucatan/Campeche setting vary event to event, with no common precursor signature and no Loop Current–Campeche merger in any pre-separation state. Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-7d4fb7c732/outputs/lc-preparation-state-2011-2017.png`.
- **Extension is necessary but far from sufficient.** Only 8 of 28 extended episodes (ridge ≥26 °N) produced one of the ten cores. The sharpest split is about loop history — 7 of 15 episodes beginning as a modest dip within an already-extended loop shed a core, versus 1 of 13 beginning after a collapse to ≤23.5 °N in the preceding 30 d (Fisher p = 0.038); pre-onset mean ridge area 50.1 ± 16.1 versus 27.7 ± 16.6 × 10³ km² (AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.64–1.00, p = 0.004); episode duration 74 ± 34 versus 41 ± 39 d (p = 0.027); peak ridge latitude 27.9 ± 0.4 versus 27.4 ± 0.5 °N (p = 0.034). Rejected as controls: deeper pre-onset retraction (the wedge runs the other way), faster extension (0.48 ± 0.35 versus 0.79 ± 0.38 km d⁻¹), loop shape/asymmetry, and the Campeche setting. A strong warm-season preference appears in the raw fields (7 of 16 May–October episodes shed versus 1 of 12 November–April, p = 0.088); after de-seasonalizing, upper-ocean heat content adds only marginal information (p = 0.15–0.30). Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-330db00bea/outputs/episode-shedding-vs-not.png`.
- **Important bound on that split:** 19 of the 20 non-shedding episodes still contain a detached SSH anomaly of at least core size for ≥10 d, and the 8/28 label shifts to 11/28 (±20 d window) or 15/28 (±30 d), so part of the "shedding efficiency" signal measures core longevity and date convention rather than detachment itself. Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-1c6bc9feb4/outputs/separate-detached-bodies.png`.

For the five eddies both lists contain, the water-mass formation date precedes the matching SSH event date by 56–191 d, when the ridge is still at 26–28 °N, whereas the SSH event date sits on a collapsed ridge (22.2 ± 1.3 °N): the two lists date the same eddy at opposite ends of one retraction cycle.

## 4. Why published estimates of the separation interval differ

Published values retrieved (abstract level only; node B1.2): shedding ≈1.1–1.6 events yr⁻¹ and mean intervals ≈8–11 months — Vukovich (1995) 11 ± 3 months (1972–1993, only rings >250 km diameter, modes at 9 and 14 months, range 6.0–17 months); Vukovich (2012) ~11 months pre-2001 versus ~9 months for 2001–2010 (16 rings in that decade versus 11 in each of the two previous); Dukhovskoy et al. (2015) 8 ± 1.8 months (1993–2010); Sturges & Leben (2000) 34 ring formations since July 1973 with interval peaks at 6 and 11 months; Leben (2005) tracking the 17-cm SSH contour; Lugo-Fernández (2007) and Lugo-Fernández & Leben (2010) 16 events each; Hall & Leben (2016) 28–30 events over 1993–2012 with pre-altimetry dates accurate only to ~±1.5 months. Saved figure: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/literature-d3b879bfac/outputs/published-lce-separation-interval-estimates.png`. Authors themselves document the disagreement (Sturges 1994: two earlier papers "used similar data but obtained remarkably different results for the primary rate of ring shedding"; Dukhovskoy et al. 2015: causes "not obvious").

What this analysis can say, component by component (node B1.4, corrected and challenged at node B1.5):

| region | corpus has no regional contrast independent of method | no | only bounded jointly with period |
| eddy identity / one-count rule | the literal named criteria give 24 detections (mean 3.5 months) and 17 with a >250 km size filter (4.1 months); a deep-retreat reading of the same 17-cm contour string gives 3 events (18.0 months) | yes, as a sensitivity | the missing rule is the largest single lever, but it is reconstructed, not read from the papers |

Saved figures: `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/statistics-771786ea98/outputs/lce-interval-spread-decomposition.png` and `/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q23/attempt-1791193824248841969-7237d69e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q23--d75a96a2504e/agents/ocean-process-20a82c7d32/outputs/lc-criterion-matched-17cm-vs-250km.png`.

**Conclusion, stated no more strongly than the evidence.** The results are *consistent with* published interval differences arising largely from what each study counts as a separation and from which count it feeds into its mean — the same fixed record spans the whole published range and beyond (3.5–20 months), the identical eddy is dated 56–191 d apart by two conventions, and a nominal "17-cm contour" criterion yields 3, 17 or 24 events depending on the unstated identity rule. But the tree did **not** separate that counting effect from a GLORYS12-specific eddy census: with one model record and no altimetry, the alternative that the published algorithms are mutually consistent and that it is this record's eddy census that differs is equally compatible with the evidence, arguably better. The safe statement is that **definitional sensitivity is large and the attribution is not identified**, that record-length sampling error alone is of the same size as the published spread, and that period/regime and region cannot be separated here. Do not read this as "GLORYS12 reproduces the published 8–11 month means" — that conclusion is only reachable post hoc, by choosing variants whose shedding rate matches the published band.

## 5. Key uncertainties that this record cannot settle

1. **No velocity fields.** No closed-contour, vorticity or Okubo–Weiss (FTLE) test is possible, so "detached ring" versus "Loop Current lobe" cannot be closed — the single closest call (2014-04-04, 86 % of ring size at 50 m) and the possible lobe character of the four "extra" joint bodies remain open.
2. **No independent altimetry.** The census-versus-convention question (does a GLORYS12-specific eddy census exist?) is not testable; acquiring altimetry was outside the sources named for this task.
3. **Published catalogues only at abstract level** (search_only mode; per-event tables and algorithm descriptions were not readable). The criterion-matched residual is therefore a null about reconstructions, not about the published algorithms; per-study attribution requires those tables.
4. **One model record and hand-set thresholds.** The amplitude cut (50 versus 45 versus 40 m) is decisive for the margin cases — including the 2011-04-04 event and the entire 2013–2014 exclusion — and the count varies 7–19 over a defensible grid.
5. **Right-censoring** at 2017-12-31 (see §2.5).

# Loop Current eddy separation in GLORYS12 (2011–2017), and why published interval estimates disagree

## Summary

Published estimates of Loop Current (LC) eddy shedding intervals span roughly 3–17 months. Working from the supplied GLORYS12 daily SSH/temperature/salinity, I identified the separation events and then reproduced the published disagreement **on a single dataset, single grid, single 7-year window** by varying only the *definition* of "separation". Mean intervals range from **4.1 to 11.3 months** across five defensible definitions, and restricting the record window alone moves the answer from **6.7 to 18.2 months**.

The dominant physical cause is that **8 of 16 contour pinch-offs (50%) reattach to the LC within 30 days**. Counting those transients as separations halves the mean interval. An independent recent study reports 58% reattachment from altimetry. A real but smaller residual remains: GLORYS12 sheds 0.86 sustained eddies/yr against 1.2–1.6 yr⁻¹ in the observational literature.

## Method

**Field.** GLORYS12V1 (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`), daily 1/12°, Gulf of Mexico 98–80°W / 18–31°N, 2557 days.

A first attempt followed the observational literature literally and thresholded the **sea-surface-height anomaly** (SSH minus the 2011–2017 time mean) at 17 cm. That fails on this model field: the time-mean SSH is itself highest in the Yucatan Channel (0.42 m), so subtracting it removes the very feature that roots the LC at the inflow. The contour shattered into drifting blobs and the "LC absent" state was falsely diagnosed on 22–60% of days. The operational Loop Current Index products in fact publish SSH with the **spatial mean removed**, not a climatological anomaly; that convention is used here, with threshold τ = 0.25 m (stable for τ ∈ 0.20–0.30 m).

**Detection.** Each day, cells with η′ ≥ τ are 8-connected-labelled. The LC is the component rooted in the Yucatan Channel inflow box that is not centred west of 89.5°W — the geographic guard that prevents the LC/eddy identity swapping the moment a ring pinches off. Eddies are the remaining components inside the Gulf of ≥25×10³ km², ≥0.15 m amplitude, ≤250×10³ km².

## Results

### Separation events and dates

| Definition | n | mean interval | SD | range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **E1** any contour pinch-off | 16 | 4.06 mo | 105 d | 27–408 d |
| **E2** sustained (no reattachment in 30 d, life ≥90 d, drifts W of 90°W) | 6 | 11.31 mo | 252 d | 106–766 d |
| **E3** major ring (E2 + ≥70×10³ km²) | 2 | 10.48 mo | — | — |
| **R1** any LC retreat below 25°N | 18 | 4.75 mo | 151 d | 14–570 d |
| **R2** sustained retreat (≥30 d retracted) | 10 | 8.36 mo | 155 d | 73–570 d |

**Sustained separations:** 2011-07-16, 2011-10-30, 2012-05-30, 2013-03-22, 2015-04-27, 2016-04-01.

### State of the LC before each separation

Every sustained separation is preceded by a prolonged, deep northward intrusion. Over the 150 days before each event: peak northern extent **26.8–28.3°N** (median 27.5°N, i.e. 0.6–1.7° beyond the 26.5°N threshold); the LC is above threshold on **25–81%** of days, with a longest *continuous* extended spell of **27–83 days** (median 36); separation follows the peak intrusion by **1–109 days** (median 66). The separation is the end state of a long-lived maximum-penetration LC, not a response to a brief surge. The least-extended precursor (2013-03-22, extended only 25% of days) also produced the smallest ring.

### Validation

Two independent checks: (i) all 16 splits were reviewed panel-by-panel (`outputs/validate_splits.png`); (ii) the detected rings carry warm salty Caribbean water — the 20 °C isotherm deepens **+100 to +140 m**, SSS rises **+0.05 to +0.15**, and the anomaly grows over the first 1–3 months. A contour artefact would carry no such subsurface signal.

## Why published estimates differ

1. **Definition is the largest single lever** (factor 2.8 in mean interval on one dataset). The E1/E2 gap is entirely the reattachment and lifetime criteria.
2. **Temporal smoothing** (a proxy for the temporal resolution a study works at): a 1-day vs 21-day running median moves the retreat count 18 → 13 and the mean interval 4.75 → 6.70 months. Weekly- or monthly-averaged fields are systematically smoother and see fewer, longer intervals.
3. **Record window**: the same 7 years sub-sampled gives 6.73 mo (2011–2013) vs 18.17 mo (2013–2017). With 2–4 events per window the mean is dominated by whichever single long gap falls inside it. The record contains a **766-day gap with no sustained separation** (2013-03 → 2015-04) that alone drags any window containing it upward.
4. **Contour threshold**: τ from 0.20 → 0.30 m raises the pinch-off count 15 → 25 while the sustained count stays 5–6.
5. **A genuine residual**: GLORYS12 sheds 0.86 sustained eddies/yr vs 1.2–1.6 yr⁻¹ observed — a factor 1.4–1.9 model deficit, smaller than and partly masked by the definitional spread.

## Blockers and limitations (honest)

- **The literature numbers are from search snippets only.** The policy for this task was `search_only`, so full texts could not be retrieved and each study's exact algorithm could not be read. Fig. 4 compares my *implementations* of the definitions against published *headline numbers*, not a line-by-line reproduction.
- **GLORYS12 is a model, not observations.** These are model events; they will not match altimetry-derived catalogues day for day.
- **The reanalysis under-sheds** (0.86 vs 1.2–1.6 yr⁻¹). Absolute intervals should be read as "what this field yields under definition X", not as a new observational estimate.
- **No independent observational event list was available** for date-by-date validation; validation rests on the internal T/S signature and visual review.
- During development the default spatial smoother differed between the notebook/figures (3-cell half-width) and the tables (2-cell), giving 17 vs 16 splits; this was found and unified to 2. An earlier "consecutive extended days before the event" diagnostic returned 0 for all events by construction and was replaced with the longest extended spell in the preceding 150 days. Both are documented in the notebook.

**FINAL RESEARCH REPORT — Loop Current Eddy Separation Events in the Gulf of Mexico (GLORYS12, 2011–2017)**

## Data & Method
- Data used (read-only): GLORYS12V1 daily fields, Gulf of Mexico bbox [98°W–80°W, 18–31°N], 2011-01-01 to 2017-12-31 (2557 days, 0.083° grid):
  - /inputs/2/zos — sea surface height (primary detector)
  - /inputs/0/thetao — temperature (used at ~92 m as a cross-check)
  - /inputs/1/so — salinity (available; not required by final detection)
- Primary metric: daily Loop Current (LC) northward extension = northernmost latitude of the 0.20 m SSH contour within the deep eastern Gulf box (91°W–84°W, 22–31°N), 5–7-day smoothed.
- Separation detection: maximal northward extension (>28.3°N) followed by rapid retraction below 26.8°N (classic extension–retraction / Leben–Vukovich-style cycle); events <120 d apart merged into one dynamical cycle.
- Independent corroboration: detached anticyclonic-ring detection (closed SSH>0.40 m regions centred west of 89.5°W not touching the eastern boundary).

## Results

### 1. Separation events, dates and intervals (table1_separation_events.csv, fig2_lc_events.png)
| # | Separation (peak) date | LC peak extension (°N) | Days extended before | Interval (d) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2011-09-03 | 29.5 | 7 | — |
| 2 | 2012-06-22 | 30.5 | 9 | 293 |
| 3 | 2013-09-18 | 28.6 | 9 | 453 |
| 4 | 2014-09-24 | 29.8 | 78 | 371 |
| 5 | 2015-10-23 | 30.6 | 304 | 394 |
| 6 | 2016-04-17 | 28.7 | 4 | 177 |
| 7 | 2016-10-16 | 30.4 | 13 | 182 |
| 8 | 2017-10-05 | 30.3 | 14 | 354 |

- **8 separation events over ~6.1 years → mean interval 318 d ≈ 1.15 events/yr** (median 354 d; range 177–453 d).
- Ring-detection episodes (13, orange shading in fig2) coincide with the major events (2011, 2013, 2015, 2016), corroborating the SSH-extent detector.

### 2. State of the LC before each separation (table1, fig2)
- Every event was preceded by a strongly extended LC (peak 28.6–30.6°N), with the LC at ~26.9–28.3°N just 10 days prior — i.e. the LC was never retracted immediately before shedding; separation followed maximal extension.
- Two regimes: short-primed events (2011, 2012, 2013, 2016-04, 2016-10, 2017; <15 d extended) and one long-resident event (2015-10; 304 d extended).

### 3. Why published separation-interval estimates differ (fig3_sensitivity.png, table2_summary.csv)
Applying different defensible event definitions to the same data:
| Trigger >X°N | Retract <Y°N | # events | Mean interval (d) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 29.0 | 25.8 | 4 | 741 |
| 28.5 | 25.8 | 5 | 556 |
| 27.5 | 25.8 | 8 | 318 |
| 27.5 | 26.8 | 18 | 142 |
| 27.5 | 27.3 | 28 | 91 |

Event counts span 4–28 and mean intervals span 91–741 days purely from threshold choice. Causes:
1. Definition of "separation": strict (only full ring detachment, 4–8 events) vs loose (every extension–retraction cycle, up to 28 events) → up to 7× rate difference.
2. Short/unequal records: intervals are intrinsically irregular (177–453 d), so short windows yield different averages.
3. Detection variable/metric: SSH-contour extent vs closed-ring counting vs 17°C-isotherm position select non-identical event sets (the 17°C-at-92 m northernmost-extent proxy proved saturated here).

## Limitations / missing evidence (honest statement)
- No literature-search tool or reference papers were supplied, so published numeric estimates could not be directly cited or compared; the "why estimates differ" conclusion is derived from my own definitional sensitivity experiment, NOT from re-analysis of those papers.
- Detection is threshold-sensitive and GLORYS12 is a reanalysis (model), not observations; exact dates carry ±days uncertainty.
- The 0.20 m SSH contour can be contaminated by shelf/coastal highs; mitigated by restricting to the deep eastern Gulf, but some ambiguity remains.
- Salinity (/inputs/1/so) was available but not needed by the final detector; LC-water (S>36.5) identification remains a possible refinement.
- 2011-01-01 is the record start, so event 1 has no computable preceding interval.

## Artifacts saved under /workspace/outputs
- fig1_lc_proxy.png — LC northern-extent proxies (single transect)
- fig2_lc_events.png — LC extension time series with ring episodes (shaded) and the 8 separation events (red)
- fig3_sensitivity.png — event count vs threshold definition
- table1_separation_events.csv — event dates, pre-separation LC state, intervals
- table2_summary.csv — headline statistics

**Bottom line:** Using GLORYS12 (2011–2017), I identify 8 LC eddy-separation events (mean interval ≈318 d, ~1.15/yr; range 177–453 d), each preceded by a strongly extended LC. Published estimates differ chiefly because "a separation event" is defined inconsistently (strict ring detachment vs every retraction cycle), because records are short relative to the highly irregular ~6–15-month interval, and because different metrics (SSH extent, closed rings, 17°C isotherm) select overlapping but non-identical event sets.

## Summary


**Data basis.** The three supplied directories are GLORYS12V1 daily-mean fields (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m` v202311): salinity `so`, temperature `thetao` (time × 40 levels, 0.49–1941.9 m) and sea surface height `zos`, on a 1/12° regular grid over 18–31°N, 98–80°W, 2011-01-01 to 2017-12-31, 2,557 days with no missing day. There are **no velocity fields, no river discharge, no winds and no independent salinity observations**. The archive resolves the Louisiana–Texas shelf with 13–24 cells between the coast and the 200-m isobath and the water column with 18 levels above 50 m; the 2011–2017 shelf-mean surface salinity is 31.7 psu against 36.2 psu in the deep Gulf (see `glorys12-gom-domain-resolution-and-signal.png`).

**How much.** There is no defensible *net* export number in these files. What can be defended, with conventions attached:

- *Standing stocks.* With one reference-free convention (top-10 m freshwater inside patches fresher than 35.5 psu, the model's collapsed shoreline step excluded): **94.3 km³ on the northern shelf and 19.6 km³ offshore, i.e. about 0.21 (defensible range 0.14–0.30) of the shelf stock appears as low-salinity surface water offshore**. If the shoreline-step cells are kept the same convention gives 152.6 km³ and 0.13; with a far-field 36.245 psu reference and the step excluded it gives 120.5 / 33.5 km³ and 0.28. The earlier headline "296 ± 67 km³ shelf, 48.5 km³ offshore, ratio 0.16" was **corrected**: the offshore residual and the ratio are not defensible as stated (they are near-cancellations whose reference-salinity sensitivity, 34 km³ per 0.1 psu, is 70 % of their own value), while the shelf stock survives in sign and order of magnitude.
- *Flux across the shelf break.* Only SSH-derived geostrophy is available. The upper 0–50 m exports the freshwater anomaly offshore at about **+155 km³/yr** (top 10 m +107 km³/yr) while 50–200 m returns about −194 km³/yr, giving a full-depth net of −38.6 km³/yr that is a ~1 % residual of a ±1,690 km³/yr two-way exchange and therefore at the noise floor; the absolute value carries roughly ±50 % sensitivity to the SSH-gradient scale and the implied net volume transport (+2.16 Sv) is physically implausible. The exporting sectors are Louisiana–Mississippi (+54.7) and Alabama–north-Florida (+86.0 km³/yr); Texas–west Louisiana (−29.1) and west Florida (−150.2) import.
- *Independent check.* The northern shelf's freshwater inventory requires an autumn removal of **190–305 (mean 253) km³/yr**, of which the upper-layer geostrophic export can account for at most about 60 % — the remaining term is not in the supplied data (wind-driven Ekman transport is not supplied).

**When.** The offshore expression is a **summer** phenomenon: the 0–10 m offshore layer peaks in July–August (86.0 km³ JJA vs 30.3 km³ DJF; monthly maximum 96.7 km³ in August), the freshest layer descends through the year (0–10 m in July–August, 10–30 m in September, 30–50 m in October, 50–100 m in April), and the northern shelf's own surface stock peaks in June–July, one to two months before the offshore surface maximum. A separate basin-wide 50–100 m freshening peaking in February exists and is robust to reference choice, but it is a water-mass/heave signature of the deep basin, not a shelf-export signature (below).

**Where.** Offshore low-salinity water concentrates between **26–29°N, 94–86°W in the northern deep Gulf and along the Louisiana–Alabama–north-Florida shelf break**; the western Gulf and Sigsbee basin stay net salty. Geostrophic export is carried by the LA–MS and AL–nFL breaks in July–September. The deep eastern basin's 50–100 m freshwater excess is a different, non-river signal.

**Which circulation features carry it — not established.** The Loop Current and its rings are the only plausible large-scale carriers present in the fields, but every discriminating test is null or negative: deep-Gulf fresh anomalies relate only weakly to Loop Current extent and ring area (daily r = +0.24, circular-shift p = 0.22), occur about 40 % *less* often over anticyclonic SSH than chance, show no advective consistency with SSH-derived flow (r = +0.04) and no net centroid displacement; the classical "Loop Current extension → ring separation → westward transport" sequence occurs **once in 2 557 days** against 0.81 expected by chance; ring separations are followed by deep-Gulf freshening in 2 of 6 cases where 2.9 are expected; and the export shows no relation to eddy kinetic energy (R² = 0.000–0.060), with more export in the *lowest*-EKE thirds of months. The export is organised at scales below ~150 km, ~65 % of the upper-layer export is transient rather than a steady current, its variability is set predominantly by the offshore-directed geostrophic flow rather than by the arrival of fresh water, and the best sub-monthly predictor is the plume/isohaline front position rather than any eddy metric. The only positive Loop-Current signal is positional and signed: a more northward Loop Current axis accompanies higher AL–nFL export at daily to intra-annual scales (r = +0.244, p = 0.007), which is not multiplicity-robust.

**How much of it is river water.** In the northern Gulf, **identifiable river/plume water reaches offshore only in the upper ~30 m and only from June to October**; the 30–100 m bands carry essentially none in any month. In June–September, 95 % of the shelf-break 0–10 m freshwater excess and 90 % of the northern-fan 0–10 m excess sits in water fresher than 35.5 psu; annually 66 % (June–September 67 %) of the northern group's reported offshore excess has a river/plume water-mass signature. By contrast, of the ~90 km³/yr of "offshore freshwater" in the deep eastern basin only ~4–10 km³ (5–10 %) has such a signature; the rest is Caribbean/Loop Current water mass plus heave read against a single deep reference box.

**Limits from the missing discharge and winds** (detail in §7): without discharge the timing and magnitude of the source cannot be tested, the autumn removal cannot be partitioned between lateral export and evaporation, and "river water" can only be inferred from a salinity threshold and T–S matching inside one assimilated model; without winds the leading published cross-shelf mechanism (Ekman transport) cannot be evaluated at all, and 42–48 % of the daily flux variance — the sub-monthly band — remains a diagnosed gap, not a null result.

---

## 1. What the supplied fields can and cannot support

GLORYS12 here resolves the shelf-to-basin freshwater contrast (mean shelf SSS 31.7 vs 36.2 psu in the deep Gulf; minimum daily SSS 5.1 near 30.2°N, 89.6°W) and a realistic Loop Current surface jet (max 1.21 m/s at 21.0°N, 86.3°W), but the archive contains **no uo/vo**, so no transport can be measured, only inferred from SSH geostrophy (which constrains the across-shelf component worst), and no model-independent check of salinity bias is possible. The 2000-m request cap also truncates the deepest ~1,000–2,000 m.

Reference figure: `glorys12-gom-domain-resolution-and-signal.png` (B2).
Saved at /import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q24/attempt-1791198594223512338-e877be18/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q24--7fc5053e9496/agents/ocean-process-4cda99e891/outputs/glorys12-gom-domain-resolution-and-signal.png

A separate check found that 389–648 of the shelf cells sit on the model's collapsed shoreline step (bottom-depth proxy ≤ 7.93 m; ~14–18 % of shelf area). Their sub-15 psu days are genuine model river water — concentrated in February–June at the Mississippi/Atchafalaya/Mississippi-Sound coasts and surface-fresher than their own bottom by 4.3 psu — but 63 % of them are within two levels of the grid minimum, so they describe a coastline step rather than a resolved offshore plume. Excluding that band lowers the shelf freshwater content by roughly 24–38 %, which is larger than any temporal uncertainty (annual-mean standard error 2.5 km³ shelf, 1.3 km³ offshore) and moves the headline ratio more than any other choice (0.13 ↔ 0.21 ↔ 0.28).

## 2. How much low-salinity water, and how much of it is offshore

**Stocks (corrected chain).** The first measurement reported 296 ± 67 km³ of shelf freshwater excess (full column, relative to a deep-Gulf reference) and 48.5 km³ in the offshore top 10 m, ratio ≈ 0.16, with a July–August offshore maximum and a 2011–2012-versus-2016–2017 decline. The robustness node **corrected** this: the 296 km³ survives in sign and order of magnitude (reproduced exactly at 295.55 km³, range 148–367 km³ across reference treatments and 236–319 km³ across domain variants, but with a 44.6 km³ per 0.1 psu reference sensitivity), the **offshore 48.5 km³ and the 0.16 ratio do not survive** (the offshore excess is a near-cancellation of a 12,333 km³ surface volume; three deep-water reference boxes supplied by the data themselves give −26.3, +14.1 and +48.4 km³; the break-even reference 36.103 psu lies inside the far-field surface salinity range), the July–August maximum survives, and the 2011–2012 versus 2016–2017 difference **does not** (it measures the difference in background trends between the reference box and the domain; with a time-varying reference the trend is −0.03 km³/yr, R² ≈ 0). The reconciliation node then put shelf and offshore on one reference-free footing and, excluding the collapsed shoreline step, reported **shelf 94.3 km³ and offshore 19.6 km³, ratio 0.208**, with the included-step variant 152.6 km³ and 0.129, and a far-field-reference variant 120.5 / 33.5 km³ and 0.278; the seasonal range of that ratio is ≈0.05 (December–January) to ≈0.38 (August). These numbers are **stocks, not exports**, and different conventions must not be averaged.

Reference figures: `gom-reconciled-shelf-offshore-freshwater.png` (B4.4), `gom_lowsalinity_maps.png` and `gom_lowsalinity_timeseries.png` (B4).

**Flux (bounded, geostrophic only).** Across the 200-m isobath (2,762 km section, 318 faces, 0–200 m): net cross-break volume transport +2.16 Sv offshore as a residual of ±10.46/−8.30 Sv; the deviatoric-velocity freshwater flux is **−38.6 km³/yr (range −17 to −86)**, i.e. net *onshore*, and it is a ~1 % residual of a **±1,690 km³/yr** two-way exchange of the same anomaly. The physically usable part is the upper layer: **0–50 m +155 km³/yr offshore (+107 km³/yr in the top 10 m)**, with 50–200 m returning −194 km³/yr; LA–MS +54.7 and AL–nFL +86.0 export, TX–wLA −29.1 and west Florida −150.2 import, and the LA–MS/AL–nFL export peaks in July–September. The naive reference-dependent flux (+266 vs −50 km³/yr) must not be quoted. **Conclusion (conditional): on this evidence the defensible export-like number is the upper-layer geostrophic anomaly flux of order 10² km³/yr offshore in July–September on the LA–MS and AL–nFL breaks; a net export of shelf freshwater cannot be demonstrated.**

**Independent storage check.** The shelf inventory requires removing 190–305 (mean 253) km³/yr in autumn (up to 48.6 km³ in October). The geostrophic upper layer supplies at most ~60 % of it. The missing term is consistent with wind-driven Ekman export or with evaporation, neither of which is in the supplied data.

## 3. When and where the offshore signal appears

- **Season and depth.** Offshore 0–10 m freshwater excess: 86.0 km³ in JJA vs 30.3 km³ in DJF, monthly maximum 96.7 km³ (August), minimum 26.7 km³ (December). The freshest layer descends through the year (0–10 m July–August, 10–30 m September, 30–50 m October, 50–100 m April–May). The northern shelf's own 0–10 m stock peaks in June–July, giving a one- to two-month shelf-to-offshore lag. Below 100 m the anomaly is a persistent salty bias against the deep reference and is not usable as freshwater.
- **Northern versus deep eastern Gulf.** The aggregated regional pass shows the 50–100 m "winter maximum" is an **eastern-basin standing feature**: `basin_E` (east of 86°W, south of 26°N) holds 66.6 / 70.9 / 65.7 / 48.1 km³ in DJF/MAM/JJA/SON, i.e. ~100 % of the deep basin's total in that band, and is positive in all twelve months (42.0–76.5 km³). The same layer's seasonal oscillation is nevertheless real and robust: with four references that cannot alias the answer it peaks in **February** and the December–May minus June–November contrast is **+45 km³** (against +18.7 km³ with the daily reference profile), the B4.3 deep-basin reference having *understated* it by a factor ~2.4 and delayed its apparent peak. It is shared between slope and basin with nearly equal salinity amplitude per unit volume, so it is a **basin-wide freshening, not a preferentially slope-band export signature**, and the summer half of the published "summer-and-winter subsurface export" picture is not supported (the 50–100 m layer is at its minimum in summer).
- **Locations.** Offshore freshening is concentrated at 26–29°N, 94–86°W and along the Louisiana–Alabama–Florida shelf break; the western Gulf and Sigsbee basin remain net salty. Shelf-to-deep co-variabilities (uncorrected, standing stocks only) are modest: AL–nFL shelf with the northern fan (r = +0.42), LA–MS with `basin_E` (+0.30 to +0.55), TX–wLA with Sigsbee/west basin (+0.31 to +0.35), west Florida anti-correlated with `basin_E` (−0.46).
- **Episode years (contested).** GLORYS12 marks 2011 as enhanced (the 7-year June–September surface maximum, 119.5 km³), 2015 as enhanced at depth only, and 2014 as not enhanced at any band, while 2012 — not a published episode year — matches or exceeds 2011. The statistical node, however, found the year-to-year offshore contrast not distinguishable from zero under three of four reference treatments, so the model's event years should be treated as **conditional on the reference choice** and not as a validated reproduction of the published 2011/2014/2015 episodes.
