## 4. Which circulation features carry it

The fields contain the two candidate structures — a persistent anticyclonic Loop Current occupying the eastern Gulf and a dense population of detached anticyclonic rings (4,229 closed-contour detections with SLA ≥ 0.15 m and area ≥ 1,500 km² west of 88.5°W over 2,557 days) — and deep-Gulf monthly-mean surface geostrophic speeds are strong (50th/90th/99th percentiles 0.18/0.53/1.09 m/s). So the fields *can* carry shelf water offshore. Whether they *do* was tested five ways, and the answer is negative or unresolved:

| Test | Result | Bearing on attribution |
|---|---|---|
| Lag/coincidence of deep-Gulf freshening with Loop Current extent and ring area | daily r = +0.24 (circular-shift p = 0.22); monthly +0.27 at lag 0; ring-area maximum only at 3–4 months, and the ring composite has the opposite sign to the ring lag-correlation | weak, not robust |
| Advective consistency | monthly surface salinity tendency vs SSH-derived advection r = +0.04; fresh-anomaly centroid no net displacement (wander 118 km/month, drift +3 km east, −1 km south) | against geostrophic advection control |
| Event sequence (Loop Current extension → ring separation → westward freshwater transport) | 10 extensions, 6 separations; separation → deep-Gulf freshening in 2/6 cases vs 2.9 expected (p = 0.89); the full three-step sequence once in 2,557 days vs 0.81 expected (p = 0.53); fresh anomalies preferentially on cyclonic SSH (61.4 % of area on SLA < 0) | classical mechanism unsupported; only the extension → separation step remains plausible (4/10, p ≈ 0.13–0.21) |
| Export vs eddy kinetic energy | monthly transient-flux anomalies unrelated to sector EKE or SSH anomaly at lags −3…+3 months (all \|r\| ≤ 0.27); LA–MS exports 47 km³/yr more in the lowest-EKE third of months; deep-basin EKE explains R² = 0.000–0.060 | contradicts eddy-carried export |
| Scale and factor decomposition | small-scale (<150 km) SSH gradient reproduces r = 0.77–0.89 of the transient flux; at daily resolution the sub-monthly meander energy has the *wrong* sign (R² = 0.024–0.037) and 42–48 % of daily flux variance lies below 31 days; flow factor dominates the transient export variance (72.1 % LA–MS, 52.4 % AL–nFL; freshwater-arrival factor 2.6 / 7.4 %) | the export is organised by fine-scale SSH structure and by the flow, not by advective arrival of fresh water |

What *does* survive is weaker and more structural: a standing spatial co-location between the export and the adjacent eddy field within each exporting sector (AL–nFL r = +0.55 to +0.66 for the time-mean part), which is degenerate with the analysis because EKE and the geostrophic flux are both built from the same SSH; a plume/delta **spatial precondition** (56.4 % of LA–MS + AL–nFL export occurs within 100 km of the Mississippi or Atchafalaya mouth, 74.3 % within 200 km) with a one-month lead of outer-shelf surface freshwater over high AL–nFL export months (r = +0.32, p = 0.000); the 34.0-isohaline front as the best sub-monthly predictor; and a signed, positional Loop Current effect (axis 1.64° farther north in high-export AL–nFL months; daily axis-latitude r = +0.244, top-5 % days +0.60σ, LC amplitude +0.78σ) that is not multiplicity-robust. For LA–MS the weak significant relations are the *wrong* sign (stronger LC or higher deep-basin sea level goes with less export).

**Statement of the attribution:** it is *consistent with* a fine-scale/frontal flushing of the northern shelf, spatially preconditioned by the river plume and only weakly steered by Loop Current position; the evidence **does not support** transport by the Loop Current or by its rings/eddies, and for the LA–MS break it contradicts the eddy-variance version of that hypothesis. Because every carrier metric and the flux itself are diagnosed from the same two fields (zos and so), and because wind and sub-surface velocity are absent, this is a failure to demonstrate, not a falsification.

## 5. How much of the offshore low-salinity water is actually river water

This is the strongest constraint on the user's question, and it splits sharply by region and depth.

- **Not river water in the deep eastern basin.** The persistent 50–100 m `basin_E` excess is not river-derived: that layer (18,107 km³) is 25.9–27.8 °C and 36.225–36.334 psu, statistically the same water as the Yucatan Channel inflow at the same depth; matched by density it is 0.012 psu *saltier* than the inflow (−6 km³ instead of +69 km³), water fresher than 35.5 psu occupies 0.09–0.65 % of the layer and carries 0.4–2.8 km³ in total, and the density-matched residual is a near-surface feature (+0.13 psu at 56–66 m, 0.00 at 78 m, −0.04 psu at 92 m). Of the ~90 km³/yr of "offshore freshwater" held by the two eastern-basin bands relative to one deep reference box, only **~4–10 km³ (5–10 %)** has a river/plume water-mass signature; the rest is the Gulf's own water-mass structure (Loop Current water at depth; the evaporatively concentrated western Gulf versus the Caribbean-fed eastern Gulf at the surface).
- **River water in the northern Gulf — but only near the surface and only in summer.** Applied to the northern shelf sectors, shelf-break bands, the northern fan and the 26–29°N/94–86°W box, the fresh-tail test gives: 30–100 m bands carry **zero** water fresher than 35.5 psu in the north in every month, while June–September 0–10 m values are 33.3 km³ on the break bands (31.5 km³, 95 %, in the fresh tail; 40.7 % of band volume in August) and 24.2 km³ in the northern fan (21.7 km³, 90 %; peak August 36.1 → 34.3 km³ with a 33.9 psu tail); 10–30 m attribution drops to 62 % and 44 %. Annually, 93 % of the northern 0–10 m excess and 58 % of the 10–30 m excess sit in the fresh tail; the northern group's 60.9 km³/yr of reported offshore excess contains **40.3 km³/yr (66 %)** with a river/plume signature (June–September: 76.4 of 113.3 km³, 67 %). The northern shelf sectors themselves hold 98 % of their June–September 0–10 m freshwater in water fresher than 35.5 psu with tail-mean salinities of 30–33 psu at the Mississippi/Atchafalaya sectors.
- **Caveats to that fraction.** The 35.5 psu tail also picks up southern-shelf (Campeche) water — the deep SW reference box carries 10.0 km³ of it in its own 0–10 m layer in June–September — so 66 % is an **upper bound for Mississippi-system water specifically**; the robust content is the north-versus-reference *location* contrast. The density-matched test cannot confirm the surface result because northern summer surface water is lighter than any water in either upstream endmember (coverage 0.00–0.19), and its large winter values are a cold fresh winter surface matched to saltier Caribbean water, i.e. a T–S structure difference rather than river water.

## 6. What the literature adds, and what it could not

A metadata/abstract-scope search (no full text was permitted) supports the mechanism set we tested — seasonal reversal of the alongshore wind field, Loop Current and Loop Current eddy interaction at the break, cyclonic Loop Current frontal eddies over the Mississippi Fan slope, storm-driven injection, and a wind-driven cross-shelf plume regime — and the standard analytic conventions: depth-integrated freshwater content as an (S_ref − S)/S_ref deficit with an explicitly chosen reference, off-shelf export as the divergence of the shelf freshwater budget or a flushing time, and plume identification by SSS/tDOC threshold algorithms or manual cataloguing in ocean colour. It also identified the one clear published disagreement we could test — a summer surface-signature plume maximum (da Silva & Castelao 2018) versus a summer-and-winter subsurface export pathway with weak surface expression (Liu et al. 2022) — and published export episodes in 2011, 2014 and 2015 (Otis et al. 2019). **No numeric offshore transport or basin freshwater content was obtainable at abstract scope, and no reference-salinity or cross-section convention could be verified**, so our numbers must not be compared to published magnitudes as if they shared a definition; the regional papers (Schiller et al. 2011; Schiller & Kourafalou 2014; Morey et al. 2002; Androulidakis & Kourafalou 2013; Dinnel & Wiseman 1986; Etter 1983; Hiron et al. 2022) were title-only in the open record. Exa returned HTTP 429 and the OpenAlex daily budget was exhausted, so the search coverage is real but incomplete.

## 7. How the missing river discharge and winds limit these conclusions

1. **No discharge → no source term, no closure, no timing test.** Every "freshwater" number is an anomaly against a chosen salinity reference, not river water. We cannot check whether the model's coastal salinity responds to observed discharge (including the 2011 Mississippi flood), so year-by-year attribution of shelf or basin anomalies to river discharge is not legitimate with these fields. The autumn shelf-inventory requirement (190–305 km³/yr removed) cannot be partitioned between lateral export and net surface evaporation, which is why the geostrophic upper layer can account for "at most ~60 %" and no more precise statement is possible.
2. **No winds → the leading published cross-shelf mechanism is untestable.** The published mechanism set makes wind-driven Ekman transport and the seasonal alongshore wind reversal central; with no wind fields we can neither add that term to the flux nor exclude it as the explanation of the 42–48 % of daily flux variance that lies below 31 days, which remains a **diagnosed gap rather than a null result**. Stronger-than-geostrophic flushing events (storms, frontal passages) are likewise invisible.
3. **No velocity field → geostrophy only, and geometry that flatters it.** The across-shelf component is the one geostrophy constrains worst; the net geostrophic volume transport (+2.16 Sv) is physically implausible and the absolute flux carries ±50 % sensitivity to the SSH-gradient scale, so only signs, patterns and layers — not absolute magnitudes — should be used. Part of the apparent export–eddy co-location is built in, because EKE and the geostrophic velocity are both derived from `zos`.
4. **No independent observations → model bias unquantifiable.** Salinity bias, assimilation increments and the collapsed coastal geometry are bounded only internally, and "river water" is inferred from T–S geometry in one data-assimilated product; a real plume can only be recognised by its freshness, not by any tracer.
5. **Sampling.** 84 monthly samples (n_eff ≈ 40–130 for daily series) and a 7-year record give low power for event statistics (only 6 ring separations) and leave the shelf residence-versus-export split weakly constrained; sub-monthly signals within each month's ~6 days of sampling are not resolved.

## 8. Unresolved uncertainties and contradictions that remain

- The shelf stock is convention-dependent (94.3 to 296 km³ across defensible definitions) and the offshore/shelf ratio is only order-of-magnitude (0.14–0.30, with the sign of some variants not robust).
- 2011–2012 versus 2016–2017 offshore contrast: supported by one reference treatment, not by the others; the model's salinification trend (+0.035 psu/yr in the offshore top 10 m) could be physical, model drift or an assimilation artefact, and cannot be settled with these fields.
- The river-water fraction of the northern offshore excess (66 %) is an upper bound because the salinity threshold also admits southern-shelf water.
- The 50–100 m basin-wide February freshening is robust as a seasonal oscillation but its interpretation as a pathway remains open; only a velocity or tracer dataset can turn any of these patterns into a pathway.
- The mechanism that actually organises the export at sub-150-km scales, and the sub-monthly band generally, is not identified by any supplied variable.

    - **B5.1 [completed]** Do deep-Gulf fresh anomalies coincide with, lag, or occur independently of the Loop Current and rings? → Only weakly and mostly without lead or lag (daily r = +0.24, circular-shift p = 0.22; monthly +0.27 at lag 0); fresh anomalies sit ~40 % less often over anticyclonic SSH than chance; the monthly salinity tendency is uncorrelated with SSH-derived advection (r = +0.04); no net centroid displacement; a carrying mechanism is **not** established; one test (centroid-displacement direction) failed numerically.

    - **B5.2 [completed]** Does the classical Loop Current extension → ring separation → westward transport sequence occur? → All three elements exist as discrete events (10 extensions with dates; 6 separations at 88.6–90.1°W, 5 of 6 drifting westward at ~−2.4 km/day; 16 freshening events, none in 2015 or 2017) but the ordering test fails: separation → freshening in 2/6 cases vs 2.9 expected (p = 0.89), the full three-step sequence once in 2,557 days vs 0.81 expected (p = 0.53), and fresh anomalies sit preferentially on cyclonic SSH (61.4 % of area on SLA < 0). Verdict: unsupported, not decisively refuted (low power, 6 separations); the extension → separation step alone remains plausible.

**Unadopted proposals of possible value if more time or data become available:** full-text verification of published magnitudes and S_ref/cross-section conventions (blocked: acquisition was search-only); wind-driven Ekman cross-shelf transport (blocked: no winds); adding uo/vo for a true three-dimensional flux and budget closure (blocked: not supplied); individual-ring tracking with a looser separation definition, and year-by-year fresh-tail shares (feasible with the supplied fields, not executed here).

# How much northern-Gulf river water reaches the deep Gulf of Mexico?

**Data:** GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1/12°, 40 z-levels (0.49–1941.9 m), 18–31°N / 98–80°W, 2011–2017 (2557 days, complete). Only temperature, salinity and SSH were supplied.

**Deliverables:** `figures/fig01`–`fig10`, `outputs/table1`–`table5` (CSV), `analysis.ipynb` (executed end-to-end, 0 errors), reusable code in `code/` (scratch diagnostics in `code/scratch/`).

## Headline answer

Net freshwater export from the northern-Gulf shelf across the 200 m isobath is **12.9 ± 3 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ (≈ 400 km³ yr⁻¹)**, against a gross exchange of 59.1 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ offshore and 46.2 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ onshore. It is concentrated off Louisiana/Mississippi (4.7 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹) and the Florida Keys (4.0 × 10³), with Texas third (3.0 × 10³) and the central Louisiana shelf smallest (0.5 × 10³).

It arrives in the deep Gulf as a **thin, patchy surface layer, mainly in August**, and it accumulates there as a standing stock that peaks at **583 km³ in August 2011** (the record Mississippi flood year) and declines to a 2017 annual mean of **39 km³**. The median thickness of water fresher than 35 anywhere in the deep Gulf is **zero**; the 99th percentile is 7.9 m.

The measured throughflow and the observed stock are mutually consistent: 12.9 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ over a ~2-month residence time gives 67 km³, matching the observed 2011–2017 mean of ~70 km³.

## When

The deep-Gulf plume has a sharp annual cycle peaking in **August** and vanishing from December to April (monthly climatology of V(S<34.5): Jan 1, Feb 1, Mar 4, Apr 17, May 32, Jun 21, Jul 99, **Aug 363**, Sep 164, Oct 30, Nov 0 km³). The shelf reservoir peaks a month earlier, in **July** (293 km³ versus 177 km³ in December), so the offshore transfer lags the shelf maximum by about a month — a residence-time lag, not a discharge lag.

Interannually the export falls monotonically in the mean: 115.9, 80.1, 53.8, 86.3, 53.4, 60.4, 39.0 km³ for 2011–2017, with August peaks of 583, 423, 427, 355, 379, 248, 179 km³. The deep-Gulf area covered by >1 m of S<35 water falls from 23.8 × 10³ to 13.2 × 10³ km².

## Where

Export is largest off the Mississippi/Atchafalaya delta and the western Florida shelf. In August 2011 the plume appears as a coherent patch of 20–25 m thickness centred near 27.5°N, 89°W, spreading east and southeast along the shelf break. The particle tracking shows the highest densities along the shelf break and the eastern deep Gulf, following the mean cyclonic rim circulation and the Loop Current.

## Which circulation features carry it

**This is where I have to report a largely negative result.** Raw correlations between deep-Gulf plume volume and the Loop Current are modest (Pearson +0.16 for LC area, +0.29 for northward extent, +0.37 for deep-Gulf EKE). But the plume and the Loop Current both have annual cycles, so part of that is shared seasonality. **After removing the seasonal cycle they collapse**: Spearman ρ = −0.00 for LC area and −0.01 for LC northward extent. Deep-Gulf EKE retains only ρ = +0.17. No lagged correlation survives the nominal 95 % level.

So the Loop Current's areal extent does **not** control how much shelf freshwater sits in the deep Gulf. What it does do is *displace* it: the per-cell correlation map shows a coherent negative patch (r = −0.4 to −0.5) at 25–27°N, 86–88°W, exactly where the current intrudes — when the LC extends, salty Caribbean water replaces fresh shelf water there. Lagrangian tracking agrees: **18 % of shelf-break water is in the deep Gulf within 30 days**, and eddy cores (Okubo–Weiss) are concentrated along the LC path and into the Florida Straits.

The honest reading is that export is set by shelf buoyancy and the wind, which I do not have — not by the LC.

## The limitation that shaped the analysis

The whole basin becomes saltier through the record: deep-Gulf mean surface salinity rises monotonically from 36.025 (2011) to 36.242 (2017), +0.036 psu yr⁻¹. Because the deep Gulf straddles any fixed reference near 36, freshwater content against such a reference is dominated by that drift — my first calculation gave a spurious monotonic decline from 139 to 19 km³. The Yucatán inflow reference drifts *more* (+0.32 psu), so re-referencing does not fix it.

I therefore estimated the volume-weighted domain-mean salinity profile as a common mode and removed its temporal anomaly. The de-drifted deep-Gulf salinity becomes flat (36.1396 → 36.1402) while genuine shelf variability survives. **All trend statements rest on this.** Part of the drift is plausibly post-2011-flood recovery and part is model/assimilation drift; with no discharge data these cannot be separated — which is itself the answer to the limitation question.

Three further caveats:
- **No river discharge** means the freshwater *content* is measurable but the attribution to a named river is not. The 2011 anomaly is consistent with the record Mississippi flood; it is not proof of it.
- **No winds** means the geostrophic velocity is very weak over the shallow shelf, where the balance is wind- and buoyancy-driven. The inner-shelf tracking beached most particles within weeks; only the shelf-break experiment is defensible, and roughly half its particles still beach within a year — an artefact that makes the 18 % deep-Gulf arrival a *lower* bound.
- **Geostrophic bias**: net volume transport across the full 200 m isobath is 2.75 Sv where it should be ~0.02 Sv. Restricted to the northern Gulf section the balance is much better (net 0.39 Sv against 26.8/26.4 Sv gross, 1.5 % imbalance), implying a section-mean velocity error of ~0.04 cm s⁻¹ and a freshwater error of order 5 × 10² m³ s⁻¹. That supports the headline number, but the full-isobath 21.8 % imbalance is why I quote ±3 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹ rather than the raw 12.9.

Two further structural notes: the 1000 m isobath number (−154 × 10³ m³ s⁻¹) is **not** a shelf export — the Loop Current and Florida Current cross that isobath, so it measures gyre recirculation; and any freshwater content integrated over the deep Gulf's whole water column (~47 000 km³ against SREF = 36) is dominated by the permanent halocline and says nothing about river water. Only the upper 100–200 m is diagnostic. Content against SREF = 36/36.5/37 gives 65.5/616.5/1976.5 km³, which is why I lead with the reference-free threshold volumes.

# How much northern-Gulf river water is exported offshore into the deep Gulf, when, where, and by which circulation features?

## Data & methods
GLORYS12V1 daily fields for 2011–2017 over the Gulf of Mexico (18–31°N, 98–80°W) were used:
- **Surface salinity (`so`, depth 0.49 m)** — 2557 daily fields (84 monthly files), the core variable.
- **Sea surface height (`zos`)** — 2557 daily fields, used to derive geostrophic currents and eddy (SLA) variance.
- **Surface temperature (`thetao`)** — loaded for context.

A bathymetry proxy was derived from the number of valid depth levels per grid cell (0 = land, increasing = deeper). Regions: **shelf** = 0–200 m (8,658 cells), **deep Gulf** = >500 m (15,856 cells), **northern shelf** band (≥28°N, 3,185 cells). Cell areas account for latitude. "Low-salinity water" (LSW) = S<35.0 (sensitivity: 34.5/34.8/35.2); deep-Gulf background salinity is 36.1.

## Key quantitative results (table1_summary.csv)

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean deep-Gulf LSW area (S<35) | 3.66×10⁵ km² |
| Maximum deep-Gulf LSW area | 1.52×10⁶ km² |
| Mean shelf LSW area | 2.07×10⁶ km² |
| **Mean export fraction** (deep share of all LSW area) | **12.7%** |
| **August mean export fraction** | **28.1%** |
| **Mean deep-Gulf freshwater content, top 5 m** | **~128 km³** (August ~407 km³) |
| corr(deep LSW area, Loop-Current eddy variance) | **r = 0.50** (p ≈ 10⁻¹⁶⁴) |

Threshold sensitivity (table2_threshold_sensitivity.csv) shows the result is robust: export fraction rises smoothly from 11.5% (S<34.5, freshest water) to 17.2% (S<35.2), i.e. the deep Gulf consistently receives ~10–17% of the total low-salinity footprint.

## When — a sharp summer–autumn signal
- **Shelf** LSW area peaks in September–October; **deep-Gulf** LSW area peaks in **August** (mean 9.8×10⁵ km²) and stays high through September.
- Export fraction is ~4% in winter and jumps to **28% in August** (fig1_lsw_timeseries.png).
- **35 of the 50 largest deep-Gulf LSW days were in August**, 13 in September, 2 in October — none in winter. Largest event: **30 Aug 2011** (1.52×10⁶ km²).
- Interannually, export was strongest in **2016** (mean 4.6×10⁵ km²) and 2012, weakest in **2017** (2.6×10⁵ km²) and 2015.

## Where — the Louisiana/Texas shelf edge
Cells with deep-Gulf LSW frequency >30% lie in a tight band at **lon −89.75° to −86.83°W, lat 28.25–29.42°N** (fig2_spatial.png) — the **Mississippi–Atchafalaya delta and Louisiana–Texas shelf margin**, where the river plume meets the shelf break and the northern edge of the Loop Current system.

## Which circulation features
Mean geostrophic speed from the 7-year mean SSH reaches **~1.0 m/s** in the eastern Gulf, tracing the Loop Current. The August salinity-anomaly map overlaid with geostrophic-speed contours (fig3_circulation.png) shows exported fresh water on the northern flank of the Loop Current / its anticyclonic meander. Deep-Gulf LSW area is significantly positively correlated with Loop-Current-region SLA (eddy) variance (**r = 0.50**), both peaking in late summer–early autumn. This is consistent with Loop-Current meanders and cyclonic frontal eddies (plus the seasonal spindown) stripping shelf water offshore during the season of maximum discharge and weakest along-shelf winds.

## Limitations (explicitly missing evidence)
- **No river discharge data**: we can identify *when* and *where* freshwater appears offshore but cannot quantify the discharge source term, the discharge-to-export lag, or the fraction escaping vs. retained on the shelf. The ~128 km³ summer deep-Gulf freshwater content cannot be used for a closed river budget.
- **No wind data**: the invoked mechanisms (wind-driven Ekman transport, frontal eddy shedding) cannot be tested directly; the Loop-Current eddy correlation is suggestive, not causal, and is confounded by the shared seasonal cycle.
- **Subsurface freshwater distribution not analyzed**: export volume is estimated for the top 5 m from a linear salinity-deficit conversion.
- **Coarse 1/12° daily surface grid** does not resolve the inner shelf/estuarine input or the narrowest Mississippi plume filaments.

## Conclusion
Over 2011–2017, GLORYS12 surface fields show low-salinity river water is routinely exported from the northern Gulf shelf into the deep Gulf, but strongly seasonally and spatially focused: ~**13% of the total low-salinity footprint sits in deep water on average, rising to ~28% in August**, equivalent to a mean deep-Gulf freshwater content of **~128 km³ (top 5 m; ~407 km³ in August)**. Export peaks in **August–September**, occurs along the **Louisiana–Texas shelf edge (−90° to −87°W, 28–29.5°N)** off the Mississippi/Atchafalaya delta, and is associated with the **northern flank of the Loop Current and its eddies**, whose variability is significantly correlated with offshore freshwater extent. Without supplied river discharge and winds, the ultimate drivers and a closed freshwater budget cannot be verified — a fundamental limitation.

Original final answer (English)
# Upper-ocean heat available to tropical cyclones in the Gulf of Mexico, June-November 2011-2017 (GLORYS12 daily temperature, salinity, sea surface height)

## Summary

- **The reservoir (quantified).** Over the Gulf of Mexico proper (ocean cells of the supplied 98-80°W / 18-31°N box, excluding its NW-Caribbean corner; 1.70x10^6 km^2) the June-November tropical-cyclone heat potential, TCHP26 = rho cp * integral of (T - 26 °C) dz down to the 26 °C isotherm, is **40.2 kJ cm^-2** (D26 = 45.3 m, SST 28.6 °C) in GLORYS12 daily fields for 2011-2017, i.e. **0.68 ZJ (6.8x10^20 J)** of excess heat above 26 °C. A unit slip of 1000x in the first returned version of this integral (6.8x10^17 J / 0.68 EJ) was **corrected** by the Loop Current attribution node; 0.68 ZJ is the value to use.
- **Structure and season.** The reservoir rises from 26.0 kJ cm^-2 in June to a 54.3-54.7 kJ cm^-2 August-September peak and falls to 18.2 kJ cm^-2 in November. It is deep-water heat: 52.3 kJ cm^-2 in the deep basin (>318 m, 59 % of area) versus 22.5 kJ cm^-2 on the shelves. The largest values are fixed to the Loop Current entrance (seasonal-mean maximum 113.7 kJ cm^-2, D26 124 m, at 21.5°N 85.2°W) and to eddies in the central Gulf (daily maximum 212 kJ cm^-2, D26 169 m, 12 Oct 2011).
- **Available vs present.** About **65 % of that heat (52 % mixed layer + 13 % barrier layer) is in the near-surface warm layer a storm's own mixing reaches directly**, 35 % lies below the isothermal layer, and 96.6 % of the whole reservoir is above 100 m: the practical constraint is stratification, not depth. The barrier-layer share is criterion-fragile (3-21 %), the "65 %" split is robust (52 % in the mixed layer, below-isothermal share 21-29 %).
- **Loop Current and eddy contribution (three different quantities, not one).** Under an explicit SSH-anomaly detection criterion, **33 % (0.22 ZJ)** of the reservoir is enclosed by Loop Current/eddy structures (24 % in the Loop Current proper, 8 % in detached anticyclones), on only 18 % of the area, and structures account for 44 % of the year-to-year variance; across defensible criteria the enclosed share spans **10-44 %**. By water mass, however, **about 98-99 % of the reservoir is the same Caribbean water that enters at the Yucatán Channel** (salinity deficit outside the mask only 0.20, 0.55 %), which makes the water-mass reading nearly tautological. No measurement here separates heat the Loop Current *delivered* from heat that merely arrived with it, and the returns give **no evidence that Loop Current or eddy variability controls the reservoir**.
- **Year-to-year variability and its control (2011-2017).** The June-November basin mean ranges **32.0 kJ cm^-2 (2013) to 46.2 kJ cm^-2 (2015)** (std 4.3, about 11 %), small beside the seasonal cycle (88 % of the daily variance of the basin mean is seasonal, 8 % year-to-year, 4 % synoptic) and beside the within-season spatial spread (about 27 kJ cm^-2). The anomaly is dominated by how deep the >26 °C layer reaches rather than how warm it is (approximately two-thirds versus one-third of the variance; ordering robust, magnitude not resolved at n = 7), is **already present in March-May and inherits 94-111 % of its variance from that state**, and its vertical shape - a surface-to-~450 m coherent anomaly dominated by thermocline heave (SSH response 11-17x the thermal-expansion prediction) - is **compatible with, but does not demonstrate**, an ocean-advection control. Eddy-activity, EKE and stratification indices fail; surface heat flux, wind forcing and Yucatán inflow transport cannot be tested with these three variables.

---

## 1. What was measured, and how strongly the numbers are worded

The literature's working measure of upper-ocean heat available to tropical cyclones is TCHP / ocean heat content relative to 26 °C, the vertical integral of the excess over 26 °C down to the 26 °C isotherm, in kJ cm^-2 with 1 kJ cm^-2 = 10 MJ m^-2 (Leipper & Volgenau 1972; Shay et al. 2000; NOAA/AOML operational product). All data-side results here use that definition, applied to the supplied read-only daily fields (temperature, salinity, sea surface height; yearly directories 2011-2017; 1/12°, 40 levels, 183 days per hurricane season, none missing).

The single most important framing limit: **every magnitude comes from one 1/12° daily-mean reanalysis**, with no independent observation supplied for validation. The model persists 29.5-30 °C water to 110-190 m at the deep end of the Gulf, which cannot be checked here; absolute levels should be read as a model estimate whose **ranking, seasonal cycle and spatial contrast are more trustworthy than its level**. Definition and domain choices, not sampling, set the internal uncertainty (Section 2).

## 2. Magnitude, seasonal cycle, spatial pattern

June-November 2011-2017, Gulf of Mexico proper:

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| TCHP26, basin mean | 40.2 kJ cm^-2 (0.68 ZJ over 1.70x10^6 km^2) |
| D26 / SST / upper-100 m mean T | 45.3 m / 28.6 °C / 26.4 °C |
| deep basin >318 m (59 % of area) | 52.3 kJ cm^-2 (D26 59.3 m) |
| shelves <318 m (41 %) | 22.5 kJ cm^-2 |
| June -> August-September peak -> November | 26.0 -> 54.3-54.7 -> 18.2 kJ cm^-2 |
| seasonal-mean maximum (Yucatán entrance, 21.5°N 85.2°W) | 113.7 kJ cm^-2 (D26 124 m) |
| largest daily value (25.3°N 86.1°W, 12 Oct 2011) | 212 kJ cm^-2 (D26 169 m) |
| yearly June-November means | 32.0 (2013) - 46.2 (2015), std 4.3 |

Climatological seasonal-mean map and the yearly series: `.../agents/ocean-process-a36b62be15/outputs/fig-gom-tchp-climatology.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-a36b62be15/outputs/fig-gom-tchp-interannual.png`.

Sensitivity (single-node result, no second estimate attempted): reference temperature 25.5 / 26.0 / 26.5 °C gives 49.9 / 40.2 / 31.4 kJ cm^-2 (-22 % / +24 %); including the excluded NW-Caribbean corner (where TCHP26 averages 105.9 kJ cm^-2) gives 50.2 kJ cm^-2 (+25 %); the vertical-integration method changes the value by +1.4 %; truncating the water column at 318 m is provably harmless. **The headline number is therefore comparable to other studies only with its threshold and domain stated.**

Comparison with published magnitudes is **not independent** (different product, domain and, for the literature, definitions read only from abstracts/metadata in search mode): published basin-mean Argo TCHP monthly values of 38 / 54 / 74 / 77 / 62 / 27 kJ cm^-2 for June-November (Potter & Rudzin 2021, as reported) sit 30-40 % above the GLORYS12 values found here for June, September and November, while operational intensification thresholds of 60 kJ cm^-2 (Mainelli et al. 2008) and 90 kJ cm^-2 (NOAA/AOML) are exceeded by the seasonal-mean basin value only in the deep basin and by individual cells in the eddy field. The direction of this difference is consistent with an under-estimate of warm-layer thickness in the reanalysis, but it is equally consistent with differing domains; it was not resolved.

## 3. How much of the heat is actually available to a storm

Using the supplied salinity with temperature, the June-November excess heat above 26 °C splits into **52 % inside the density mixed layer** (mean MLD 25.3 m), **13 % in a salinity-controlled barrier layer** (mean thickness 6.0 m, from MLD to isothermal-layer depth 31.2 m) and **35 % below the isothermal layer**; 96.6 % of the reservoir lies above 100 m. Highest-heat years store their excess deeper (r(TCHP26, fraction below ILD) = -0.82).

Spatially (Gulf proper): 52 kJ cm^-2 in the deep basin (57 / 13 / 30 %), **82 kJ cm^-2 on the SE banks / Florida Straits (47 / 12 / 40 %)**, 20 kJ cm^-2 on the northern shelf (61 / 14 / 25 %); a barrier layer is present over 81 % of the area and is thicker in the deep Gulf (6.1-7.1 m) than on the shelf (3.7 m).

Two honest qualifications. (i) The barrier-layer heat share is **criterion-fragile: 13.4 % with the standard criteria, 2.9 % with a stricter density criterion and 21.2 % with a looser temperature criterion (3-21 %, a factor of 7)**; the below-isothermal share is comparatively robust (21-29 %). (ii) The reduction of the stratification partition under-integrates the ~8 % of the Gulf whose whole column is warmer than 26 °C (bottom-limited SE banks), leaving those heat magnitudes about 6 % low; an attempted fix did not take effect, and no figure was rendered for this partition, so the spatial claim rests on region statistics (this is the one visually requested-type view that was **not** delivered). No observed mixed-layer, barrier-layer or salinity profile was supplied, so none of these stratification quantities is validated against observation.

## 4. The Loop Current and its eddies: how much, and in what sense

Three returned numbers describe three different quantities and must not be substituted for one another:

| reading | value | what it measures |
|---|---|---|
| enclosed share | **33 % (0.22 ZJ)** of the 0.684 ZJ reservoir; 24 % Loop Current proper (0.17 ZJ) + 8 % detached anticyclones (0.06 ZJ); 18 % of the area; mean TCHP 81 and 58 inside vs 33 kJ cm^-2 outside | heat sitting inside an SSH-anomaly-defined structure at a given time |
| criterion range | **10-44 %** across defensible detection criteria (21.3 % in a transient-only, climatology-removed version) | how much of the headline is definition; about 11-12 percentage points of the 33 % is the quasi-permanent Loop Current |
| variance share | **44 %** of the year-to-year variance of the June-November mean | how much of the interannual signal lies in the structure mask (but the map derives from the same thermocline signal it attributes, and the annual *background* correlates better with the basin mean, r = 0.77, than the Loop Current 0.41 or eddy 0.48 contributions) |
| water-mass share | **~98-99 %** | almost the whole reservoir is Caribbean/Yucatán-Channel water (salinity deficit outside the mask 0.20, i.e. 0.55 %); near-tautological given the Gulf's single oceanic connection |

Figures: `.../agents/ocean-process-2f54348a18/outputs/fig-gom-lc-eddy-structures.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-2f54348a18/outputs/fig-gom-lc-eddy-attribution.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-87815f12d5/outputs/gom-warm-layer-origin-ts.png`.

What this supports: **about a third of the standing reservoir, and roughly half of its year-to-year variance, sits in Loop Current/eddy structures rather than in the basin background.** What it does not support: that the Loop Current *delivers* that heat. The only demonstrably non-Caribbean water in the reservoir is a thin river-influenced layer over the Mississippi/Atchafalaya shelf holding about 2 % of the heat (heat-weighted freshwater fraction 0.0039 over the reservoir, 11.4 % on that shelf), and no geometric mask or temperature-salinity pair can separate heat carried in the Loop Current from heat that merely entered with it. A formal interpretation review concluded that the evidence fits **one inherited deep warm-layer/thermocline state seen twice**, not a Loop Current control.

Applying the same detection criterion to the preceding March-May gives the same structural footprint (structure area 0.168 of the Gulf in spring versus 0.178 in June-November), and **62 % of the spring excess heat already sits inside Loop Current/eddy structures** (against 32.5 % in June-November, because in spring the only >26 °C water is Loop Current/eddy water). The structural anomaly carries over (r = 0.84) but supplies only 21 % of the variance and 22 % of the magnitude of the June-November structural contribution, and about a third of the seasonal enclosure lies on cells that were not structure-frequent in spring. Figure: `.../agents/ocean-process-422fba613c/outputs/fig-gom-lc-eddy-preseason.png`. So the structural share and the pre-season inheritance found in Section 5 are **consistent, not competing** - the structures act as a pre-season carrier, with the season amplifying the spring anomaly about 3.4x.

## 5. What controls the year-to-year variability

| candidate class | result (n = 7 seasons) | status |
|---|---|---|
| warm-layer thickness / temperature | D26, mixed-layer temperature, SST correlate r = 0.90-0.92 with the seven seasonal means (p <= 0.006); the anomaly is dominated by warm-layer thickness (thickness 0.666 / temperature 0.353 / cross -0.019; reproducible; bootstrap thickness share 0.31-0.98, ordering robust in 86 % of resamples and every leave-one-year-out fit) | **supported as a description**; the number is not resolved |
| Loop Current extension from SSH | r = 0.90 at a 0.15 m SLA threshold but 0.43-0.96 across reasonable thresholds; fails to lead the reservoir; the Loop Current corridor is the *worst* regional predictor of the season (D26 r = 0.58 vs 0.93 shelf, 0.86 Gulf) and adds no significant skill beyond the basin mean (partial r = 0.25, p = 0.58) | present but index-dependent; not established as a control |
| eddy activity | EKE 0.54-0.56, eddy area 0.35-0.38, separation-like events 0.57, >0.15 m SLA area 0.38 - all p > 0.17 | **not supported** (sharpest discriminating negative result) |
| stratification / salinity | SSS r = 0.58, barrier-layer thickness -0.33, MLD +0.29, max N^2 -0.35, all p > 0.17; annual reservoir vs freshwater content r = 0.38 n.s. | **not supported** |
| timing / pre-season state | the seasonal anomaly is already present in June (r = 0.80) and in March-May (r = 0.92, p = 0.003); an exact covariance partition gives **94-111 % of the variance to the pre-season state and 0 % (negative) to the in-season June-November change**, and the in-season change is anti-correlated with the pre-season state (r = -0.83 to -0.68): the season relaxes a pre-existing anomaly | **supported** |
| vertical structure of that pre-season state | March-May anomalies coherent from the surface to ~450 m (r = +0.76 at 0 m, +0.70 at 22 m, +0.10 at 92 m, +0.74 at 266 m, +0.74 at 454 m; deep salinity anomaly r = +0.81 at 266 m); a single rigid vertical displacement of the mean stratification explains 76-83 % of the March-May profile variance over 30-520 m; SSH response 0.8 cm per kJ cm^-2, 11-17x the uniform thermal-expansion prediction | **supported**; mass-field (thermocline heave) anomaly |
| mechanism (advection vs surface flux) | the heave-shaped, basin-wide spring anomaly is compatible with ocean advection, but a spring surface heat flux acting through mixed-layer deepening and eddy restratification can also warm the column coherently to several hundred metres; no partial correlation is significant | **not discriminated** |
| surface heat flux, wind forcing, Yucatán/Caribbean inflow transport | not testable: no flux, radiation, wind-stress or velocity variable is supplied | untestable here |

Figures: `.../agents/statistics-3ba52b5a46/outputs/fig-gom-tchp-controls.png`, `.../agents/statistics-f16f3bb131/outputs/fig-gom-tchp-preseason-memory.png`, `.../agents/statistics-df7f57450b/outputs/gom-tchp-d26-split-reproducibility.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-4d93a9db36/outputs/fig-b111-marmay-structure.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-4d93a9db36/outputs/fig-b111-marmay-composite-maps.png`, `.../agents/ocean-process-4d93a9db36/outputs/fig-b111-ssh-heat-endmembers.png`.

Note on the corrected record: one node's check of the D26 series disagreed with the series used for the thickness/temperature split by about +5.6 m. That discrepancy was traced to the check, not to the series (independent derivation of D26 = 45.20 m versus 45.45 m; the discrepant series differed by a multiplicative factor of 1.12-1.15 by year), so the published split is reproducible; the correction is recorded here because the earlier checkpoint circulated the discrepant value.

**Reading, stated no more strongly than the evidence:** the year-to-year differences in the heat available to Gulf storms in 2011-2017 are dominated by how deep the >26 °C layer reaches, are set before the hurricane season begins (in March-May, not mid-winter), are basin-wide rather than Loop-Current-corridor-specific, and are carried in the mass field. Whether the pre-season control is an ocean-advection process or an atmosphere-driven thermal process remains unresolved at n = 7 with no flux, wind or velocity data.

## 6. Limits and unresolved uncertainties (all named)

1. **No independent validation was possible.** No observed TCHP, D26, mixed-layer, barrier-layer or salinity profile was supplied, so every absolute magnitude (including the 40.2 kJ cm^-2 reservoir and the 6 m barrier layer) is a property of this GLORYS12 reanalysis, and the literature review found no published Gulf-specific validation of it. Its warm layers (29.5-30 °C to 110-190 m) are unvalidated. This needs Argo/altimetry-derived TCHP or MLD, which is outside this delivery.
2. **"Delivered" versus "present" Loop Current heat cannot be measured** with temperature, salinity and SSH; it needs velocity, a transport or a tracer experiment.
3. **Seven seasons.** The 5 %-level critical |r| is 0.75; multiplicity over ~25 candidate indices and a Bonferroni correction over ~56 lead windows mean the individual p-values are exploratory. The true precision of "67 % vs 35 %" and of the LC-extension correlation is not established.
4. **No storm data entered the analysis.** The user's "available to tropical cyclones" is answered as a reservoir, its accessibility (Section 3) and its variability; whether the basin-integrated state maps onto the heat actually encountered along best tracks is untested and needs TC best-track data.
5. **Residual biases.** The stratification partition under-integrates bottom-limited columns by ~6 % on 8.3 % of the area; the barrier-layer share is criterion-fragile (3-21 %); the surface-freshwater estimate is a sub-grid model parameterisation.
6. **Untestable drivers** (surface heat flux, wind stress, Yucatán inflow transport) and the previous-season-to-spring carry-over (only six Nov->Apr year-pairs exist in the delivery) remain open; they need data this task does not have.

Closed without action: the general definitional-sensitivity node (already answered by the baseline node) and the proposed updates of the delivered reports' secondary refinements (Lagrangian identity of individual eddies, longer-record repetition, transport budgets, observational MLD validation), each of which needs data that is not in the delivery or would not change the conclusions above.

# Upper-ocean heat available to tropical cyclones in the Gulf of Mexico, and the role of the Loop Current and its eddies

**GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis, 2011–2017 · June–November**

---

## 1. Data and method

**Data (read-only, never copied or modified).** `CMEMS_Gulf/{thetao,so,zos}` — GLORYS12V1 (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1/12° daily, 40 z-levels (0.49 m → 1941 m), 217 × 157 grid points, 2557 days covering 2011-01-01 → 2017-12-31.

**Metrics computed on every day at every grid point** (`code/preprocess.py`):

| quantity | definition |
|---|---|
| TCHP | ρc_p ∫₀^D26 (T − 26 °C) dz, ρc_p = 4.093 × 10⁶ J m⁻³ K⁻¹, in kJ cm⁻² |
| D26, D20 | isotherm depth by linear interpolation between model levels |
| MLD | σ₀(10 m) + 0.03 kg m⁻³ criterion (gsw); ILD = 0.2 °C criterion; BLT = ILD − MLD |
| stratification | σ₀(100 m) − σ₀(10 m) |
| OHC100, MLH | heat above 26 °C over 0–100 m; ρc_p(SST−26)·MLD |

**Domain.** The downloaded box spills into the Caribbean and the Atlantic, so an explicit Gulf-of-Mexico polygon is applied (hugging the Florida coast, crossing the Florida Straits, closing south of the Yucatan Channel). Analysis is done on the **deep Gulf** — inside that polygon *and* deeper than 200 m — **984 840 km²**. The shelf (1 150 040 km² of the polygon) is retained only in the maps: on the shelf TCHP is small and dominated by the exact isotherm depth, which would blur the Loop Current signal without adding heat a storm can use.

**Loop Current / eddy detection** (`code/prep_masks.py`). The 17 cm dynamic-height-anomaly contour (the operational Gulf convention) applied to SSH with the **daily Gulf-of-Mexico mean removed**. Connected components touching the Yucatan Channel box (87.6–84.6 °W, 20.8–23.0 °N) are the Loop Current; detached components > 20 000 km² are warm-core eddies; 5 000–20 000 km² are tracked as an alternative "extended" definition; 1 000–5 000 km² are flagged but not used.

The choice of SSH reference was tested explicitly (`code/compare_reference.py`). Removing the **7-year** mean instead injects a spurious seasonal cycle into the LC extent (annual maximum 30.6 °N — the basin mean blooming in summer, not the LC). The daily-mean reference gives a mean LC northern extent of **26.0 °N, range 23.6–28.5 °N**, reproducing the published statistics (Leben et al. 2005: 26.2 ± 0.95 °N; Dukhovskoy et al. 2015: 25.8 ± 1.2 °N). The daily-mean reference is used throughout.

---

## 2. How much heat is available

Averaged over all June–November days of 2011–2017, the deep Gulf holds **TCHP = 50.2 ± 19.4 kJ cm⁻²**, i.e. **494 EJ** (4.9 × 10²⁰ J) of excess heat above 26 °C on an average hurricane-season day. The seasonal march is large (Fig. 2): D26 deepens from ~13 m in February to ~66 m in late October, SST peaks at 30.1 °C in August, MLD shoals to ~18 m in June–July, and TCHP rises from ~20 kJ cm⁻² in May to ~70 kJ cm⁻² in October before collapsing in November as the mixed layer deepens and entrains cold water.

**Area above operational thresholds** (June–November mean): 46.9 % of the deep Gulf exceeds 50 kJ cm⁻², **9.3 % exceeds 90 kJ cm⁻²** (the Gulf "hot spot" threshold for rapid intensification), and 3.2 % exceeds 120 kJ cm⁻².

---

## 3. Contribution of the Loop Current and its eddies

**They are a small area holding a disproportionate share of the heat, and they own the hot spot.**

| | June–November 2011–2017, deep Gulf |
|---|---|
| Loop Current area | 104 250 km² (10.6 % of the domain) |
| Detached eddies (> 20 000 km²) | 50 500 km² (5.1 %) — on average 0.78 eddies present per day |
| **Feature area combined** | **154 750 km² = 15.7 % of the deep Gulf** |
| **Share of total TCHP** | **30.6 %** |
| **Share of the area with TCHP > 90 kJ cm⁻²** | **87.4 %** |
| Excess heat above the no-feature background | 61.2 EJ (LC) + 18.8 EJ (eddies) = **80 EJ** |

**TCHP inside the Loop Current is 99.3 ± 24.7 kJ cm⁻², inside detached eddies 67.2 ± 32.0, outside any feature 42.6 ± 18.2** — a factor of 2.3 between the LC and the background Gulf. The corresponding 26 °C isotherm depths (Fig. 3c) are ~104 → 122 m inside the LC through the season, ~80 → 100 m inside eddies, and 36 → 60 m in the background — squarely consistent with published values for the LC (120–150 m) and for Gulf Common Water (40–50 m).

Two structural results are worth stating plainly:

- **The features are not a marginal embellishment.** 87 % of the water warm enough to support rapid intensification sits inside an LC or an eddy, even though those features cover only 16 % of the deep Gulf. A storm's exposure to high-TCHP water is essentially a question of whether its track crosses the LC/eddy field.
- **The Loop Current proper dominates the eddies.** The LC alone is 10.6 % of the area but carries 61.2 EJ of the 80 EJ excess; the detached eddies carry the rest. The result is insensitive to the eddy-size cut: with the "extended" definition (> 5 000 km²) the feature area rises to 16.3 % and the heat share to 31.3 %, and the hot-area share stays at 87 %.

---

## 4. What controls the year-to-year variability

Seasonal (June–November) deep-Gulf TCHP ranges from **38.1 kJ cm⁻² (2013) to 58.9 (2015)** — a spread of 21 kJ cm⁻², or 55 % of the lowest year. Correlations with candidate controls across the 7 seasons:

| control | r | p |
|---|---|---|
| D26 | **+0.93** | 0.002 |
| OHC 0–100 m | +0.99 | < 0.001 |
| TCHP outside features (background) | **+0.83** | 0.020 |
| SST | **+0.81** | 0.027 |
| MLD | +0.43 | 0.33 |
| LC northern extent | +0.31 | 0.50 |
| LC area | +0.31 | 0.50 |
| eddy area | −0.09 | 0.84 |
| stratification, barrier layer | ≈ 0 | ns |

**The dominant control is the background Gulf, not the Loop Current.** An additive decomposition of the seasonal TCHP anomaly into feature intensity, background intensity and feature area gives variance shares of **71 % background intensity, 20 % feature intensity, 8 % feature area** (the three terms reconstruct the observed anomaly with r = 0.998). 2013, the coldest season, is cold because the background was cold (−7.3 kJ cm⁻²) *and* the features were weak (−3.6); 2015, the warmest, is warm in both (+3.1 and +2.6) and had the largest feature area (+2.3).

At the daily, deseasonalised timescale the same story holds: a regression of TCHP on SST, D26, MLD and stratification explains **R² = 0.875** (n = 1281 days), with **SST contributing 63 % of the variance and D26 29 %** — MLD and stratification contribute nothing once SST and D26 are included. Locally, TCHP is a surface-enthalpy and thermocline-depth problem; the Loop Current modulates *where* the heat is, but the year-to-year swing in basin-wide heat is set by how warm the surface is and how deep the 26 °C isotherm sits.

The Loop Current's own variability is largely decoupled from the total: LC area and northern extent are essentially uncorrelated with seasonal TCHP (r = +0.31, ns) and *negatively* correlated with eddy area (r = −0.80), reflecting the shedding cycle (a retracted LC builds area while a shed ring is still attached; after detachment the eddy area rises). Note also 2017: the mean TCHP inside detached eddies collapses to 14 kJ cm⁻² because that season's eddy was shed only at the very end of the record (0.14 eddies/day), a reminder that with 7 seasons the eddy statistics are noisy.

---

## 5. Validation, robustness and honest caveats

**What was checked**

- The vertical integration was validated independently: on a real profile (18.00 °N, 87.25 °W, 1942 m), TCHP from `code/preprocess.py` is 86.245 kJ cm⁻² versus 86.249 from a fine-grid (1 m) trapezoid truncated at D26 — a difference of 0.004 kJ cm⁻². This check is cell 2 of the notebook and runs live.
- A subtler point is visible in that cell: trapezoidal integration on the *raw* z-levels without truncation gives 86.656, biased high by 0.4 kJ cm⁻² because it counts the layer containing 26 °C in full. The production code truncates at D26.
- LC detection was validated against published LC-extent statistics, and the SSH-reference sensitivity is quantified in `outputs/reference_sensitivity.csv`.
- The eddy-size threshold was bracketed (results above), and the `deep` mask was tightened mid-analysis after an early version let the deep Caribbean inflate the "background" — the headline heat share moved from 16 % to 31 % when this was fixed.

**Caveats**

- **TCHP is a 26 °C-referenced metric and is undefined in winter.** In February–March parts of the domain have SST below 26 °C, so the SSH-detected features can overlie water with TCHP ≈ 0. This does not affect the June–November results (SST ≥ 26 °C essentially everywhere in the deep Gulf) but it is why the annual-mean numbers in the tables are not physically meaningful and why the analysis is season-focused.
- **A just-shed ring adjacent to the Yucatan Channel is classified with the Loop Current**, since the classifier only requires contact with the channel box. This inflates LC area slightly in shedding months and is the likely source of the LC-area/eddy-area anticorrelation.
- **Seven seasons is a small sample.** All the year-to-year correlations use n = 7; only D26, SST, background TCHP and OHC100 reach p < 0.05. The decomposition variance shares are descriptive, not a significance test.
- **GLORYS12 is a reanalysis, not observations.** Its LC eddy-shedding statistics are model-dependent, and the 1/12° grid plus 3D-VAR assimilation of along-track altimetry will smooth sub-mesoscale frontal structure. The absolute TCHP values should be read as internally consistent, physically plausible, and consistent with published Gulf ranges (LC OHC 125–150 kJ cm⁻², Texas Bight ~35 kJ cm⁻² during Harvey) — not as a substitute for observed TCHP.
- **Literature context** was obtained under the `search_only` policy (search results and public snippets only; no full-text downloads). The numeric literature values quoted above are from search snippets and should be verified against the primary sources before being cited in a publication.
- No storm-track data was supplied, so "available to tropical cyclones" is quantified as the heat field and its thresholds, not as a track-integrated exposure for named storms. That would be the natural next step.

---

## 6. Deliverables

**Notebook:** `analysis.ipynb` (workspace root, 18 cells, executed end-to-end with outputs saved — includes the live TCHP validation, the domain/mask statistics, all result tables, and inline display of every figure).

**Code (`code/`):** `preprocess.py` (daily 3-D → 2-D diagnostics), `prep_ssh.py` (SSH anomalies), `prep_masks.py` (bathymetry + LC/eddy mask), `build_dataset.py` (daily regional index table), `analysis.py` (all figures + tables, sectioned: `maps cycle features annual controls hovmoller exposure`), `compare_reference.py` (SSH-reference sensitivity), `viz_style.py` (shared palette/style).

**Figures (`figures/`):** `fig01_hurricane_season_maps.png` (seasonal-mean TCHP, D26, MLD, SST, LC/eddy frequency), `fig02_seasonal_cycle.png`, `fig03_feature_contribution.png`, `fig04_annual_series.png`, `fig05_index_correlation.png`, `fig06_tchp_vs_controls.png`, `fig07_hovmoller.png` (TCHP along the LC axis with the LC-extent time series), `fig08_exposure.png`. Exploratory diagnostics used during method development are kept separately in `figures/exploratory/`.

**Derived data (`outputs/`):** `daily/gom_daily_YYYY.nc` (2557 days of fields), `daily_indices.csv` (2557 × 55 daily index table), `gom_lc_mask.nc`, `gom_bathy.nc`, `gom_ssh_daily_2011_2017.nc`, `lc_metrics_daily.csv`, `reference_sensitivity.csv`, `jjason_maps.npz`, and the five result tables `table_{seasonal_stats,feature_contribution,annual_indices,index_correlation,tchp_decomposition}.csv`.

**Bottom line.** In the deep Gulf of Mexico during June–November, the upper ocean holds ~50 kJ cm⁻² of cyclone-available heat on average (494 EJ total). The Loop Current and its detached eddies occupy 16 % of that area but hold 31 % of the heat, are 2.3× warmer than the background, and contain 87 % of the water exceeding the 90 kJ cm⁻² rapid-intensification threshold. Year-to-year variability, however, is not controlled by the Loop Current: 71 % of the seasonal TCHP variance comes from the background Gulf's own intensity (SST and D26), against 20 % from feature intensity and 8 % from feature area. The Loop Current governs *where* the heat is; the background state governs *how much* there is.

Original final answer (English)
# Research Report: Upper-Ocean Heat Available to Tropical Cyclones in the Gulf of Mexico (2011–2017)

## Data & Methods
- **Source:** GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (CMEMS cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m): thetao, so, zos.
- **Domain:** 18–31°N, 98–80°W; 40 depth levels (0.5–1942 m), 157×217 grid; daily, hurricane season (Jun–Nov) of 2011–2017 (183 days/yr, 1281 days total).
- **Metric — Tropical Cyclone Heat Potential (TCHP):** rho*cp*integral(T−26°C)dz from surface to the 26°C isotherm (rho=1025 kg/m3, cp=3994 J/kg/K), in kJ/cm2. Local points reach ~193 kJ/cm2; Gulf-wide daily means 5–60 kJ/cm2.
- **Loop Current (LC)/eddy mask:** daily SSH anomaly (zos minus Gulf ocean mean) > +10 cm.
- **Gulf interior mask** excludes Caribbean (S of 21°N/E of 87.5°W) and Atlantic (S of 22°N/E of 83°W); area-weighted by cos(latitude).

## 1. How much upper-ocean heat is available during the hurricane season?
Season-mean Gulf-wide TCHP ranges from **24.2 kJ/cm2 (2013)** to **34.7 kJ/cm2 (2015)** — a max/min ratio of ~1.4. The pooled seasonal cycle peaks in **August–September**, tracking seasonal warming and maximum TC activity, then declines into November (Fig 2).

## 2. Contribution of the Loop Current and its eddies
- LC/anticyclonic-eddy waters occupy only **~17–21% of the Gulf area** yet contain **30–44% of total Gulf TCHP**.
- Mean TCHP inside the LC/eddy mask is **61–90 kJ/cm2** vs **28–39 kJ/cm2** in the background — an **enhancement ratio of 1.9–2.9x**.
- 2014 and 2015 had the largest LC eddy coverage and deepest warm layers; 2013 had the weakest SSH anomaly (+0.004 m) and lowest Gulf TCHP.

## 3. What controls the year-to-year variability?
Correlations of seasonal-mean Gulf TCHP vs. predictors (n=7):
- Gulf top-50 m temperature: r=0.93, p=0.003
- Gulf mean SST: r=0.91, p=0.005
- Gulf mean D26 (26°C depth): r=0.90, p=0.006
- LC-region mean SSH: r=0.69, p=0.08
- LC TCHP area fraction: r=0.04, p=0.93

**Interpretation:** Interannual variability is primarily driven by the integrated thermal state of the upper Gulf — top-50 m temperature and the depth of the 26°C isotherm (D26), which together explain ~80–85% of seasonal-mean TCHP variance. The **Loop Current/eddy field is a spatially concentrating amplifier (2–3x local enhancement)** rather than the dominant basin-scale driver. Salinity is nearly invariant (top-50 m S = 35.64–35.81 psu) and does not drive the interannual signal.

## Deliverables (saved under /workspace/outputs)
- **Figures:** fig1_tchp_ssh_maps.png, fig2_tchp_timeseries.png, fig3_yearly_variability.png, fig4_controls.png, fig5_salinity.png
- **Tables:** table1_yearly_summary.csv, table2_correlations.csv
- **Report:** README_report.md

## Limitations / Missing Evidence (stated honestly)
- No in-situ (Argo/glider) validation nor independent SST cross-check (offline environment).
- No literature-search tool available; methods follow standard TCHP and SSH-based eddy definitions but no external citations are verifiable here.
- Eddy identification uses a single fixed +10 cm SSH-anomaly threshold; no eddy tracking (Okubo-Weiss/closed-contour) was applied.
- n=7 years limits statistical power; the LC-SSH correlation (p=0.08) is suggestive but **not significant at 5%**. Multiple regression/variance decomposition was avoided to prevent overfitting.
- Salinity used only as a supporting descriptor; a full barrier-layer computation was not performed.

Original final answer (English)
# How much subsurface temperature and salinity variability can be inferred from sea surface height in the Gulf of Mexico (GLORYS12, 2011-2017)?

## Summary

In the supplied GLORYS12 daily fields (1/12° grid, 18-31°N, 98-80°W, 40 levels from 0.494 to 1941.9 m, 2557 days) sea surface height (SSH) is a **useful proxy for thermocline temperature and for deep thermocline salinity, and a poor one for the surface layer, for the shelves and for salinity in general**. The coupling is almost entirely *vertical heaving of the background stratification*, so its strength is set by how much of a subsurface anomaly is displaced mass rather than a water-mass (spiciness) anomaly: temperature anomalies track SSH from roughly 80 m down to about 1000 m, salinity anomalies only where the halocline is also the pycnocline (about 156-460 m in deep water).

Concretely, for daily anomalies after removing the seasonally varying mean, with SSH at the same point:

* **Temperature**: recoverable variance R² peaks at **156 m (R² = 0.73)** and stays above 0.5 down to about **660 m**, above 0.25 to about 1310 m, and reaches the no-skill floor near **1650 m**; it falls below 0.5 already above about 150 m and is only **0.16 at 0.5 m**.
* **Salinity**: R² peaks at **222 m (0.60)** and collapses much shallower - below 0.5 at about **410 m**, below 0.1 at about **750 m**, dead below about **800-900 m**; in the top 20 m it is 0.03 or less.
* These are **in-sample values reproduced out of sample** (fit 2011-2015, score 2016-2017, and the reverse split: temperature 0.72-0.83, salinity 0.59-0.66 in the thermocline), so they are not an overfitting artifact.

Regionally and seasonally, using areal-mean anomaly series at 109.7 m over the full 2557-day record, temperature skill is high in the deep basin across the seasons (0.49-0.93 over the deep, shelf-adjacent and Campeche/Yucatan boxes, the weakest single case being the Loop Current box in MAM at 0.34, so no deep box or season collapses to no skill) and **fails in the two freshwater-influenced shelf boxes** (northern Gulf shelf 0.15-0.40, Mississippi plume 0.26-0.31, leave-one-year-out R² ranging down to -0.18). Salinity at that depth fails nearly everywhere (R² < 0.13) and works only in the 156-460 m band of deep water. The surface failure is **physical, not a lead-lag artifact**: allowing SSH to lead or lag by up to 20 days moves the optimum to lag 0 for temperature at all 40 levels and to lag 0 to +2 days for salinity, leaving the failure depths unchanged.

Two limits dominate the result. First, all three fields come from **one SSH-assimilating reanalysis**, so the demonstrated coupling is a property of that model's internally consistent density field, not an independent observational verification. Second, the record is only seven years of strongly autocorrelated daily fields (lag-1 correlation 0.86-1.00; effective sample size 0.4-7.5 % of season-days), so shelf and salinity verdicts are sign-unstable while the deep-box temperature verdicts are robust.

## What was analyzed

Verified data geometry (from the depth-profile node): 1/12° grid, 18-31°N, 98-80°W, 40 depth levels 0.494-1941.9 m, 2557 daily records with a static land/bottom mask. Gulf-wide SSH anomaly variance splits as **34.4 % seasonally varying mean, 45.6 % in the >~1-month band and 20.0 % in the <~1-month band** (ocean-mean total 0.01586 m², σ = 12.6 cm), and the deseasonalized SSH field is multi-modal (20 EOFs = 87.4 % of variance), so no single baroclinic/steric mode describes it. These variance splits define the timescales the whole analysis is conditioned on.

## How much, and at which depths

![SSH-recoverable fraction of subsurface temperature and salinity variance versus depth, in-sample and out-of-sample, by frequency band, with the no-skill floor](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-35504d0c27/outputs/b111_ssh-recoverable-fraction-vs-depth.png)

The collocated-SSH profile above is the central quantitative answer. **A correction matters for it**: an earlier value (R² = 0.399 for temperature at 186 m, 0.350 for salinity at 222 m) was produced with the monthly climatology subtracted twice from the SSH predictor and is **superseded** by R² = 0.73 at 156 m and 0.60 at 222 m; the earlier within-month numbers were correct and were reproduced exactly.

Measured structure of the relation:

| Property | Temperature | Salinity |
|---|---|---|
| Peak R² (deseasonalized, collocated, daily) | 0.73 at 156 m | 0.60 at 222 m |
| R² at 0.5 m / top ~20 m | 0.16 (lag-allowed ceiling 0.155-0.22) | 0.03 (ceiling 0.032-0.038) |
| R² falls below 0.5 | ~660 m (upward crossing near 150 m) | ~410 m |
| R² falls below 0.25 / 0.1 | ~1310 / ~1640 m | ~640 / ~750 m |
| At the no-skill floor (R² ≈ 0.07, autocorrelation-adjusted) | below ~1650 m | below ~800-900 m |
| Out-of-sample (2011-2015 → 2016-2017 and reverse) | 0.72-0.83 in the thermocline | 0.59-0.66 in the thermocline |

Timescale dependence is as important as depth: in the thermocline the **month-mean anomaly band (>~1 month) is the most recoverable** (temperature 0.78 at 156 m, salinity 0.65 at 222 m), the within-month band is about 0.15 lower and decays faster, and the mean annual cycle is strongly recovered near the surface for temperature (0.77 at 47 m) but only 0.32-0.37 for salinity above 150 m. Consistently, 15-day low-passing raises R² by 0.03-0.05 at every level without moving the lag optimum away from zero. In other words, **SSH constrains the slowly varying mass field, not the fast, thin surface layer**.

A related check on the operational form of the same question is negative: replacing pointwise regressions with a multivariate SSH predictor of the whole profile **did not help and often hurt out of sample** (median leave-one-year-out profile R² over 9 regions × 4 seasons × 15 depths fell from +0.302 to -0.096 for temperature and from +0.056 to -0.632 for salinity). That is a result about an *unregularised* predictor that cannot be fitted from seven year-blocks; a deliberately low-dimensional, basin-scale-inclusive variant did beat the single region-mean predictor in 15-26 of 36 temperature cells and in most salinity cells (effect positive in 97 % of cells), but the gain lay **below the design's detection floor** (≈1.4 R² units per cell at 80 % power), so it is a bound rather than a proven improvement. Salinity inference is not rescued by any form tested.

## Where and when the relation holds or fails

![Regional and seasonal skill maps of SSH against subsurface temperature (109.7 m) and salinity (222.5 m), with region-by-season skill heatmaps](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/statistics-59aabfec9b/outputs/gom-ssh-subsurface-skill-mapview-B15.png)

![Depth-season companion view of the same 2011-2017 skill assessment](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/statistics-59aabfec9b/outputs/gom-ssh-subsurface-skill-depth-season-B15.png)

These figures are the areal-mean-series assessment for **every day of 2011-2017** (no temporal subsampling), 15 depths, 9 a-priori region boxes, 4 seasons. One number in the assessment's own narrative was **corrected** afterwards: the Loop Current box at 109.7 m spans R² 0.34-0.93 across seasons, not 0.81-0.93, because MAM drops to 0.34.

**Where it holds (temperature, ~110 m):** Loop Current (R² 0.34-0.93; DJF series correlation 0.901 with bootstrap 95 % CI [0.79, 0.95], LOO 0.78), deep central Gulf (0.64-0.81, LOO 0.43-0.61), deep west (0.57-0.84, LOO 0.47-0.82), west Florida shelf (0.56-0.85), Florida Straits (0.66-0.76), Bay of Campeche (0.61-0.73), Yucatan shelf (0.49-0.66).

**Where it fails:** the northern Gulf shelf (0.15-0.40; LOO -0.18 to 0.16) and the Mississippi plume box (0.26-0.31; LOO -0.02 to 0.11); the surface layer everywhere (temperature R² ≈ 0.05-0.2 in MAM-JJA above ~30 m); the abyss (0.33 at 1245 m, 0.04 at 1942 m); and salinity at almost all shallow and shelf locations (R² < 0.13 at 109.7 m except Bay of Campeche 0.12-0.24, Yucatan shelf 0.13-0.38 with negative sign, and west Florida shelf in SON 0.41).

**When:** temperature holds in the deep boxes in every season, but the surface layer fails most strongly in summer, when the mixed layer is thin (0.06 at 21.6 m in August with a mixed layer of 18-20 m; 0.30 in Jan-Mar versus 0.09 in Jul-Sep at 0.49 m). Depth is the dominant axis for both variables, and salinity's useful band sits 150-300 m deeper than temperature's.

**How firm is this:** for the deep boxes the sign is unambiguous and the effect large (R² 0.5-0.9 with bootstrap lower bounds 0.29-0.88). For every shelf box and for salinity the daily fields' autocorrelation (lag-1 0.86-1.00; n_eff/n ≈ 0.004-0.075, i.e. only about 3-50 effectively independent season-samples per region × season, and only 7 year-blocks for the bootstrap) leaves intervals that span zero (e.g. Yucatan shelf JJA temperature [0.51, 0.80], northern Gulf shelf MAM [0.02, 0.61], deep central Gulf JJA salinity [-0.57, 0.50]). Those verdicts should be read as **"not distinguishable from zero with this record"**, not as measured failures.

## Why

![Heaving decomposition of the SSH-subsurface relation](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-913b613551/outputs/ssh-subsurface-heaving-decomposition.png)

![Regional maps behind the heaving and failure analysis](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-913b613551/outputs/ssh-subsurface-regional-maps.png)

1. **The coupling is heaving of the mean stratification.** Over roughly 78-900 m, vertical displacement of the 7-year mean profile carries 0.94-1.02 of cov(T′,SSH′) and 0.86-1.03 of cov(S′,SSH′), and R²(heaving T, SSH) is within 0.01-0.05 of R²(T′,SSH). The non-heaving residual has almost no SSH signature (R²(spiciness, SSH) ≤ 0.02 at 156-644 m). An independent re-derivation reproduced the attribution (heave share 0.98/1.03/1.15/1.13 at 155.9/318.1/643.6/902.3 m) but gave R²(T′,SSH′) 0.04-0.12 lower when the density anomaly was linearised about the 7-year mean α, β instead of evaluated with TEOS-10 day by day - a reminder that these ratios are method-sensitive at the 0.1 level.

2. **The failures are the mirror image.** Where an anomaly is *not* displaced mass, SSH cannot see it:
   * upper ~40 m: the near-surface anomalies sit in a shallow, seasonally varying mixed layer that is only weakly coupled to the coherent subsurface structure (θ-θ vertical coherence 0.85-0.93 between 92 and 222 m at lag 0, versus r = 0.26 between 0.5 m and 110 m); this is why no lead time helps;
   * shelf and Mississippi plume: steric height accounts for only 0.22-0.34 of SSH variance there versus 0.82 in the deep basin, so the local SSH contains a large non-steric (mass/barotropic, wind and freshwater) part, and temperature R² is correspondingly 0.36-0.49;
   * below ~1000 m: the mean stratification is too weak to define a heaving projection (R² 0.33 at 1245 m, 0.04 at 1942 m);
   * salinity everywhere shallow: the haline anomalies are strongly density-compensated with temperature (corr(spice T, spice S) = 0.97-0.99), so they are "invisible" to SSH, and the useful salinity band is where the halocline coincides with the pycnocline.

3. **Which timescales carry the thermocline skill.** Splitting the Gulf-wide covariance shows the **non-seasonal band carries the thermocline relation** (share of cov(T′,SSH′) rising from 0.66 at 77.9 m to 0.73-0.76 over 156-902 m; salinity 0.75-0.86), while the **phase-locked seasonal cycle carries the surface relation**; the two shares cross between 56 and 78 m, so the outcome is depth-dependent rather than one band winning. This is stable to leave-one-chunk-out jackknife (f_M stays 0.70-0.80 when any 2-7-month chunk is removed).

![Band-resolved, heaving-based attribution of the SSH-subsurface relation](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-7ef92bbb14/outputs/ssh-heaving-eddy-vs-seasonal.png)

4. **The Loop Current eddy label is not demonstrated.** Splitting that non-seasonal band at 12 months gives a **near-even split**: the 2-12 month (eddy-shedding scale) fraction is 0.503 at 155.9 m, 0.515 at 318.1 m and 0.527 at 643.6 m, never reaching 0.67 anywhere, and it is *lowest* in the eddy-rich eastern basin (0.493-0.514) and higher in the western deep basin (0.564-0.598) - the opposite of what an eddy-shedding explanation predicts. Robustness variants keep the ratio in 0.43-0.63 with the >12-month band always ≥ 40 %.

![Two-year versus multi-year split of the non-seasonal thermocline covariance](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-99d68f1ef0/outputs/band-split-eddy-vs-interannual.png)

Because timescale is not mechanism, this node's honest verdict is that the SSH-linked thermocline heaving is carried by non-seasonal variability whose 2-12-month and multi-year parts are comparable, and that its attribution to Loop Current eddy shedding remains **an inference from SSH structure, unsupported by any kinematic evidence available in these three fields**.

![Regional and spatial skill of the SSH-subsurface relation](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-35504d0c27/outputs/b111_regional-and-spatial-skill.png)

![Depth-lag dependence of SSH-subsurface skill, with vertical coherence and the seasonal split](/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q26/attempt-1791210541206451339-8c57b6ec/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q26--9d726b0d59e7/agents/ocean-process-e35daeb095/outputs/b1111-1-lag-dependence-of-ssh-subsurface-skill.png)

5. **Where these Gulf results stand against the literature.** A search-only review found a consistent theoretical prediction - SSH inference should be best in the thermocline of strongly baroclinic eddy fields and worst in the mixed layer, in density-compensated salinity regimes, in freshwater/coastal regimes and at long periods - and the Gulf results are **consistent with** every one of those predictions. The largest gap is that **no published Gulf-of-Mexico-specific, depth-resolved SSH-to-subsurface variance fraction was found**, so the depth/region/season expectations used here come from theory and analogues (tropical Pacific, South China Sea, Tasman, Southern Ocean, Mediterranean/Arabian Gulf), not from a GoM benchmark. Quantitative anchors elsewhere range from ~72-80 % of variance explained for SSH-plus-in-situ subsurface temperature at 4° × 4°/1-year scales, to machine-learning reconstructions with R² ≈ 0.93/0.86 that **also use SST and SSS as predictors** and are therefore not pure SSH skill. The observed deep-basin steric share of SSH variance (0.82) is numerically close to the ~20 % steric-versus-baroclinic bias reported in the altimetry literature, which supports treating the shelf steric deficit (0.22-0.34) as a genuine partition effect rather than a parsing artifact.

## Limits, contradictions and what would be needed next

* **Single reanalysis, SSH-assimilating.** All conclusions describe the internal coupling of GLORYS12's density field, which assimilates satellite SSH. An independent test would need observed profiles (Argo/gliders) or at least non-SSH-assimilating fields.
* **No velocity, surface-flux, river-discharge or bottom-pressure fields were supplied**, so "mixed-layer/surface-flux", "shelf barotropic" and "freshwater" are consistency-supported interpretations rather than demonstrated forcings, and the eddy attribution cannot be made kinematic.
* **Statistical power.** Seven years and autocorrelated daily fields leave only ~7 independent year-blocks; shelf and salinity verdicts are bounded, not measured, and the multivariate gain is bounded below the detection floor.
* **Convention mixing is a real hazard.** Two different estimands coexist here and are kept separate throughout: pointwise collocated R² (depth profile; peak 0.73/0.60) and areal-mean-series R² (regional/seasonal tables; 0.49-0.93 for deep-box temperature). One intermediate analysis reported per-band pooled values above 1.0 in some regional conventions and explicitly flagged that the per-band numbers need one consistent domain before quantitative use; the headline values cited above come from conventions that do not have that problem (the corrected non-seasonal-band value 0.87 at 155.9 m versus the pointwise 0.78 at 156 m is a method difference of this kind, not a contradiction).
* **One branch failed and was superseded in place.** The first regional/seasonal attempt returned no skill estimate (compute exhaustion after 2011-2012); its replacement completed the full 2557-day assessment, and the numbers quoted here are from the replacement plus its correction.
* **Residual uncertainties named but not closed:** the magnitude of the multivariate gain (below the design's detection floor); whether the 6-12-month part of the non-seasonal band is eddy shedding or annual-frequency amplitude modulation; whether the compensating shelf spiciness signal is riverine or advective; and the shelf/plankton-box definition sensitivity (a-priori rectangles rather than objective provinces).
