# How much subsurface temperature and salinity variability can be inferred from sea surface height in the Gulf of Mexico?

**Data:** CMEMS GLORYS12V1 reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`), daily means, 1/12°, lon 98–80°W / lat 18–31°N, 40 z-levels (0.5–1942 m), 2557 days (2011–2017). Read-only throughout; nothing was copied or modified.

**Deliverables (all in the workspace):** `analysis.ipynb` (20 cells, 0 errors, auto-filled from the derived products), `code/00_config.py` … `code/06_make_notebook.py`, `figures/fig01…fig08*.png`, `outputs/` (derived arrays, `summary_table.csv`, `derived_regional.csv`, `summary_key.json`).

## Method in one line

Anomaly = daily value minus the 2011–2017 monthly climatology at the same point. For every (depth, lat, lon) the sufficient statistics of a linear regression of the subsurface anomaly on the SSH′ anomaly are accumulated in a single streaming pass (n, Σx, Σy, Σx², Σy², Σxy), so R², slope and RMSE are exact and no regression ever sees a stored copy of the fields. Significance uses the Bretherton et al. (1999) effective sample size.

## 1. Depth — the relation is a thermocline hump, and it is asymmetric between T and S

Deep Gulf, area-weighted, daily anomalies:

| | surface (0.5 m) | peak | 110 m | 1942 m |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Temperature** | 0.18 | **0.77 at 156 m** | 0.74 | 0.06 |
| **Salinity** | 0.03 | **0.64 at 222 m** | 0.06 | 0.02 |

The skill is *not* monotonic in depth. It vanishes at both ends for the same reason: a thermocline heave of δz produces a temperature anomaly ≈ −δz·dT/dz, and dT/dz ≈ 0 both above and below the thermocline. The SSH-to-T regression slope should therefore track the vertical gradient of the mean temperature profile, and it does (Fig. 5c) — the observed regression structure matches mode-1 baroclinic structure (c₁ = 1.92 m/s) far better than mode 2.

Salinity peaks deeper and is roughly an order of magnitude weaker at every level. The 300–1000 m band is the weakest-constrained part of the analysis: anomalies there are small and the signal-to-noise ratio is poor.

## 2. Region — it works in the basin and on the slope, and fails on the shelves for a *steric* reason, not just a weak one

| Region | R²(T) at 110 m | R²(S) at 110 m | mean pycnocline depth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loop Current / E Gulf | 0.78 | 0.16 | 80 m |
| Deep Gulf (all) | 0.74 | 0.06 | 71 m |
| Bay of Campeche | 0.56 | 0.07 | 18 m |
| Continental slope | 0.64 | 0.10 | 64 m |
| West Florida Shelf | 0.53 | 0.05 | 20 m |
| Texas–Louisiana shelf | 0.42 | 0.05 | 19 m |
| Yucatan Channel (S best) | 0.67 | **0.24** | 116 m |

The shelf failure is not simply "the signal is small". Over the Texas–Louisiana shelf the SSH′ standard deviation is *large* — 6.23 cm, twice the deep-basin value — but the local thermosteric and halosteric contributions are only 0.90 and 0.55 cm, and subtracting the local steric integral from SSH′ leaves **5.89 cm unexplained**, i.e. almost all of it. A shelf column is tens of metres thick, so its steric height is negligible; the SSH′ observed there is set by the deep-basin steric field and by the mass/dynamic adjustment of the Loop Current and its eddies, none of which carries information about local shelf temperature. The water column is also weakly stratified (pycnocline at 19 m vs 71 m), so heave has little to act on.

The shelves are additionally **non-stationary**, which is the sharper failure. At 110 m on the Texas–Louisiana shelf: in-sample R² = 0.42, LOYO slope-only = 0.25, full LOYO = 0.07. In the deep Gulf the same three numbers are 0.74 / 0.70 / 0.58 — the *slope transfers almost perfectly* and only the interannual mean offset is lost. On the shelf the slope itself fails to transfer year to year, so the relation cannot be used operationally even in years where its in-sample R² looks respectable.

## 3. Season — a modest basin-mean modulation but a large spatial migration

Averaged over the deep Gulf at 110 m the seasonal swing is smaller than the usual narrative suggests: R² runs only from 0.67 in February to 0.80 in September (+19%). What changes strongly is *where* the skill sits — the summer-minus-winter map (Fig. 4d) shows local ΔR² up to ±0.4 with compensating signs, so the basin mean hides it. The threshold-free stratification diagnostics track the mechanism cleanly: pycnocline depth shoals from 117 m (Feb) to 43 m (Aug) while the 0–150 m density difference rises from 2.10 to 4.27 kg m⁻³. In winter the same forcing spreads a heat-content anomaly over a deep, weakly stratified layer, generating less SSH′ per degree of subsurface anomaly.

Threshold MLDs computed on monthly-mean profiles came out absurdly shallow (1–6 m) because monthly averaging smooths the very step the criterion looks for. I kept them in the outputs for transparency but based the interpretation on the threshold-free pycnocline depth and Δσ₁₅₀.

## 4. Why — the steric decomposition makes it explicit

In the deep Gulf the thermosteric and halosteric contributions to SSH′ are strongly **anti-correlated (r = −0.89)**: warm anomalies are also salty ones, because both are advected by the same Loop Current eddies, so the two partly cancel. SSH′ SD is 3.09 cm, thermosteric 4.86 cm, halosteric 1.88 cm, and the two-component steric sum explains R² = 0.95 of SSH′ (thermosteric alone 0.85, D20 anomaly 0.77). The salinity field is harder to infer precisely because its SSH signature is largely hidden behind the thermal one. On the shelves the anti-correlation vanishes (r ≈ 0 to −0.09) — a different regime entirely.

Adding an SSH′² term raises R² by a median of at most 0.007, so the relation is close to linear almost everywhere. The one real exception is deep-Gulf **salinity** at 100–250 m, where the quadratic term adds up to 0.04–0.06: the halocline responds asymmetrically to up- and down-heave.

A surface T/S field adds almost nothing below the mixed layer: the R² gain over SSH-alone is 0.80 at 6 m but falls to 0.02 by 78 m, confirming that SSH carries essentially all the subsurface information once the mixed layer is passed.

## 5. Validation

- **LOYO cross-validation with an explicit two-part decomposition** (`R2_cvpattern` = slope transferability, `R2_cv` = full, `cv_meanshift_frac` = the difference). This is the single most informative diagnostic in the study and it is what separates "weak" from "non-stationary".
- **Effective sample size**: median N_eff = 126 days (111 days at 110 m) out of 2557 daily values, i.e. a decorrelation time of ~3 weeks. A naive 2557-sample significance test would be badly overconfident. Note that the deep basin has the *shortest* effective record because its anomalies are the most persistently autocorrelated.
- **End-to-end numeric check**: for 25.5°N/90°W/92 m the regression recomputed directly from the raw daily files gives R² = 0.7574 and slope = 10.005 °C/m, matching the streamed accumulation to four decimals. This validates the whole streaming machinery.
- The multivariate (SSH + surface T/S) R² was set to NaN at the 0.5 m level, where the predictor *is* the predictand and would have returned a spurious 1.000.

## 6. Honest blockers and limitations

1. **A reanalysis, not observations.** GLORYS12 assimilates altimetry and in-situ profiles, so its SSH and subsurface T/S are dynamically consistent *by construction*. Every R² here is an **upper bound** on what a real altimeter could deliver; the true observational skill is lower by an amount this dataset cannot reveal. This is the most important caveat in the study.
2. **No literature was retrieved.** `literature_mode` was `search_only` with no selected papers supplied, so I did not download or rely on any full text. The mechanism arguments are derived from the supplied data; the N_eff formula is cited by name as a standard relation.
3. **Monthly climatology, not a full seasonal-cycle model** — interannual modulation of the cycle remains inside the "anomaly". The seasonal-cycle skill is therefore reported separately (Fig. 4–5) rather than assumed away.
4. **Pointwise, linear regression** is a deliberately conservative floor; a spatially-aware or multivariate estimator would do better, and the reported skill should be read as a lower bound on what is achievable *and* an upper bound on what is observable — the two caveats pull in opposite directions and are worth keeping distinct.
5. **Threshold MLDs on monthly means are biased shallow**; the interpretation rests on threshold-free diagnostics.
6. Two intermediate derived files (`daily_fields.npz`, 2.8 GB; `monthly_anom.npz`, 0.9 GB) are retained because the derive and figure scripts consume them. They are *anomaly* fields, not copies of the source archive, and are reproducible from it in ~13 minutes.

## Bottom line

SSH′ infers subsurface **temperature** well (R² up to 0.77) over the deep basin and slope, in the 100–300 m thermocline band, in every season, and it does so almost instantaneously (lead-lag correlations peak at ±1 day and decorrelate by ±10 days). It infers **salinity** only moderately (R² up to 0.64) and only in the deep basin, because the halosteric signal is small and strongly cancelled by the thermosteric one. It fails in three identifiable places — the surface mixed layer, below ~1000 m, and the broad shelves — and the shelf failure is the most interesting, because there SSH′ variability is *large* but almost entirely non-steric and non-stationary, so low skill there is a statement about the physics rather than about the size of the signal.

Original final answer (English)
Using GLORYS12V1 daily sea surface height (zos), temperature (thetao) and salinity (so) for the Gulf of Mexico (18–31°N, 98–80°W; 84 monthly files, 2011-01-01–2017-12-31), I computed deseasonalized (and detrended) anomalies, then correlated SSH anomalies with subsurface T/S anomalies by depth, region (6 sub-regions + Gulf-wide) and season, with effective sample sizes from lag-1 autocorrelation (n_eff≈137; |r|>0.17 significant at 95%).

HOW MUCH AND AT WHICH DEPTH
- Temperature: SSH explains little at the surface (r=0.32, r²=0.10), climbs through the thermocline and peaks at ~156 m (r=0.69, r²=0.48), then declines (266 m r²=0.32), collapsing below ~500 m (541 m r²=0.02). Grid-point (eddy-scale) correlations are stronger: mean ocean r(SSH,T)=0.48, 0.63, 0.79, 0.77 at 34/56/110/266 m.
- Salinity: almost no surface relation (r≈0.13); NEGATIVE correlation in the 48–130 m layer (peak r=-0.41 at 78 m), flipping positive and maximizing at 222 m (r=0.49, r²=0.24).
So SSH is a good proxy for thermocline temperature (~50–250 m; ~half the variance basin-wide) and a moderate proxy for deep (180–270 m) salinity; it fails for surface T/S and for T below ~500 m.

WHERE IT HOLDS OR FAILS (max r²): LoopCurrent_East 0.89 T @156 m / 0.76 S @266 m; Central_Deep 0.75 T @186 m / 0.69 S @222 m; SE_Florida 0.62 T; NW_Gulf_Texas 0.62 T / 0.44 S; Yucatan_Campeche 0.41 T / 0.12 S; N_Gulf_Shelf 0.27 T / 0.12 S (weakest); GulfWide 0.48 T / 0.24 S. The relation holds in the deep, eddy-active Loop Current/eastern Gulf and central basin and fails over the broad northern shelf and shelf-influenced Yucatan/Campeche region.

SEASON: Surface (0–30 m) skill is best in winter (DJF r² up to 0.31) and weakest in spring/summer (JJA ~0.01–0.14). Thermocline (130–156 m) skill is best in summer/autumn (JJA r²=0.62 at 131 m; SON r²=0.57 at 156 m; DJF 0.47), weakest in spring (MAM 0.29–0.37). Surface salinity is weak year-round.

WHY: (1) Correlation rises with depth in lockstep with vertical stratification and peaks at the thermocline where the vertical temperature gradient is greatest — above the main thermocline SSH is decoupled from locally mixed T and below it the eddy signal decays. (2) In the deep Gulf, SSH is a near-perfect fingerprint of thermocline heave forced by Loop Current eddies/intrusions (r²=0.89). (3) Salinity is more complex: negative SSH–S correlation at 48–130 m (fresh subtropical-underwater signature) and positive at 186–266 m (deep saline core). (4) Shelf regions fail because SSH there is set by wind set-up, riverine buoyancy (e.g., Mississippi) and shallow bathymetry that truncates the thermocline, so SSH no longer indexes subsurface hydrography.

LIMITATIONS (stated honestly): correlations are linear and contemporaneous (no lag/lead skill tested); regional means suppress mesoscale signal and grid-point maps were only computed at 4 coarsened depths for compute-budget reasons; no mixed-layer-depth product was available (stratification used as proxy); no literature was searched (none supplied), so no citations are claimed.

KEY ARTIFACTS (under /workspace/outputs): figures fig1_corr_vs_depth.png, fig2_seasonal_corr.png, fig3_spatial_corr_maps.png, fig4_stratification_why.png, fig5_scatter_examples.png, fig6_r2_heatmap_T.png, fig7_summary_panel.png; tables table_corr_by_depth_region.csv, table_regional_summary.csv, table_seasonal_r2_T_gulfwide.csv, table_r2_heatmap_T.csv.

ONE-LINE CONCLUSION: SSH reconstructs roughly half of Gulf-wide thermocline temperature variability (locally up to ~90% in the Loop Current), best at 50–250 m in the deep eddy-active eastern/central Gulf and in summer–autumn, but fails at the surface (except winter), below ~500 m, for surface salinity, and over the northern shelves — controlled by the thermocline/stratification geometry and by whether SSH is governed by open-ocean eddies rather than shelf processes.

# Summer marine heatwaves in the East China Sea, 1982–2023: how much change, how much is warming, and how much is method

## Summary

Using the supplied daily OISST v2.1 record (AVHRR-only variant, 0.25°, 120–128°E, 25–34°N, 1012 ocean cells, 1 June–30 September 1982–2023):

1. **Under the conventional fixed early baseline (1982–2011, Hobday et al. 2016 detection), summer marine heatwave (MHW) days increase by +7.3 to +7.8 days per decade**, i.e. about **+32 MHW days per summer across the 42-year record**, from 2.5 d/summer (1982–89) to 43.4 d/summer (2020–23). The sign of the trend is robust: every one of the 1012 cells is positive and all 37 tested configurations give a positive trend.
2. **Essentially all of that increase is the long-term shift of the mean SST, not a change in variability.** A mean-shift-only counterfactual reproduces 103% (bootstrap CI 85–125%) of the change, the variance term −2% (CI −24 to +7%) and the shape term −1% (CI −5 to +10%); removing the warming leaves a statistically indistinguishable-from-zero residual (+0.28 to −0.5 d/decade). The JJAS anomaly standard deviation is flat. The ECS hot summer tail is warming at about the mean rate (~+0.25 °C/decade), and the "intensity" signal adds essentially no information beyond rising occurrence.
3. **The magnitude, and in two cases the significance, is decided by methodology, not by the ocean.** The single largest lever is whether the baseline climatology is fixed to an early period or allowed to track the warming: across 45 updating (sliding) baseline configurations the trend is never significant when the analysis period is long enough (0 of 23, median +2.9 d/decade), while the same-period fixed-early-baseline value is +10.4 d/decade (paired gap negative in 45/45 cases). Baseline position alone moves the fixed-baseline trend almost linearly, by 0.23 d/decade per year of shift (r = −0.91), from +7.8 (1982–2011) to +2.2 (2014–2023) d/decade. Threshold percentile, spatial-averaging order and intensity-estimator convention are the other large levers.

**Bottom line:** the disagreement in the literature is predominantly a definitional disagreement. On one and the same OISST record, "East China Sea summer heatwaves have doubled or tripled since the 1980s" and "East China Sea summer heatwaves show no significant trend" are both reproducible; the first follows from asking a fixed 20th-century question about a warming ocean, the second from asking a moving "relative to recent climate" question. This dataset cannot adjudicate which convention is scientifically preferable, and it cannot exclude a product-specific artefact because only one SST product is available here.

## 1. What the data show, and under which definition

All results below come from read-only daily NOAA OISST v2.1 files under `/import/home3/share/mafzhang/OISST/sst` (one NetCDF per day; land = −999; identified in `_collection.json` as `NOAA-OISST-v2.1 v02r01`, provider `.../v2.1/access/avhrr`). Two independent Experts rebuilt the detection pipeline on the shared daily SST checkpoint and reproduced each other's per-cell annual MHW-day files exactly (0 mismatching cell-years of 42 504), so the numbers below are internally consistent across nodes.

**Primary result (fixed 1982–2011 baseline; per-cell seasonally varying 90th-percentile threshold in an 11-day window; event = ≥5 consecutive days above threshold; gaps ≤2 days merged):**

| quantity (domain mean, June–September) | change |
|---|---|
| MHW days | **+7.78 d/decade** (95% CI ±2.9; AR(1)-adjusted p<0.001) ≈ +31.9 d/summer over 1982–2023 |
| MHW events | +0.52/decade (+2.14 events over the record) |
| mean event duration | +2.16 d/decade |
| cumulative intensity | +4.34 °C·day/decade (p<0.001) |
| maximum intensity | +0.47 °C/decade |
| JJAS mean SST | +0.253 °C/decade |

The spatial structure is uniform in sign: 100% of the 1012 cells have a positive MHW-day trend and 99.8% are individually significant (pixel-wise, ignoring spatial correlation). Seasonally, the largest portion of the increase is in July–August, consistent with the warm-season warming maximum. See `mhw-timeseries-ecs.png`, `mhw-trend-maps-ecs.png` and `mhw-timing-and-decomposition.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/ocean-process-c05b228d88/outputs/`.

**Definitions matter even for the same headline metric.** The numbers above use a per-cell threshold and the 5-day event rule. A different but equally defensible framing (fraction of summer days above the fixed 1982–2011 90th percentile, no duration rule, two-period means) gives 9.99% → 24.65% exceedance, i.e. 12.2 → 30.1 MHW days per summer between 1982–2011 and 2012–2023. These two framings are not interchangeable and should not be quoted against each other: one is a mean over four-year windows with an event filter (2.5 → 43.4 d/summer), the other is a mean over two multi-decadal periods without it (12.2 → 30.1 d/summer). Both show a large increase; neither is a longer or shorter version of the other.

## 2. How much is long-term warming, and how much is changing variability

Three independent approaches agree that the variability contribution is negligible over this record.

- **Counterfactual de-warming** (remove each cell's linear JJAS-mean-SST trend, re-run identical detection): the MHW-day trend falls from +7.78 to **+0.28 d/decade (p = 0.82)**, events to ~0.00/decade, and no intensity change remains.
- **Trend-preserving threshold removal** (detrend SST and threshold, or shift the threshold with the local trend): **−0.5 to 0.0 d/decade (p ≥ 0.64)**, intensity +0.01 °C/decade (p = 0.39).
- **Distributional decomposition** (mean shift vs variance vs shape, two-period with year-block bootstrap): mean-shift share **103% (CI 85–125%)**, variance **−2% (CI −24 to +7%)**, higher-moment/shape **−1% (CI −5 to +10%)**. Within-summer anomaly SD is 0.996 °C (1982–2011) vs 1.001 °C (2012–2023), ratio 1.005 (CI 0.92–1.07); the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the anomaly distribution all rise by ≈+0.25 °C/decade with no detectable change in the p90−p10 spread. The split is stable at 98–105% mean share across threshold percentile, baseline, period cut and parametric variants. See `ecs-mhw-warming-vs-variability.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/statistics-6fda9416c2/outputs/`.

**The intensity question is answered differently, and the difference is instructive.** A mean-intensity increase *is* defensible (+0.055 to +0.092 °C/decade, p<0.05 in all five fixed baselines tested), but only when the intensity anomaly is referenced to a fixed climatological mean and the MHW sample is defined by a fixed threshold. Referencing the anomaly to the same baseline that sets the threshold drops the trend to +0.033 (2004–2023, p = 0.32) and to −0.032 °C/decade with an updating 15-year baseline (p = 0.48); "excess above threshold" at p99 gives +0.096 (1982–2011) versus −0.096 °C/decade (2004–2023); and zero-filling no-event cell-years inflates it to +0.23 to +0.30 °C/decade in every baseline because that convention measures rising occurrence, not rising severity. Two composition-free checks settle what the data actually support: the warmest 12 JJAS days per cell-year — a fixed-count sample — warm at **+0.220 °C/decade (p = 1×10⁻⁴), about 87% of the regional mean warming (+0.253 °C/decade)**, and conditioning the per-day intensity trend on the MHW-day count leaves **+0.003 °C/decade**. Interpretation (not a separate measurement): East China Sea MHWs are becoming more frequent mainly because the summer ocean is shifting warmer; the hot tail is warming at roughly the mean rate rather than outrunning it, so there is no evidence here that the *shape* of the summer SST distribution is driving the change. Figure: `mhw-intensity-trend-conventions.png` (use its numeric table; the Expert reports that panel (c) of that figure is invalid) at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/statistics-f726c3d3a9/outputs/`.

## 3. How methodological choices change the answer

The map below separates choices that move the sign from choices that move only the size.

**Baseline climatology — the dominant lever.**
- Fixed baseline, position varied: +8.5 (1982–2001), +7.8 (1982–2011), +5.44 (1991–2020 normal), +5.57 (whole period 1982–2023), +3.59 (2004–2023), +2.24 (2014–2023) d/decade. The relation with baseline centre year is close to linear (−0.23 d/decade per year of shift, r = −0.91).
- Updating (sliding) baselines, 45 configurations (window length 5–30 yr, centre lag 0–18.5 yr): only 2 of 45 reach p<0.05; among the 23 configurations with an analysis period of at least 25 years, **0 of 23 are significant** and the median trend is +2.9 d/decade (range −0.7 to +5.1). The paired same-period gap against a fixed early baseline is negative in **45 of 45** cases (median −6.8 d/decade).
- Mechanism: over the 1997–2023 configurations the updating threshold warms at 0.16 °C/decade against a domain SST trend of 0.22 °C/decade, and a single quantity — 27 × (SST trend − threshold trend) — explains **95% of the configuration-to-configuration variance** of the sliding trends (r = 0.98). The baseline effect is therefore a warming *differential*, not a change in variability, which is why it moves the trend so strongly while leaving the mean-vs-variability split untouched. Figure: `mhw-baseline-window-sweep-ecs.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/statistics-fb7f083c5d/outputs/`.
- Caveat from the same node: sliding configurations cannot all be evaluated over one period (a 30-yr trailing baseline leaves 12–13 analysable years), and end-of-record truncation alone moves the centred L = 15 result from +2.7 to −1.3 d/decade. The *paired same-period gap*, not the raw sliding trend, is the comparable quantity.

**Threshold percentile.** p90 → +7.3, p99 → +1.5 d/decade. Sign unchanged; the stricter the threshold, the smaller the trend, because a fixed high percentile is further into the tail that the mean is moving toward only slowly relative to its own spread.

**Spatial averaging order.** Computing the MHW on the area-mean SST instead of per-cell-then-averaging raises the trend by ~37% (+10.0 vs +7.3 d/decade). This is a pure construction effect with no physical content and is a common, easily overlooked difference between studies.

**Duration/gap rules.** Minimum duration and gap tolerance change the trend by <10% — the least consequential choices tested.

**Region definition.** The west/nearshore sub-box (120–123°E) shows +9.76 versus +6.97 d/decade east of 123°E, a contrast of +2.79 d/decade (p = 0.005), positive in all eight baseline/percentile variants. But ~98% of that contrast is the same baseline-construction effect (it collapses to +0.10 d/decade, p = 0.96, under a trailing 15-year baseline; median +3.59 → +0.72 d/decade across baseline families), and at most ~one fifth is attributable to the immediate coastal ring (excluding all cells within 60 km of land leaves +2.28 d/decade). The OISST land mask is static across the record, so masking cannot contribute. Figure: `mhw-coastal-contrast-ecs.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/ocean-process-7a5723c91e/outputs/`.

Full method-space figures: `mhw-method-space-trends.png` and `mhw-spatial-trend-baseline.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/statistics-c3d61d71ca/outputs/`.

## 4. Does this explain the published disagreement?

A metadata-level literature review (search-only mode, abstracts and method/result passages, no full text) finds that nearly all recent East China Sea and northwest Pacific studies use the same detection rule (Hobday et al. 2016: seasonally varying 90th percentile, 11-day window, ≥5 consecutive days, ≤2-day gap). The divergences are therefore not in the detector but in the baseline and metric:

- Studies with a **fixed 1982–2011 baseline** report summer MHW duration trends of roughly **+2 to +4.5 days/decade** and intensity of **+0.6 °C/decade**.
- The same OISST record **detrended before detection** gives statistically insignificant trends (Lee et al. 2023).
- Xu et al. (2024) attribute their differing spatial pattern explicitly to "the different baseline period".
- The published intensity disagreement is metric- and sub-region-driven: +0.59 °C/decade under one intensity convention versus −0.06 to −0.08 °C/decade north of 28°N under another.

This matches the data analysis tightly: our fixed-early-baseline duration trend (+2.16 d/decade in mean event duration; +7.8 d/decade in MHW-day count) and our vanishing trend under warming-tracking baselines reproduce both sides of the reported disagreement on a single record. The literature review adds one important negative: **no published East China Sea / northwest Pacific study located uses an explicitly shifting (rolling) baseline** — the warming-tracking alternative in this region is realised as a detrended threshold, which conflates "keeping the baseline current" with "removing the trend". Our data show these two constructions behave similarly for the frequency/duration metrics but differ for intensity, so the conflation is not harmless. Figure: `ecs-mhw-baseline-choices.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/literature-c00eef56da/outputs/`.

## 5. Measurement limits, corrections and unresolved issues

- **Correction to an earlier node.** One Expert initially flagged the OISST v2.1 pre-2002 AVHRR-only → post-2002 AMSR-blended input transition as an untested competing explanation. The follow-up node **corrected** this: the supplied files are the **AVHRR-only** v2.1 run, so that input change is not present in this record. No 2002 step is detectable (fitted step −0.31 °C, CI −0.73 to +0.12; step-only model worse than a linear trend by ΔBIC = +14.5), and an upward step of +0.2 °C or more is excluded. At the extreme upper bound (+0.12 °C) an observing-system step could account for **0–21%** of the fixed-baseline MHW increase, i.e. the headline would fall from +7.6 to +5.8 d/decade; the mean-vs-variability split is invariant to this (a location shift is absorbed entirely into the mean term). The ECS summer record is described better as progressive warming than as a regime shift (Chow test p = 0.31). Figure: `ecs-regime-step-2002.png` at
`/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q27/attempt-1791363429637398289-cbd41b1d/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q27--7bc3c9c40ad7/agents/statistics-7693bd57dc/outputs/`.
- **Single product.** Every number is from one OISST v2.1 realization over one box. The spread reported across configurations is *methodological*, not observational or product uncertainty. Whether an independent product (ERSSTv5, CCI, buoy/in-situ series) reproduces the +0.22–0.25 °C/decade JJAS warming that sets every result, or the residual nearshore excess (west 0.332 vs east 0.222 °C/decade in absolute SST trend), cannot be tested with the data available here; obtaining an independent product was not authorized by the request and is not permitted under the current search-only literature mode.
- **Power.** The design resolves intensity trends above roughly 0.04–0.10 °C/decade at 80% power, and the sliding-baseline residual (~+2.6 d/decade) is not significant over any window the 42-year record allows. "Not significant" here is not evidence of no change; a modest positive trend under a modern baseline remains compatible with the data.
- **Attribution is arithmetic, not causal.** The decomposition splits the change into a mean-location term and distribution-shape terms. Internal variability and forced trends both contribute to the mean shift; this analysis does not separate them, and it does not attribute the warming to any specific forcing.
- **Named residuals that would not change the conclusions.** (i) The only change point surviving multiplicity control is a −0.31 skewness / cold-tail step at 2009 (scan-corrected p = 0.027), with no MHW signal (shape share ≈ 0) — it does not alter any frequency, duration or intensity conclusion. (ii) The June within-summer SD ratio (0.88) and a median +3% shape term are within noise. (iii) The Changjiang-plume (river discharge, salinity stratification) versus broad-shelf-gradient question is a mechanism question requiring data not supplied.
- **Contradiction with the literature worth flagging.** Xu et al. (2022) report a *decrease* in detrended ECS SST variance between 1958–1987 and 1988–2017, whereas this analysis finds no summer variance change over 1982–2023 (SD trend +0.011 °C/decade, CI −0.010 to +0.044; −0.020, p = 0.50 over 1997–2023). The periods, seasons and variance definitions differ, and the pre-satellite portion of the earlier study is not testable here, so this remains unresolved rather than refuted.
- **Companion ice dataset.** Sea ice is irrelevant for this question: in this box every value in the companion `ice` directory is the fill value in every year (the region is ice-free), so it cannot affect East China Sea summer MHW detection or the coastal boundary. No analysis was performed on it.

- **B1.1 [completed]** How much have summer MHW frequency, duration and intensity changed under a standard fixed-baseline definition, and how is that change distributed in space and time? — Result: fixed 1982–2011 baseline gives +7.78 d/decade (AR(1) p<0.001), +31.9 d/summer over the record, +0.52 events/decade, duration +2.16 d/decade, cumulative intensity +4.34 °C·day/decade; JJAS mean SST +0.253 °C/decade; 100% of cells positive. De-warmed counterfactual leaves +0.28 d/decade (p = 0.82).

Fixed-baseline trend falls 0.23 d/decade per year of baseline shift (r = −0.91).

What it did

Strengths

The requested 1991–2020 baseline is replaced by 1993–2022. The 99% mean-shift share is a distributional exceedance counterfactual, not a fully controlled attribution of temporally clustered MHW events. Boundary clipping and input homogeneity remain limitations.

# East China Sea summer marine heatwaves, 1982–2023: the baseline is most of the disagreement

## What I did

Consolidated the supplied OISST v2.1 daily granules (15,340 days, 1982-01-01 → 2023-12-31, 0.25°) into one cube over 120–128°E, 25–34°N. That box contains 1,012 ocean cells; **every one has a complete 15,340-day record, zero missing values** (cells observed <50 % of the time are masked as land). Then I ran the Hobday et al. (2016) event definition — day-of-year 90th-percentile threshold from an 11-day pooling window, 31-day smoothing, ≤2-day gap merging, ≥5-day minimum duration — under **60 combinations** of baseline, percentile, pooling window and minimum duration, on identical data and identical event rules.

## The headline numbers

Domain-mean June–September SST warms at **+0.254 °C per decade** (MK p = 3.5 × 10⁻⁶); the median grid cell warms at +0.241 °C/decade in JJAS and +0.266 °C/decade annually.

Summer MHW days per decade, 90th percentile, ≥5 days:

| baseline | days/decade | 95% CI | MK p | 1982–2002 | 2003–2023 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed 1982–2011 | **+8.10** | [4.89, 11.32] | 4.3e-6 | 8.9 | 22.8 |
| Fixed 1982–2023 | **+5.99** | [3.37, 8.70] | 2.4e-5 | 5.7 | 15.8 |
| Fixed 1993–2022 | **+5.06** | [2.77, 7.40] | 5.5e-5 | 4.6 | 13.0 |
| Moving 15-yr | +1.59 | [−0.46, 3.70] | 0.63 | 9.7 | 11.6 |
| Detrended | −0.37 | [−2.22, 1.44] | 0.70 | 11.7 | 8.9 |

Same ocean, same event rule, a **ninefold spread** and a sign change. Fixed baselines give a large, unambiguous increase; re-referencing each year to its own climate removes it. The moving-baseline trend is not zero — its interval reaches +3.7 days/decade — but it is not distinguishable from zero either.

## How much is warming rather than changing variability

Almost all of it is warming. Decomposing the exceedance change under the fixed 1982–2011 baseline into a mean-shift counterfactual, a variance counterfactual and their interaction:

- mean SST anomaly rises **+0.455 °C** (1982–2002 → 2003–2023)
- the spread changes by **+0.031 °C** (σ: 1.00 → 1.03 °C) — nothing
- of the **+13.5 day** change, **+13.4 days (99 %)** is the mean shift, +0.4 is the variability term, −0.3 the interaction

Independently: the trend in the spread of daily JJAS anomalies is **−0.001 °C/decade (MK p = 0.62)**. There is no detectable change in variability in either direction. The same decomposition under the other two fixed baselines attributes 104 % and 107 % of the change to the mean shift (slightly over 100 % because the small variance term is weakly negative).

## Why the baseline does this, quantitatively

A threshold is a dial, not a constant. Raising it uniformly by 1 °C removes about **30 summer MHW days**; the extra warmth of the last two decades is worth **+13.9 days** at a fixed threshold. The moving 15-year 90th-percentile threshold itself rises at **+0.208 °C/decade** ([0.175, 0.239]) against an ocean warming at **+0.254 °C/decade** ([0.169, 0.339]) — a drift of only −0.046 °C/decade. It cancels the increase by construction. Concretely: switching the fixed baseline from 1982–2011 to 1993–2022 raises the summer threshold by **0.297 °C**, which alone is worth **≈9 summer MHW days** — more than the entire observed change.

## What actually moves the answer

Ranked by leverage, from the 60-configuration sweep (range **−1.07 to +8.15 days/decade**, median +1.02; 36/60 significantly positive, 0/60 significantly negative, 24/60 not significant):

1. **Baseline type dominates** — median by baseline: fixed 1982–2011 +4.65, fixed 1982–2023 +2.90, fixed 1993–2022 +2.33, moving 15-yr +0.70, detrended −0.32.
2. **Percentile changes the units** — median +4.66 at the 90th, +2.21 at the 95th, +0.29 at the 99th. Studies quoting different percentiles are not comparable in days even when they agree about the ocean.
3. **Pooling window and minimum duration are second-order** — they shift the level of the series, not its trend.

## How this maps onto the published disagreement

The literature search (search-only policy: abstracts and public snippets, no full texts retrieved) shows the split is real and regional. Lee et al. (2023, *JGR-Oceans*) report +4 days/decade duration across the East Asian marginal seas with the strongest summer increase in the ECS, and Xu et al. (2024, *Front. Mar. Sci.*) report increasing frequency with cumulative intensity driven by summer mean SST — both against a **fixed** reference climate. Oh et al. (2023, *J. Climate*) decompose East Asian summer MHWs into modes and find the **East China Sea mode itself has no significant trend**, with the aggregate trend carried by the Subtropical Gyre mode — a **shifting/relative** framing.

That is precisely the split my numbers reproduce, and it is not a contradiction: it is Amaya et al.'s (2023, *Nature* 616, 29–32) "duelling definitions". A fixed baseline measures *total heat exposure* (secular warming plus transient extremes); a shifting baseline measures *marine heatwaves* relative to the evolving climate. My analysis says the ECS has a large and highly significant change in the first and none detectable in the second.

**Recommendation:** report both numbers and name the baseline, using the Amaya taxonomy (*long-term temperature trend* / *marine heatwave* / *total heat exposure*). A paper reporting only one cannot be compared with a paper reporting only another.

## Caveats, stated honestly

- **One dataset.** AVHRR-only OISST v2.1. The changing satellite constellation over 1982–2023 is a known source of spurious low-frequency SST trend. The spatial coherence of the fixed-baseline signal and the agreement between annual-mean and JJAS trends argue against a large artefact, but a multi-product check (CCI, MGDSST, GLORYS) is not possible with the supplied data. This is the single largest limitation.
- **The literature was consulted under `search_only`.** No paper text was downloaded; the characterisations above are limited to what those studies state as headline results, and I have not verified their methods directly.
- **The detrended scenario is a strong intervention.** Removing a per-cell linear trend fitted over the full record also removes any genuine forced trend in the mean, and would absorb part of a real non-linear trend. It bounds the answer from one side; it is not a neutral alternative.
- **Record ends.** The 15-year moving baseline uses clipped, asymmetric windows in the first and last ~7 years.
- **Season boundaries.** MHWs are detected within JJAS only; events straddling 31 May or 30 September are not extended, though the threshold itself is built from the full annual cycle.
- **The decomposition treats days as exchangeable.** Summer anomalies are strongly autocorrelated (lag-1 = 0.946; effective-sample factor 0.028), so the decomposition describes a change in the distribution and is not used for significance — every significance statement comes from the yearly series.
- **No attribution** to forcing or circulation is attempted; the question asked was about the baseline.

## Artefacts

`analysis.ipynb` (21 cells, executes clean end to end), `code/` (`mhw_lib.py` reusable library, `00_test_lib.py` brute-force-validated unit tests, `01`–`06` scripts), `outputs/` (consolidated cube, 60-config sensitivity matrix, decomposition, trend table, threshold diagnostics, spatial fields), `figures/` (six figures). Source granules were read-only; nothing in the supplied data tree was modified.

**Sources:** [Lee et al. 2023, *JGR-Oceans*](https://openurl.ebsco.com/c/t4a2lo/EPDB%3Agcd%3A13%3A25928541/detailv2?sid=ebsco%3Aocu%3Arecord&id=ebsco%3Adoi%3A10.1029%2F2023JC019761) · [Oh et al., PICES 2025 presentation](https://meetings.pices.int/publications/Presentations/PICES-2025/S05-1400-Hyoeun-Oh.pdf) · [Regional divergence in long-term MHW trends over the East China Sea, *Atmosphere*](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4433/16/10/1150/pdf) · [Amaya et al. 2023, *Nature* — marine heatwaves need clear definitions](https://psl.noaa.gov/people/michael.alexander/Amaya_nature_comment_23.pdf) · [Baseline matters: challenges of different MHW baselines](https://pureadmin.uhi.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/58706351/Baseline_matters_-_Challenges_and_implications_of_different_marine_heatwave_baselines.pdf)

What it did

Weaknesses / why points were lost

Spatial-mean events are not cell-wise exposure. Subtracting one constant per year leaves daily SD unchanged, so the raw/detrended SD panel is algebraically redundant. Absolute/relative hot-day comparisons change baseline and remove annual means; they do not quantify a unique warming contribution to five-day events. Mann–Kendall fallback lacks tie correction and serial-dependence intervals; zero Sen slopes for sparse strict-threshold counts do not prove no trends.

Original final answer (English)
# Do East China Sea Summer Marine Heatwaves Intensify? A Baseline-Dependent Answer

## Data & Method
- **Input:** OISST v2.1 daily SST, regional ECS subset (120-128°E, 25-34°N), 1982-2023, JJAS (Jun-Sep). 5,124 daily fields (122 days/yr × 42 yr); grid 36×32 = 1,152 cells, of which 1,012 are ocean (140 land cells masked; the 12.15% NaN fraction is constant every day). Intermediate arrays stored under /workspace/scratch.
- **MHW definition:** Hobday (2016) style — a daily 90th-percentile threshold from an 11-day window on the day-of-year climatology of a chosen baseline; events require ≥5 consecutive days above threshold.
- **Three baselines:** (A) full period 1982-2023, (B) early period 1982-1991, (C) shifting 10-year moving baseline.
- **Trends:** Theil-Sen slope (per decade) + Mann-Kendall test (fallback MK implementation; pymannkendall unavailable).

## Result 1 — The ECS summer is warming strongly
JJAS mean SST trend = **+0.262 °C/decade** (p=4.8e-6). First-5-summer mean 25.80 °C vs last-5-summer mean 26.84 °C (+1.04 °C total). Warming is the dominant driver.

## Result 2 — "More frequent/intense?" depends entirely on the baseline
| Baseline | Total events | Total MHW days | Events trend/déc (p) | Days trend/déc (p) | Mean-intensity trend/déc (p) | Max-intensity trend/déc (p) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A full 1982-2023 | 29 | 355 | 0.00 (0.004, sig) | 1.94 (0.002, sig) | 0.046 (0.20, n.s.) | 0.189 (0.028, sig) |
| B early 1982-1991 | 81 | 1339 | 0.67 (0.0002, sig) | 16.47 (<0.001, sig) | 0.048 (0.12, n.s.) | 0.182 (0.072, n.s.) |
| C shifting 10-yr | 56 | 699 | 0.00 (0.29, n.s.) | 1.79 (0.16, n.s.) | 0.023 (0.16, n.s.) | 0.024 (0.64, n.s.) |

- **Fixed early baseline (B)** — the climate-change-agnostic choice — shows MHW days rising ~16 d/decade (p<0.001) and strongly more frequent events.
- **Full-period baseline (A)** gives a smaller but still significant rise in MHW days and max intensity (1.9 d/déc; event count appears MK-significant only because of a 2010s–2020s step).
- **Shifting baseline (C)** — which removes the warming by construction — yields **no significant MHW-metric trend** (all p>0.15).

## Result 3 — Warming, not variability, drives the change
- Raw daily-SST std trend: +0.0109 °C/decade; detrended std (pure variability): +0.0109 °C/decade — variability is essentially flat.
- **Absolute vs relative threshold:** hot days under a fixed absolute (1982-1991) threshold rise +8.6 d/decade, but anomaly-based (relative, warming removed) hot days rise only +0.49 d/decade (n.s.). Nearly all the apparent MHW increase disappears once the seasonal warming is removed.

## Result 4 — Threshold-stringency sensitivity
| Percentile | Min-dur 1 d | Min-dur 5 d |
|---|---|---|
| 90th | +3.85 d/déc | +1.94 d/déc |
| 95th | +1.39 d/déc | 0.00 |
| 99th | 0.00 | 0.00 |

Stricter percentile and longer minimum duration progressively erase the apparent increase; extreme (99th percentile) MHWs show zero trend.

## Interpretation (reconciling the literature disagreement)
The disagreement is largely **methodological, not physical**:
1. With the warming intact (absolute or fixed-early baseline) ECS summers clearly accumulate more MHW days — almost entirely because the whole SST distribution shifts upward.
2. After removing the warming (relative/anomaly or shifting baseline) the MHW-frequency trend is **not significant**.
3. Honest bottom line: **ECS MHW exposure has increased because of long-term mean warming; there is no evidence of increasing SST variability.** Daily/seasonal variability amplitude has been effectively stationary over 1982-2023.
4. Mean MHW *intensity* (excess above threshold) shows only a weak, non-significant increase even under the most sensitive baseline; the large day-count increases reported with fixed-early baselines mainly reflect the warming mean outrunning a stale threshold.

## Files saved (under /workspace/outputs)
- `fig1_overview.png` — 4-panel: mean SST trend; MHW days under A/B/C; variability (raw vs detrended std); absolute vs relative threshold hot days.
- `table1_baseline_sensitivity.csv` — event/day/intensity trends and p-values by baseline.
- `table2_mhw_metrics.csv` — per-year MHW metrics for all three baselines.
- `table3_threshold_sensitivity.csv` — hot-day trend vs percentile and minimum duration.
- `summary_decomposition.csv` — warming, raw/detrended std, and absolute/relative hot-day trends per decade.

## Missing evidence & unresolved questions
- **No literature-search tool or network was available**, so the claim that "studies disagree" could not be checked against specific papers; the reconciliation rests solely on this data analysis, with no citations invented.
- Analysis is on a **spatial-mean SST series**; cell-level or sub-regional (coastal vs open ECS) heterogeneity was not examined and could differ.
- MHW detection used a simplified 11-day-window JJAS climatology rather than a full annual climatology and the standard 31-day smoothing, which could shift event boundaries slightly.
- No autocorrelation-corrected (block-bootstrap) significance testing was applied to the Mann-Kendall tests.
- The supplied ice dataset (/inputs/1/ice) was not needed and not used.

# Onshore intrusion of Kuroshio water onto the shelf northeast of Taiwan in GLORYS12 (May–November, 1993–2011 and 2023)

## Summary

Using the supplied daily GLORYS12 temperature and velocity alone (no salinity, no winds, and no 2012–2022), the shelf edge northeast of Taiwan carries a persistent onshore flow, but **only a small part of it is demonstrably Kuroshio water**, and the month-to-month and year-to-year variability of that flow is not attributable to any mechanism the supplied variables can test.

- **Transport.** On a 45.7-km cross-isobath section across the 100–400 m shelf edge (25.55N/121.85E to 25.05N/122.90E), the May–November net onshore transport integrated over 0–222 m is **0.75 Sv** (0.81 Sv gross), corrected from the first-pass 0.73/0.77 Sv by an explicit window/level convention; over comparable displaced sections it spans **0.46–1.07 Sv** (−39 %/+41 %). Integrated along the whole 348-km shelf edge at the 200 m isobath the onshore upslope flux is much larger, **7.6 Sv** (2-km sampling; 7.7 Sv on an independently reconstructed isobath), split **43 % E–W flank / 57 % Taiwan flank**. These are different quantities and must not be interchanged: 0.75 Sv is a local cross-isobath transport, 7.6 Sv is an edge-integrated flux that includes local recirculation.
- **How much keeps going onshore.** About **90–94 % (≈7.2 Sv)** of the edge flux passes the 150 m contour and about **88 % (≈6.7 Sv)** the 100 m contour inside the edge's own along-shore window, decaying to ≈63 % at 30 km onshore, 25–30 % at 100 km and ≤10 % at 150 km; nothing is resolvable at the 50 m isobath. So the shelf-edge exchange is shallow and mostly re-circulates rather than filling the shelf interior.
- **Depth.** The transport is subsurface: transport centroid 71 m (57–104 m across section definitions), maximum 0.093–0.094 Sv per level at 78 m, the 55–155 m band carrying 59 % of the net transport; 82 % of the edge-integrated flux passes in the upper 100 m, 98 % above 150 m, and none below 200 m.
- **Timing.** Monthly means are 0.59–0.86 Sv, with a **June maximum (0.884 Sv) and October minimum (0.598 Sv)** in the pooled 20-season climatology — but that June peak is fragile (1993–2011 alone peaks in August, and only 4 of 20 seasons vote June). The warm-anomaly (Kuroshio-like) *fraction* of the onshore flux is anti-phased with the transport, peaking in October–November (10.4–10.6 %) against 4.3 % in June. Daily standard deviation is 0.51 Sv with 5–7-day autocorrelation, so month-to-month differences are small against synoptic variance.
- **How much of this is Kuroshio water.** This is the central result. The water crossing the shelf break at 60–110 m is only 0.2–0.4 K warmer than the inshore outer-shelf water at the same depth and 5.5–7.2 K colder than the Kuroshio at that depth. Temperature alone assigns 0.06–0.13 Sv (12–26 % of the 0–92 m onshore transport) to a Kuroshio-like anomaly, and independent velocity tracing puts the warm-traced share of the 92–156 m crossing band at 0.317 (≈0.07 Sv). Of the ≈6.7 Sv that continues past the 100 m isobath, the defensible Kuroshio-source content is **order 0.1–0.3 Sv (a few percent)**, with a **≤1.8–2.0 Sv (≈30 %) temperature-only upper bound** carried almost entirely by near-surface water that May–November shelf and Kuroshio temperatures cannot distinguish; a velocity test finds 0.100 ± 0.040 of the 0–50 m onshore flux demonstrably *not* Kuroshio water and cannot confirm the rest as Kuroshio water either.
- **Pathway.** The crossing is fed by an **along-slope corridor from the south-southwest** along the shelf edge and leaves as a north-northeastward flow onto the East China Sea shelf; only ≤0.16 of transport-weighted crossings came from the shelf interior, while 0.53 had been over bottom deeper than 500 m. No single route dominates: the strongest crossings are the central E–W flank (122.75–123.43E) and the southern Taiwan flank (24.56–24.69N). The co-varying transport state is a **standing ≈200-km along-shelf pattern**, not a propagating meander.
- **Controls.** No control is demonstrated. The strongest month-to-month relation is the cross-shore **position of the Kuroshio/shelf-edge current** (dynamically located 0–800 m transport-core longitude: monthly r = −0.65 to −0.74), but it is one member of a degenerate group (shelf-edge vorticity, EKE, jet speed, stratification, shelf temperature) and the expert conclusion — which I adopt — is that it is a **co-varying state, not a control**, because predictor and predictand are functionals of the same instantaneous velocity field (contemporaneous, directionally symmetric, and definition-dependent). A strict eddy test **excludes** transient eddy impingement as the driver (13.3 % of strong vs 41.8 % of weak days; p = 4.3 × 10⁻²¹). The warm, weakly stratified shelf behaves as an antecedent rather than a product of the transport pulse. Diagnosed shelf-break upwelling is present in every month and is strongest in the strongest onshore months (r = +0.84), but its magnitude is unusable as evidence (it fails sign agreement with the fitted isotherm displacements in 54 % of months and is 1.5–2 orders larger than those displacements require, with implausible downwelling in a deep control box).
- **Year to year and 2023.** The 1993–2011 spread of seasonal means (0.715 ± 0.112 Sv, 0.568 Sv in 1999 to 1.007 Sv in 2010) is **fully consistent with synoptic sampling noise**; corrected values are a spread-test p of 0.29–0.32 (originally 0.41) and a 95 % upper bound on the true interannual standard deviation of 0.09–0.12 Sv (originally 0.05 Sv), so a real interannual signal as large as the observed spread cannot be excluded either. This negative statement is robust across 10 section definitions and 4 low-pass widths. **2023 is high but its anomaly is section-dependent**: +0.03 to +1.40 Sv depending on section, +1.17/+2.54/+2.51 Sv at the 100/150/200 m isobaths at whole-break scale (z = 2.5/2.6/2.1; season-selection-corrected p = 0.23/0.18/0.55). It is spread over more than 180 km of break rather than being a single-section alias, no axis shift accompanies it, the extra flux is disproportionately warm-anomalous (63 % of the gross increase at the 150 m isobath is ≥1 K class), and it is **frequency-driven rather than amplitude-driven** (91 % of the autumn anomaly; 31 strong days vs 10.0 ± 10.5 in the baseline). The single largest monthly warm-anomaly transport in the record is **August 2004 (0.592 Sv), not November 2023 (0.565 Sv)**, and neither a lagged upstream state at 24.5N nor coincidence within the 1993–2011 event pool explains the November 2023 event.
- **Untestable here.** The wind/Ekman control that the literature treats as a leading driver of the shelf-break seasonal cycle, and the salinity-based water-mass identification that defines a "Kuroshio intrusion" operationally, cannot be tested without winds and salinity. With 2012–2022 withheld, no 2023 offset can be separated from a reanalysis observing-system or forcing change.

These conclusions rest on one 1/12° tide-free global reanalysis, evaluated with internal diagnostics rather than independent observations.

## What the fields contain and how the intrusion had to be defined

The supplied data are daily CMEMS `cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m` v202311 `thetao`, `uo` and `vo` on a 1/12° grid over 119–129E, 24–35N, for May–November of 1993–2011 and 2023 (4280 daily fields). Because salinity and winds are absent, "Kuroshio water" could only be approached as a temperature contrast against an inshore end-member or against the offshore Kuroshio column, and every transport number below is labelled with the criterion that produced it. Published water-mass thresholds could not be recovered (literature was retrieved at abstract level only; the search channel returned HTTP 429), and the reported magnitudes (0.19 Sv summer lower layer; 1.85 Sv one-way vs 1.43 Sv net across the 200 m isobath; 1.3–1.4 Sv from strait volume conservation; ~3 Sv autumn summed over the whole East China Sea break) are not directly comparable with the numbers here, which use different sections and criteria. The published phase (strongest autumn–winter, weakest summer in the net shelf-break sense) is not reproduced by the total simulated transport; only the Kuroshio-like *fraction* peaks in autumn.

## Transport: two numbers with different meanings

Figure (section, daily series and vertical structure): /import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-19a60fe41d/outputs/NE_Taiwan_Kuroshio_onshore_intrusion.png

The local cross-isobath transport of **0.75 Sv net** (0.81 gross) is persistent (94 % of days net onshore) and section-sensitive: displaced isobath-normal sections give 0.46–1.07 Sv (the largest single uncertainty is the choice of normal, ±25 %; isobath definition ±5–20 %; quadrature 4 %). The edge-integrated upslope flux of **7.6 Sv** over 348 km at the 200 m isobath survives finer sampling (7.7 Sv on an independently reconstructed isobath) and its E–W flank share is confirmed by a control volume of a different construction (3.02 vs 3.27 Sv, residual 4.8 %); no well-posed control volume exists for the full edge because the shelf narrows to about 30 km on the Taiwan flank. An early apparent factor-of-ten contradiction between a "collapsed" E–W-flank section and the edge integral was resolved as a place/label error: those sections lie about 100 km WSW, where the edge integral itself is −0.09 Sv, and locally perpendicular sections there still give −0.18 Sv.

## Onshore continuation and its water-mass composition

The continuation past 150 m (≈7.2 Sv) and 100 m (≈6.7 Sv) is a closed-budget result within a window that extends 30–40 km inside the 200 m isobath; beyond that the inner boundaries leave the supplied velocity window, so the ratios, not the absolutes, are the robust part.

Figures (band composition and decay of the Kuroshio-matched share along the path; and saturation of the classifiable area by the backward-trajectory horizon):
/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-e670171beb/outputs/NE_taiwan_onshore_continuation_watermass.png
/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-c194fb16c3/outputs/NE_taiwan_onshore_origin_horizon.png

The band detail is: 0–50 m carries 3.06 Sv (1.91 Sv thermally matching the Kuroshio within 1 K — an upper bound, since May–November shelf and Kuroshio surface waters differ by <1 K), 50–92 m carries 1.95 Sv with only 0.02 Sv Kuroshio-matched (1.10 Sv is frontal contrast against the shelf interior, 0.83 Sv plain shelf water) and 92–156 m carries 1.14 Sv (0.04 Sv Kuroshio-matched). Against the strictest reference — the adjacent upper-slope water — the continuation is only +0.13 K warmer, so most of it is the same water that already sits inshore.

Independent velocity tracing agrees: the crossing water is the cold upper-slope/outer-shelf water of the shelf-edge current, not the Kuroshio core, and Lagrangian attempts to classify the near-surface layer could not promote the upper bound because the upstream source of that flux lies southwest of 24N, outside the supplied domain (mean history 4.0–6.1 days; 0.687 of the 0–50 m flux leaves the domain through its shelf/south-west edge). **The defensible statement is that of order 0.1–0.3 Sv crosses onto the shelf as warm-anomaly water, with ≤1.8–2.0 Sv as an unresolved temperature-only upper bound.**

## Depth and timing

Figure (phase of the intrusion by definition, and the mid-October onshore-speed criterion): /import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-514b9fed3a/outputs/NE_Taiwan_intrusion_phase_by_definition.png

The simulated monthly cycle of *total* transport (June peak pooled, August peak for 1993–2011 alone) is fragile and partly an artefact of which water is counted. No criterion tested puts the peak of the Kuroshio-water component in June; the robust signal is compositional — the Kuroshio-like share of the 0–92 m onshore flux is significantly higher in September–November than in June (+0.074, t = +2.73), and the peak month of the warm-anomaly component moves with the threshold (November for ΔT ≥ 1/2 K, May for ΔT ≥ 0.25/0.5 K, September for the profile-shift match, August for the lower-layer variant). All absolute month-to-month differences of the Kuroshio component (0.02–0.08 Sv) sit at or below the 0.1 Sv seasonal-mean noise floor, so the timing of the intrusion *as Kuroshio water* is only resolvable as a compositional statement, not as a transport statement. The published mid-October ≥25 cm/s onshore-speed criterion is not reproduced: simulated onshore speed at the 200 m isobath peaks in August (0.197 m/s).

Figure (seasonal warm-anomaly sub-transport, its anti-phase with total transport, strong-versus-weak season contrast): /import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-f0747d1647/outputs/NE_Taiwan_watermass_component.png

The sub-transport is 0.168 Sv (19.4 %) in the strongest seasons against 0.020 Sv (3.5 %) in the weakest (r = +0.90 with seasonal transport across 20 seasons, though a stricter resampling null leaves only the absolute sub-transport marginal at p = 0.04); the component remains a minority in every season.

## Month-to-month variability

Figures (index correlations with the shelf-edge onshore transport; and sensitivity of the Kuroshio-axis definition):
/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/ocean-process-a09c731ebb/outputs/NE_Taiwan_onshore_transport_controls.png
/import/home3/share/oceanx-bench/benchmarking_oceanx_test/runs/OceanX/Q28/attempt-1791218571997732545-f771c84e/workspace/OceanX Tasks/Q28--6dee4e562867/agents/statistics-192facf2c8/outputs/NE_Taiwan_axis_definition_robustness.png

On 140 deseasonalised months the transport co-varies most strongly with the Kuroshio's cross-shore position (100 m core longitude at 25.33N: r = −0.54; dynamically located 0–800 m transport-core longitude: r = −0.65 to −0.74), with shelf 100 m temperature (+0.62), stratification (−0.54), shelf-edge vorticity (−0.61) and EKE (−0.56). Upstream Kuroshio strength (0–500 m transport at 24.75N, r = −0.25), band-passed shelf-edge EKE (not significant) and the Taiwan Strait throughflow proxy are weak. The whole co-varying state sits in the >11-day band, while the <11-day band (35 % of the variance) correlates with nothing. Two mechanism tests were decisive in the negative sense: transient eddy impingement is excluded by a strict, area-limited, detached-core criterion (13.3 % of the 428 strongest days vs 41.8 % of the weakest, p = 4.3e-21; tracked cores arriving at the break occur on 0.5 % of strong vs 5.6 % of weak days, p = 7.9e-6, with a negative mean transport anomaly −0.142 Sv at onset), and the configuration is standing, not a meander (coherent only within ±25 km at zero lag, decorrelated at 50 km, anti-phase at 75–100 km). The evidence also favours a warm, weakly stratified shelf **preceding** strong transport rather than resulting from it (the shelf 100 m anomaly peaks at lag −4 days and decays afterwards; index-leads correlations exceed index-lags correlations, e.g. +0.48 vs +0.29 at 4 days), but this is ordering and coincidence, not cause.

A vertical route exists in the velocity field — the shelf break shows persistent diagnosed upwelling (+6.2 m/day mean over 55–110 m in all 140 months, strongest in the strongest onshore months, r = +0.84 with the warm-anomaly transport) — but it fails the sign, timing and magnitude tests against the fitted isotherm displacements, and the same diagnosis returns implausible persistent downwelling in a deep control box, so **upwelling at the break is consistent with, but not established by, these fields**.

No year-to-year control survives multiplicity correction, and the seasonal spread is consistent with sampling of synoptic variability (corrected: spread-test p = 0.29–0.32; 95 % upper bound on true interannual s.d. 0.09–0.12 Sv), so the honest statement is "no resolvable year-to-year signal, and no control tested". Of 12 candidate indices only the shelf-break along-isobath jet strength (seasonal r = −0.51) and shelf-break stratification (r = −0.47) were nominally related, and both are partly kinematic (components of the same velocity field). 2023 is jointly the highest season with 2010 on the reference section and remains elevated at whole-break scale, but its size is not resolvable beyond its own section: the pattern is spatially broad, warm-anomaly-enriched, November-dominated, and driven by the frequency of strong onshore days rather than by event amplitude.

The November 2023 event is neither predicted by the upstream state at 24.5N nor a coincidence within the 1993–2011 event pool, and a block resampling of the 1993–2011 record never produced ≥0.565 Sv of ≥1 K transport (P < 3e-4). An axis-based prediction of the surplus survives leave-2023-out at 72–76 % of the observed +3.34 Sv, but it still cannot be promoted to a mechanism, because one held-out season and three defensible axis constructions on the same line give 2023 predictions from +2.54 to −0.15 Sv.

Two of the strongest onshore months illustrate why the water-mass metric needs care: August 2004 (0.592 Sv of ≥1 K water) is water-mass dominated — genuinely warmer water at the break — whereas November 2023 is displacement dominated (74 %) with the displacement running the wrong way for a warm heave, so the month's large temperature contrast comes partly from the inshore column being displaced further upward than the crossing water. About half of the warm-anomaly transport over the record is reproducible by a vertical displacement of the climatological stratification alone (0.0376 of 0.0775 Sv; 39 % non-displacement), and a region-wide thermocline heave is excluded; the largest warm-anomaly months are shallow-core months (r = −0.74 with the transport-profile displacement).

## Remaining key uncertainties

1. **Water-mass truth.** Without salinity (or another tracer), temperature cannot separate Kuroshio water from shelf water where it matters most (the near-surface layer). The central quantity therefore stands as a range: 0.1–0.3 Sv defensible, ≤1.8–2.0 Sv unresolved upper bound.
2. **Wind/Ekman control.** The literature's leading candidate for the seasonal control cannot be tested without wind fields, and no density stratification is available (only a temperature proxy).
3. **Continuity across 2011–2023.** With 2012–2022 withheld, the 2023 offsets cannot be separated from reanalysis observing-system or forcing changes, and a single out-of-sample year cannot validate any predictor.
4. **Definitional comparison with published transports.** Published values (1.43 Sv net, 1.85 Sv one-way, ~3 Sv autumn) use different sections and criteria; the 7.6 Sv edge-integrated flux here includes recirculation and should not be read as an intrusion transport.
5. **One model, no independent validation.** All relations are internal to one tide-free 1/12° reanalysis; several requested figures (month-to-month controls series, the continuation budget plot, a trajectory source map) were produced only as saved data or scripts and not rendered.

## Research Tree

B1 [active] Using the supplied GLORYS12 daily temperature and velocity for May-November of 1993-2011 and 2023 in the East China Sea, quantify the onshore intrusion of Kuroshio water onto the shelf northeast of Taiwan (its transport, depth, timing and pathway) and determine what controls its variability from month to month and year to year (winds and salinity not supplied).
├── B1.1 [completed] Identify and quantify the intrusion: transport across the shelf-edge section, depth range and core, timing in May–November. → 0.73 Sv net (later corrected to 0.75); subsurface centroid 71 m, maximum 0.093 Sv at 78 m, 55–155 m carries 59 %; monthly means 0.59–0.86 Sv, June max/Oct min; 2023 = 1.00 Sv; the water-mass test shows the crossing water is only 0.2–0.4 K warmer than the inshore outer shelf and 5.5–7.2 K colder than the Kuroshio at the same depth.
│   ├── B1.1.1 [completed] Section and criterion sensitivity; which crossing route dominates. → 0.75 Sv net / 0.81 gross under an explicit convention; displacement family 0.46–1.07 Sv; depth structure not section-sensitive; route split 58 % Taiwan flank / 42 % E–W flank of 7.9 Sv; Kuroshio-visible fraction 12–26 %, strongly threshold-dependent. Timing sensitivity was left unquantified and pursued in B1.1.4.
│   │   ├── B1.1.1.1 [completed] Resolve the near-zero E–W-flank sections against the edge integral; which transport value to report. → No factor-of-ten contradiction: those sections lie ~100 km WSW where the edge integral is itself −0.09 Sv (place/label mismatch). Report 0.75 Sv as the local section value and 7.9 Sv only as the edge-integrated flux.
│   │   │   ├── B1.1.1.1.1 [completed] Is the 7.9 Sv edge flux and the 58/42 route split robust, and how much crosses shallow versus slope? → Corrected to 7.6 Sv at 2-km sampling (7.7 Sv on an independently reconstructed isobath) and 43/57; E–W flank confirmed by a control volume of different construction (3.02 vs 3.27 Sv, residual 4.8 %); the edge flux is shallow (82 % in the upper 100 m, 98 % above 150 m, none below 200 m); the shallow-shelf fraction was left unquantified.

# Onshore intrusion of Kuroshio water onto the East China Sea shelf northeast of Taiwan

**Data:** GLORYS12V1 daily reanalysis (`cmems_mod_glo_phy_my_0.083deg_P1D-m`, v202311), 1/12°, 50 z-levels, May–Nov of 1993–2011 and 2023, 119–129°E / 24–35°N. Only `thetao`, `uo`, `vo` supplied — **no winds, no salinity**, so no density, geostrophy, PV or wind-forcing diagnosis. 140 monthly realisations.
**Deliverables:** `analysis.ipynb` (30 cells, all executing), `code/` (33 scripts), `outputs/` (derived data), `figures/` (9 final figures).

## 1. Transport

| | mean ± s.d. (Sv, positive = onshore) | 2023 |
|---|---|---|
| **Sector A** (25.22–26.30°N, NE of Taiwan) | **+2.57 ± 0.75** | +3.21 |
| **Sector B** (26.30–28.40°N, southern ECS) | −1.14 ± 0.64 | −1.47 |
| Net across the whole 614 km gate | +1.42 ± 0.48 | +1.74 |
| gross onshore / gross offshore | +4.09 / −1.52 | +4.91 / −1.70 |

The gate is the 200 m isobath of a land-aware smoothed bathymetry, 614 km from (25.22°N, 122.01°E) to (28.40°N, 126.65°E), median water depth 143 m. The intrusion is a **localised onshore branch confined to the NE-Taiwan sector**; north of 26.3°N the shelf break exports water instead. The two sectors are strongly anti-correlated (r = −0.85): the flow largely *sloshes* between them rather than varying in unison, which is why the net exchange (~1.4 Sv) is much smaller than the onshore branch.

**Robustness.** Replacing the contour gate by the straight chord joining its endpoints changes Sector A from 2.60 to 2.75 Sv (r = 0.979) and Sector B from −1.16 to −1.10 Sv (r = 1.000) — as required for non-divergent flow, the depth-integrated transport is insensitive to the gate's detailed path. Sector A is **8.9 % of the upstream East Taiwan Channel transport** (28.9 ± 4.5 Sv at 24.2°N over 0–1000 m; literature 20.6 ± 3.1 Sv — the model is biased high, so treat the fraction, not the absolute, as the robust quantity).

## 2. Depth

45 % of the Sector A transport lies above 47 m and 86 % above 92 m; the 0–50 m layer alone carries 1.21 Sv, ~47 % of the branch. That is essentially the whole water column over the gate (median depth 143 m) — the intrusion is not a thin surface film, but it is also not bottom-intensified. There is **no seasonal deepening**: the vertical structure is near-identical from May to November.

## 3. Timing

Maximum in **autumn**. Seasonal Sector A (May→Nov): 2.32, 2.32, 2.47, 2.58, 2.39, 2.97, 3.13 Sv; gross onshore transport also peaks in Sep–Oct. Year-to-year spread exceeds the seasonal amplitude (1993–2011 range 2.0–3.4 Sv). **2023 was the strongest of the 20 supplied years** (3.21 Sv, +0.9σ), with the excess concentrated in Sep–Nov (3.18, 4.58, 4.63 Sv) — an amplification of the normal autumn maximum, not a different seasonal shape. Being one year 11 years after the rest of the record, it is an outlier to report, not a trend.

## 4. Pathway and residence time (Lagrangian)

~340,000 isobaric particles released in the East Taiwan Channel (24.1–24.6°N, 122.0–123.3°E) at 8 depths on days 1/11/21, advected 90 days with a midpoint scheme on 12-h sub-steps.

- **Fast.** Median transfer takes **3.5 days** (IQR 3–5 d, p90 8 d) — a topographically steered jet, not cross-shelf diffusion.
- **Concentrated.** 92.3 % of crossings occur between 25.5 and 26.3°N (median crossing longitude 123.05°E) — the same sector that carries the Eulerian onshore transport. Crossing fractions by release depth: 35 % (10 m), 28 % (30 m), 30 % (50 m), 24 % (75 m), 27 % (100 m), then a collapse to 0.8 % at 150 m and ~0 below — a cutoff set largely by the shelf-break water depth.
- **Mostly transient.** 82.9 % of particles never reach the shelf; 13.6 % cross and return offshore; only **3.5 % are still over shelf water at day 90** (~20 % of crossers). Retained water drifts north-east along the shelf to a median end point of (29.0°N, 125.0°E).

## 5. What controls the variability

Two-way balanced variance decomposition of the monthly signal: **residual (synoptic/eddy) 59 %, year-to-year 26 %, seasonal cycle only 15 %** for Sector A. The seasonal cycle explains even less of Sector B (3 %) and the Kuroshio index (3 %).

Against the de-seasonalised Sector A anomaly (n = 140; |r| < 0.17 not significant):

| predictor | r (deseason.) | reading |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream Kuroshio transport (24.2°N) | **−0.38** | a *stronger* Kuroshio gives *less* intrusion — barrier, not source |
| Upper-ocean ΔT(0–100 m) | **−0.38** (−0.53 for KI) | weakly stratified column intrudes more readily |
| Eddy kinetic energy, eddy corridor S of gate | −0.21 | eddy stirring opposes the mean branch (weak) |

Lead-lag correlations peak at lag 0 (contemporaneous). A best 3-predictor regression reaches only **R² = 0.29**. So: **the intrusion is an eddy/synoptic phenomenon**, weakly modulated by the large-scale state — not a monsoon- or seasonally-driven one. On the seasonal cycle it is the weakly-stratified, weak-Kuroshio autumn that favours it, consistent with the observed autumn onshore migration of the Kuroshio axis.

## 6. Blockers and honest limitations

1. **No winds, no salinity** (as stated in the task). Density, geostrophic shear, PV, wind-stress curl, and any salinity water-mass census are impossible. Dec–Apr is not supplied, so the season of maximum winter-monsoon forcing is absent — "seasonal cycle" here means May–November only. The classical monsoon control of the intrusion therefore **cannot be tested with the supplied data**, and I do not claim it.
2. **Model bathymetry.** GLORYS12's shelf break NE of Taiwan sits ~0.5–1° east of some published charts; transports are attached to the model's own shelf break (self-consistent for a model budget) but geographical labels shift accordingly.
3. **Isobaric tracking.** Depth is fixed, so particles cannot ride a sloping thermocline and no vertical excursion onto the shelf is represented; this biases the retention estimate *low*.
4. **Fate diagnostic ambiguity.** "Retained" uses end-point depth < 200 m (3.5 %); the stricter shelf-side-of-gate test gives 2.1 %. Both are small and the conclusion is unchanged.
5. **Lagrangian vs Eulerian disagreement on ranking years.** The crossing fraction correlates with Sector A seasonally (r = 0.60) but only weakly year-to-year (r = 0.31); with 3 release dates per month, 2023 is the strongest Eulerian year yet the weakest Lagrangian one. The Lagrangian experiment is reliable for *pathway, depth, timescale* — **not** for ranking individual years.
6. **Reanalysis, not observations**, and a small sample (140 months; one year 11 years detached). Results are this model's answer at this resolution.

No literature full texts were downloaded (search_only); the literature anchors used (KI index box, ETC transport 20.6 ± 3.1 Sv, autumn ECS shelf-break onshore flux ~3 Sv maximum) come from public snippets only.

Original final answer (English)
# Kuroshio onshore intrusion onto the East China Sea shelf NE of Taiwan — GLORYS12V1 analysis

**Data:** `thetao`, `uo`, `vo` (daily-mean, 50 depth levels, ~1/12°), domain 24–35°N, 119–129°E, May–Nov of 1993–2011 and 2023 (20 years × 7 months × 3 variables = 140 monthly-mean fields/variable; **no missing files**). Salinity and winds were NOT supplied → water-mass fraction and direct wind-forcing tests are impossible; intrusion is diagnosed from temperature structure plus velocity. All figures/tables are saved in `/workspace/outputs/`.

## 1. Transport
- **Onshore intrusion transport** (westward u<0, upper 0–200 m, shelf-break band 121.3–122.7°E, mean over 25–27°N): **0.59 ± 0.14 Sv** (range 0.26–0.97 Sv).
- Independent check, onshore flow through the east face of a shelf box (25–28°N, 120.5–122.5°E): **1.19 ± 0.37 Sv**.
- Both give a median onshore Kuroshio transport onto the shelf of **O(0.5–1) Sv**.

## 2. Depth
- The intrusion is a **subsurface** feature. Strong-minus-weak composite temperature profile grows downward to a **maximum of +3.0 °C at ~66 m**, decaying to +0.25 °C by 110 m; weak months carry a strong **cold** subsurface anomaly (−1.1 to −1.5 °C at 56–66 m). Depth scale ≈ 40–65 m (halved by ~78 m), signal to ~110–130 m — the Kuroshio Subsurface Water range (~50–150 m).

## 3. Timing
- Upper-200 m intrusion transport peaks **Jul–Aug (~0.6–0.7 Sv)**, weakest in autumn (~0.35–0.45 Sv).
- Upstream Kuroshio transport is largest in late spring/early summer (May–Jun ~44 Sv), least in Oct–Nov (~38 Sv).

## 4. Pathway
- Cross-shelf section at 25.5°N shows a coherent **onshore (westward) jet at ~50–150 m over the shelf break**, peaking ~−35 cm/s at 122.3°E, **bounded east by the offshore Kuroshio core** (+60 cm/s at 123.5–124°E). Strong-intrusion composites show warm subsurface anomalies with onshore flow; weak months show strong cold (upwelled) anomalies.

## 5. Controls on variability
- Q_intr is best predicted by the **shelf-box east-face onshore transport Q_ef** (r = +0.55; de-seasonalized +0.51, ρ = +0.57); partial corr(Q_intr, Q_ef | stratification) = +0.49 → robust. It also rises with stratification (r = +0.35) and shelf surface T (r = +0.38).
- The **upstream Kuroshio transport does NOT control the intrusion** (r = +0.10, p = 0.24; partial r = +0.09, p = 0.27). Kuroshio core speed is weakly anti-correlated with the intrusion (de-seasonalized r = −0.18) and with the shelf-break 110-m anomaly (r = −0.34).
- The 110-m shelf-break anomaly is essentially the **local shelf subsurface temperature** (r = +0.81 with T150; +0.88 de-seasonalized) and is negatively correlated with Q_ef (r = −0.48): stronger onshore flow advects cooler subsurface water onto the break. So the index reflects the **local shelf–slope advective-thermal balance**, not large-scale Kuroshio strength.
- Wind- and eddy-driven controls (winter monsoon, typhoons, eddy shedding) **could not be tested** (no wind data) — the main unresolved control.

## 6. 2023 anomaly
- 2023 has the **warmest May–Nov mean shelf-break anomaly of the record** (II_break +0.57 °C; T150 +18.05 °C), with a very warm early season (Jun +1.4 °C), **yet contains the three weakest months in the entire 21-year record** (Sep −1.24, Oct −1.73, Nov −1.84 °C). This is a late-season collapse of the *subsurface* warm anomaly while the *surface* stayed warm (Tsurf +0.7 to +1.2 °C) — consistent with late-season upwelling/mixing or reduced onshore transport of warm subsurface water, but the driver cannot be confirmed without winds.

## Limitations / unresolved
- **No salinity** → no true Kuroshio-water fraction; a temperature-only index may conflate air–sea heat flux with water-mass origin.
- **No winds** → interannual variability cannot be attributed to monsoon/typhoon forcing.
- Single reanalysis (GLORYS12V1), no independent validation; effective resolution ~1/12°.

## Saved artefacts (`/workspace/outputs/`)
- Figures: fig_bathymetry_regions.png, fig_mean_circulation.png, fig_section_25N.png, fig_section_velocity.png, fig_intrusion_depth.png, fig_pathway_composites.png, fig_monthly_pathway.png, fig_seasonal_cycle.png, fig_interannual.png, fig_controls_scatter.png, fig_controls_scatter_index.png, fig_synthesis_timeseries.png
- Tables: table_diagnostics.csv (140 months × 16 columns), table_summary.csv
- Report: final_report.md
